cards.title: P versus NP
cards.formal: Does every language with polynomially bounded, polynomial-time verifiable certificates admit a deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm? Equivalently, do there exist a deterministic Turing machine A and constants C,k such that, for every encoded Boolean formula F of bit length n, A decides whether F has a satisfying assignment and halts within $C(n+1)^k$ steps? The algorithm must give the correct answer on every input.
cards.definitions: A language is a subset of the finite binary strings. P consists of languages decided by one deterministic multitape Turing machine with worst-case running time \(C(n+1)^{k}\) for some constants C,k. NP consists of languages L for which there are a deterministic polynomial-time verifier V and a polynomial p satisfying $x\in L\iff\exists y\in\{0,1\}^{\le p(|x|)}:V(x,y)=1$. The verifier's time is polynomial in the combined input length. SAT is the language of well-formed Boolean formulas with at least one satisfying assignment; malformed encodings are rejected. Fix any ordinary explicit binary encoding of formulas using AND, OR, and NOT. The question concerns uniform deterministic computation, with no advice, oracle, or error probability. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\) or \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) in the deterministic uniform model defined here. Equality requires that every NP language have a polynomial-time decision algorithm; inequality requires that at least one NP language have none.
cards.why: This is the basic test of whether efficient verification entails efficient solution. It organizes the complexity of optimization, search, logical reasoning, and many graph problems, while motivating the development of general algorithmic lower-bound techniques.

importance.reason: The central boundary between efficient verification and efficient computation, with implications throughout TCS. It is the highest-priority landmark in the complexity category.

progress.text: The Cook–Levin completeness theorem identifies Boolean satisfiability as NP-complete; Karp reductions connect it to many standard combinatorial problems. This establishes equivalent targets, rather than a separation.

Relativization and subsequent natural-proofs and algebrization barriers delimit broad approaches to separation. The natural-proofs obstruction to general circuit lower bounds is conditional on sufficiently strong pseudorandomness assumptions.

Williams proves that NEXP is not contained in polynomial-size nonuniform ACC circuits, using faster satisfiability algorithms to obtain lower bounds. ACC has constant depth and modular counting gates. Both the larger language class and the restricted circuit model matter; this does not prove \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\).
The Clay Mathematics Institute continues to list P versus NP among its unsolved Millennium Prize Problems.

cards.status_note: The Clay Mathematics Institute lists P versus NP as unsolved, checked on 11 September 2026. The cited restricted-circuit lower bounds and proof-method barriers do not resolve the uniform decision problem.

context_blocks.text: A proposed assignment to a Boolean formula is easy to check: evaluate the formula under that assignment. Finding a satisfying assignment seems to demand a different kind of work because the assignment is missing. The question asks whether this difference can always be overcome with only polynomial computation. It is a worst-case statement about arbitrarily long inputs, so extensive experiments on current SAT solvers cannot settle it.

NP-completeness makes SAT a representative of an entire class. A polynomial-time reduction converts any NP verification problem into a satisfiability instance while preserving its answer. Consequently, one polynomial-time SAT algorithm would supply polynomial-time decision procedures for all NP languages. It would also allow witnesses to be recovered by asking a sequence of decision questions about their successive bits.

The two possible answers have different practical limits. \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\) would not by itself give a small polynomial exponent or an implementation useful at realistic sizes. \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) would establish some worst-case superpolynomial difficulty, but would not imply an exponential lower bound, hardness of typical instances, or the existence of secure cryptography. Those are stronger or differently quantified claims.

Many successful lower bounds impose restrictions on the competing computations, such as bounded circuit depth or the absence of negation. Removing those restrictions is a central obstacle. Conversely, theorems about relativization, natural proofs, and algebrization identify limitations of particular proof methods. These results do not decide P versus NP.

cards.title: P versus PSPACE
cards.formal: Does every language decidable by a deterministic Turing machine using polynomial working space have a deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm? Equivalently, do there exist a machine A and constants C,k such that A decides truth of every closed quantified Boolean formula of encoded length n in at most $C(n+1)^k$ steps?
cards.definitions: P consists of languages decided by one deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed polynomial worst-case time bound. PSPACE consists of languages decided by one deterministic Turing machine which halts on every input and visits at most \(C(n+1)^{k}\) work-tape cells, for some constants C,k, on inputs of length n. The input is read-only and is not charged as work space; a fixed finite tape alphabet is used. PSPACE imposes no polynomial time bound. A closed quantified Boolean formula has the form \(Q_{1}x_{1}\cdots Q_{m}x_{m} \varphi (x_{1},\ldots ,x_{m})\), where each \(Q_{i}\) is \(\exists\) or \(\forall\), quantified variables are distinct, and \(\varphi\) is an explicitly encoded Boolean formula using AND, OR, and NOT, with no free variables. Every quantifier ranges over \(\{0,1\}\). The number of quantifiers and their alternations may grow with n; the input is not restricted to a fixed number of blocks. Use any standard explicit binary encoding, reject malformed inputs, and count its full bit length n. Truth means the usual nested Boolean quantifier semantics. This language, TQBF, is PSPACE-complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions. No oracle, advice, randomization, or promise is allowed. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{PSPACE}\) or \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{PSPACE}\). The first outcome asserts a deterministic polynomial-time decision procedure for every polynomial-space language; the second asserts a polynomial-space language with no deterministic polynomial-time decision procedure.
cards.why: This asks whether reusing a feasible amount of memory can provide computational power beyond feasible running time. It is a central unresolved separation even when the allowed language class is enlarged from NP to all of PSPACE, and it organizes the complexity of quantified reasoning, games, and verification.

importance.reason: A defining question about the relationship between the two basic computational resources, time and working memory. It is a top-priority foundational class separation.

progress.text: Quantified Boolean formulas provide a PSPACE-complete target. Chandra, Kozen, and Stockmeyer characterize deterministic polynomial space as alternating polynomial time.
Shamir proves \(\mathrm{IP}=\mathrm{PSPACE}\), giving an interactive-proof characterization without resolving deterministic polynomial-time computation.

Williams proves the \(O(\sqrt{t \log  t})\) space simulation of time-t multitape machines, improving the decades-old \(O(t/\log  t)\) bound. It yields fixed-exponent time lower bounds for linear-space languages.
Williams’ MFCS invited survey discusses this simulation and further space-complexity developments. It supplies no separation of the unions P and PSPACE.

cards.status_note: Primary-source review and a search for subsequent results on 11 September 2026 found no resolution. Williams’ 2025 simulation and August 2026 MFCS survey concern time-space bounds; neither states an equality or separation of P and PSPACE.

context_blocks.text: Time measures the total number of computation steps; space measures how much information the machine retains at once. Space can be reused. For example, a machine can evaluate a quantified formula by recursively exploring possible choices and reusing its work area when it returns from a branch. The resulting computation may inspect exponentially many choices while keeping only a polynomial amount of information.

Alternating quantifiers express a finite game of choices: existential moves try to make the final formula true, and universal moves challenge them. For example, \(\forall x\exists y (y=x)\) is true because y may depend on x, whereas \(\exists y\forall x (y=x)\) is false. Both variables range over \(\{0,1\}\). A winning strategy for a longer formula can have exponentially many branches even though each play has polynomial length. Polynomial-time alternation captures exactly PSPACE.

The inclusion \(\mathrm{P}\subseteq \mathrm{PSPACE}\) is immediate, but its strictness is unknown. \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) would imply \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{PSPACE}\) because \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq \mathrm{PSPACE}\). A proof of \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), however, would collapse the polynomial hierarchy without automatically giving a polynomial-time algorithm for formulas with an unbounded number of quantifier alternations. This separates the present question from merely solving satisfiability.

The theorem \(\mathrm{IP}=\mathrm{PSPACE}\) characterizes the same space class through interaction: a polynomial-time randomized verifier can check claims from an unbounded prover using a bounded-error interactive protocol. The prover’s assistance is a resource. Removing the prover to obtain an ordinary deterministic polynomial-time algorithm is not a consequence of that characterization.

Williams’ time-to-space simulation gives a concrete advance in the comparison of these resources. For time bounds \(t(n)\ge n, a\) time-t multitape computation can be simulated in \(O(\sqrt{t \log  t})\) working space. A consequence is that some linear-space languages require time \(n^{2- \varepsilon}\) for every \(\varepsilon >0\). The lower-bound exponent remains bounded: the result does not exhibit a polynomial-space language outside every polynomial time bound.

cards.title: L versus P
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{P}\)? Equivalently, does the Circuit Value Problem have a deterministic algorithm that always halts and uses \(O(\log (n+2))\) bits of working memory on an input of binary encoding length n?
cards.definitions: L consists of total decision languages recognized by a fixed deterministic Turing machine with a read-only input tape and a fixed finite number of initially blank read/write work tapes over fixed finite alphabets. The input can be revisited freely; all visited work-tape cells count toward space, but the read-only input itself does not. For each language there must be a constant C such that every n-bit input uses at most \(C \log _{2}(n+2)\) work bits and the machine halts. Acceptance is a final state, not a long output tape usable as memory. A halting machine in this model has only polynomially many possible configurations on a fixed input, so its time is automatically polynomial. P is the class of languages decided by uniform deterministic Turing machines in \(O((n+2)^{c})\) time for some fixed c. Circuit Value receives an explicit topologically ordered DAG of AND, OR, and NOT gates, Boolean input values, and one designated output gate, and asks whether its value is 1. The entire gate and input encoding counts toward n; malformed encodings are rejected. There are no random bits, oracle, advice, auxiliary catalytic tape, or restrictions on circuit depth. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{P}\) or \(\mathrm{L}\ne \mathrm{P}\) in the read-only-input model defined here. Equality means that every polynomial-time decision language admits a halting deterministic logarithmic-space machine; inequality means that at least one such language admits none.
cards.why: This is a fundamental question about how much memory efficient computation needs. It asks whether all of polynomial-time reasoning can be reorganized around logarithmic working storage, and connects circuit evaluation, graph reachability, recomputation, and the structure of space-bounded complexity.

importance.reason: A canonical unresolved boundary between time and memory, asking whether any polynomial-time decision problem intrinsically needs more than logarithmic workspace.

progress.text: Ladner’s logspace completeness theorem for Circuit Value supplies a universal P-complete problem for the question.
Reingold proves undirected connectivity is in L. This resolves a major special case of low-memory graph computation without handling all directed reachability or P-complete problems.
Williams obtains the \(O(\sqrt{t \log  t})\) deterministic space simulation and square-root-type circuit-evaluation space bounds. These remain far above logarithmic space in the general case.
Blais’s logarithmic-space notes explicitly state that strictness between these basic classes remains unknown and fix the read-only-input convention needed to formulate the question.

cards.status_note: The Winter 2026 logarithmic-space notes explicitly leave the basic containments unresolved. A primary-source and later-result search on 11 September 2026 found no resolution of L versus P. The square-root-space simulation remains above logarithmic space for general polynomial-time computations.

context_blocks.text: A polynomial-time algorithm may keep a large table of intermediate results. A logarithmic-space algorithm has room for a fixed number of indices into its input: one position among n symbols needs about \(\log _{2} n\) bits. It can revisit the read-only input and recompute intermediate values, but it cannot retain an arbitrary n-bit table. The question asks whether this severe memory restriction still permits every polynomial-time decision task.

Circuit Value is a concrete complete problem for P under logarithmic-space reductions. Evaluating gates in topological order uses polynomial time and readily stores their values. An alternative may recompute gate values, but shared dependencies make naive recursive expansion expensive in both stack space and repeated work. Completeness says that a logarithmic-space solution to this one task would extend to all polynomial-time decision problems.

Logarithmic workspace already forces polynomial time for a halting deterministic machine: revisiting the same full configuration would produce an infinite loop. Consequently the question does not grant unlimited superpolynomial recomputation while retaining membership in L. The polynomial time exponent can nevertheless depend on the machine, so lower bounds for one fixed time budget are insufficient.

\(\mathrm{L}\subseteq \mathrm{NL}\subseteq \mathrm{P}\), where NL allows nondeterministic logarithmic-space computation. A proof that \(\mathrm{L}\ne \mathrm{NL}\) would therefore separate L from P, but \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{NL}\) would not itself settle \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{P}\). Reingold resolves undirected reachability in logarithmic space; directed reachability remains a separate NL-complete target, and Circuit Value represents the potentially larger class P.

Recent time-to-space simulation substantially improves general upper bounds without reaching logarithmic space. Williams simulates time t in \(O(\sqrt{t \log  t})\) space and obtains an analogous square-root-type space bound for Boolean circuit evaluation. With polynomial t, the guarantee is still polynomial space. This advances the tradeoff while leaving the much smaller \(O(\log  n)\) target unresolved.

sentences: Logarithmic-space computation can retain only a few input indices and counters while repeatedly rereading the input.
The question asks whether that memory always suffices for every polynomial-time decision problem.
Evaluating a supplied Boolean circuit is a representative complete task.
Shared dependencies make naive recomputation expensive, while storing all intermediate gate values exceeds the space budget.
The project tests whether efficient computation fundamentally needs substantial working memory or can always reorganize its information into an extremely small state.

cards.context:
A polynomial-time algorithm may keep a large table of intermediate results. A logarithmic-space algorithm has room for a fixed number of indices into its input: one position among n symbols needs about \(\log _{2} n\) bits. It can revisit the read-only input and recompute intermediate values, but it cannot retain an arbitrary n-bit table. The question asks whether this severe memory restriction still permits every polynomial-time decision task.

Circuit Value is a concrete complete problem for P under logarithmic-space reductions. Evaluating gates in topological order uses polynomial time and readily stores their values. An alternative may recompute gate values, but shared dependencies make naive recursive expansion expensive in both stack space and repeated work. Completeness says that a logarithmic-space solution to this one task would extend to all polynomial-time decision problems.

Logarithmic workspace already forces polynomial time for a halting deterministic machine: revisiting the same full configuration would produce an infinite loop. Consequently the question does not grant unlimited superpolynomial recomputation while retaining membership in L. The polynomial time exponent can nevertheless depend on the machine, so lower bounds for one fixed time budget are insufficient.

\(\mathrm{L}\subseteq \mathrm{NL}\subseteq \mathrm{P}\), where NL allows nondeterministic logarithmic-space computation. A proof that \(\mathrm{L}\ne \mathrm{NL}\) would therefore separate L from P, but \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{NL}\) would not itself settle \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{P}\). Reingold resolves undirected reachability in logarithmic space; directed reachability remains a separate NL-complete target, and Circuit Value represents the potentially larger class P.

Recent time-to-space simulation substantially improves general upper bounds without reaching logarithmic space. Williams simulates time t in \(O(\sqrt{t \log  t})\) space and obtains an analogous square-root-type space bound for Boolean circuit evaluation. With polynomial t, the guarantee is still polynomial space. This advances the tradeoff while leaving the much smaller \(O(\log  n)\) target unresolved.

cards.title: Nonuniform \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\) versus \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\)
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\subsetneq \mathrm{NC}^{1}\) for the nonuniform circuit classes defined below? Equivalently, does there exist a Boolean function family \(f=(f_{n}:\{0,1\}^{n}\to \{0,1\})\) in \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) such that for every fixed depth \(d\ge 1\), exponent \(k\ge 1\), and constant \(M\ge 1\), there is an n for which every depth-at-most-d majority circuit computing \(f_{n}\) exactly has size greater than \(M(n+1)^{k}\)?
cards.definitions: A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with input nodes \(x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}\), optional constants 0,1, and one output. Depth is the maximum number of gates on an input-to-output path. Size is the number of gates plus the number of wires; if an input is repeated at a gate, each occurrence counts as a wire. A majority circuit has AND and OR gates of arbitrary positive fan-in, NOT gates of fan-in one, and MAJ gates of arbitrary positive fan-in m, with output 1 exactly when strictly more than \(m/2\) inputs equal 1. \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\) consists of all families with such circuits of size \(M(n+1)^{k}\) and depth at most d for every n, for some constants M,k,d depending on the family. \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) consists of families with circuits over AND, OR, NOT, with fan-in at most two (one for NOT), size \(M(n+1)^{k}\), and depth at most \(b \log _{2}(n+1)\), for fixed M,k,b. Circuits may share intermediate gates. Both classes are nonuniform: an arbitrary separate circuit may be chosen for each input length, without any requirement to compute its description. The output must be correct on every input; no randomness, approximation, promise, or distributional error is allowed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\subsetneq \mathrm{NC}^{1}\) or \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}=\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) for the nonuniform families defined here. Strictness requires a single \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) family with no polynomial-size constant-depth majority-circuit family; equality requires that every \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) family admit such a family.
cards.why: One of the central small-circuit questions: whether a constant number of counting layers can perform every logarithmic-depth Boolean computation. A resolution would clarify the power of threshold circuits, finite-group computation, and the role of sequential dependence in parallel computation.

importance.reason: A flagship unresolved containment between basic circuit classes, with explicit complete problems and connections to arithmetic, algebraic automata theory, and lower-bound amplification.

progress.text: Hesse, Allender, and Barrington place division and iterated multiplication in DLOGTIME-uniform \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\), demonstrating the arithmetic power already available at constant depth.

Chen and Tell show how improvements in the depth dependence of superlinear wire lower bounds for certain \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\)-complete problems would yield superpolynomial \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\) lower bounds.
Dawar and Evans characterize uniform \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) with typed monoids and unary generalized quantifiers. The containment comparison remains open.

Chen, Tal, and Wang prove superquadratic gate lower bounds for depth-two weighted threshold circuits for an \(E^{\mathrm{NP}}\) function; the result does not supply an \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) separation against every constant depth.

cards.status_note: The source and subsequent-work checks on 11 September 2026 found no equality or separation of these nonuniform classes. The 2026 depth-two result concerns a function in \(E^{\mathrm{NP}}\) and polynomial circuit size; the typed-monoid result concerns uniform classes. These conclusions have different quantifiers and models from the target.

context_blocks.text: The two models trade different resources. A majority gate can aggregate arbitrarily many bits in one step, whereas a binary Boolean gate sees only two. \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) permits logarithmically many layers of binary computation. A majority of polynomially many bits can itself be computed by a polynomial-size logarithmic-depth Boolean circuit, so a constant number of majority layers gives \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\subseteq \mathrm{NC}^{1}\). The open issue is whether counting in a fixed number of layers can also replace every logarithmic-depth computation.

Arithmetic tasks are an instructive warning against judging depth from familiar sequential algorithms. Hesse, Allender, and Barrington prove that integer division and iterated multiplication have even DLOGTIME-uniform \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\) circuits. A binary long-division procedure takes many dependent steps, but that procedure does not establish a lower bound on all circuits for division. These arithmetic problems therefore cannot serve as the missing separation.

There are concrete complete problems on the \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) side. Evaluating a Boolean formula, and evaluating a product of elements of the fixed permutation group \(S_{5}\), capture \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) under very simple reductions. \(S_{5}\) consists of the 120 permutations of five objects, with permutation composition as its operation. Chen and Tell study these complete problems in their lower-bound amplification results.

Chen and Tell prove a conditional amplification theorem connecting certain mildly superlinear wire lower bounds to a separation of the full classes. Its hypothesis imposes a specific quantitative dependence on circuit depth. Thus a lower bound proved only at one fixed depth, or with an insufficient exponent at growing constant depths, is a different statement from their theorem’s hypothesis and from the conjecture here.

Dawar and Evans give an algebraic characterization of uniform \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) using typed monoids in FSTTCS 2025, extending earlier work on uniform \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\). Typed monoids allow infinite algebraic structures while restricting recognition through finitely many types. This supplies another mathematical language in which to compare the classes. Their theorem is a characterization, not a separation, and its uniform scope must be kept distinct from this card’s formulation.

Chen, Tal, and Wang’s 2026 preprint proves \(n^{2.5- \varepsilon}\) gate lower bounds for depth-two linear-threshold circuits computing a function in \(E^{\mathrm{NP}}\). Here \(E^{\mathrm{NP}}\) allows deterministic time \(2^{O(n)}\) with an NP oracle. A linear-threshold gate tests a weighted sum, while this card fixes unweighted majority gates. More decisively, the result treats one depth, a polynomial size bound, and a hard function not shown to belong to \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\). The target here concerns an \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) family against every fixed depth and every polynomial size bound.

cards.title: Berman–Hartmanis conjecture
cards.formal: For every pair of languages \(A,B\subseteq \{0,1\}\)* that are NP-complete under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, does there exist a bijection \(f:\{0,1\}*\to \{0,1\}\)* such that f and \(f^{- 1}\) are computable in deterministic polynomial time and, for every string \(x, x\in A\) if and only if \(f(x)\in B\)?
cards.definitions: A language is a set of finite binary strings, including a specified membership decision for every string; malformed encodings are therefore part of the language convention. NP consists of languages L for which \(x\in \mathrm{L}\) exactly when some witness of length polynomial in |x| is accepted by a deterministic polynomial-time verifier. A many-one reduction from L to A is a total deterministic polynomial-time function g with \(x\in \mathrm{L}\) iff \(g(x)\in A\). A is NP-complete if \(A\in \mathrm{NP}\) and every \(\mathrm{L}\in \mathrm{NP}\) reduces to A in this sense. The desired f is a permutation of all finite binary strings, taking members to members and nonmembers to nonmembers. Its running time is polynomial in its input length, and its inverse has a polynomial bound in the inverse input length. The algorithms and polynomial bounds may depend on the fixed pair A,B, but not on the particular input string. No advice, oracle, randomness or length-preservation requirement is allowed. This is the unconditional conjecture; \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) is not an assumption.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that every pair of polynomial-time many-one NP-complete languages is polynomial-time isomorphic, or prove that some pair has no bijection with both directions computable in polynomial time. The statement is unconditional: \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) is not an added hypothesis.
cards.why: A fundamental test of what NP-completeness means beyond mutual reducibility: does it impose one efficiently reversible structure on all complete decision problems? It links padding, cryptographic inversion, uniformity and the limitations of relativizing methods.

importance.reason: A defining structural-complexity conjecture about the entire NP-complete degree, stronger than P≠NP and supported by substantial restricted-model theorems and oracle barriers.

A later-source search on 11 September 2026 located the 2025 recovery-reduction preprint, which still uses it as a conjectural hypothesis, and found no resolution. Its truth-table recovery consequence is conditional.

context_blocks.text: NP-completeness normally identifies problems by their ability to simulate one another. A reduction may map many distinct instances to the same target instance, leave most target strings unused, and erase information that would be needed to reconstruct its input. The isomorphism conjecture asks for a much more rigid relationship: an efficiently reversible relabelling of the entire instance space. Its claim includes every artificially constructed NP-complete language, not only the familiar examples used in applications.

The distinction is visible in the quantifiers. Choosing one clever reduction from SAT to another problem and discovering that it is many-to-one says nothing decisive about whether some other reduction could be a bijection. Conversely, an abstract bijection between two infinite sets is not enough: it might take exponential time to compute or invert. The conjecture requires both computations to be efficient, while allowing a polynomial change in the lengths of instances.

Padding supplies the strongest classical evidence. A paddable language has an efficient injective way to append arbitrary recoverable auxiliary information without changing the answer. For satisfiability, fresh variables and a suitably delimited formula encoding can carry extra bits while preserving whether the original formula has a satisfying assignment. Berman and Hartmanis used padding to show that the standard NP-complete examples known at the time are polynomial-time isomorphic. The unresolved step is proving that arbitrary complete languages possess enough recoverable structure.

The connection with one-way functions depends on more than difficulty inverting a particular reduction. An NP-complete language can have many reductions from SAT, and invertibility of one map does not determine whether a different efficient isomorphism exists. The Hartmanis problem column distinguishes one-way functions, scrambling functions and easy-cylinder hypotheses; these additional structural conditions are not interchangeable.

Oracle results go in both directions. Kurtz, Mahaney and Royer construct random-oracle counterexamples using scrambling functions. Fenner, Fortnow and Kurtz construct a different oracle setting in which the conjecture holds. These are results about relativized computation, where the algorithms can query a supplied set. They do not settle the ordinary conjecture, but they show that an argument valid uniformly across all such oracle settings cannot choose its truth value.

Restricting the completeness reductions can produce affirmative theorems. Agrawal, Allender and Rudich prove an isomorphism theorem for sets complete under nonuniform \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\) reductions, with nonuniform depth-three \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\) circuits computing the isomorphisms and their inverses. Here \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\) means polynomial-size Boolean circuits of constant depth with unbounded-fan-in AND and OR gates and negations. Both the restricted completeness hypothesis and the availability of nonuniform circuits matter; dropping them would be a stronger statement.

Agrawal and Watanabe further relate structural assumptions about one-way functions to nonuniform isomorphisms. Under their stated hypotheses they obtain P/poly isomorphisms, permitting polynomial advice that depends on input length. This does not provide the uniform polynomial-time algorithms demanded here. The broad question remains whether NP-completeness itself forces reversible structure, or whether some complete languages have an intrinsically different organization of their yes and no instances.

Nareddy and Mishra’s 2025 preprint studies recovery of Boolean truth tables after random corruptions. It states the Berman–Hartmanis conjecture explicitly and derives, conditionally on it, recovery guarantees for every NP-complete language after partitioning instances by the length of their image under an isomorphism. This is an application of the conjecture as a hypothesis, not a proof of it.

cards.title: Expected linear-time integer sorting for every word length
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform Las Vegas word-RAM algorithm and a constant \(C\) such that, for every \(n\ge2\), every integer word length \(w\ge\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\), and every list \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\), the algorithm outputs the list in nondecreasing order with expected running time at most \(Cn\)?
cards.definitions: The input occupies n words, with one unsigned w-bit key per word; repeated keys are allowed. The output must contain exactly the input multiset in nondecreasing numerical order, with no stability requirement. The machine is sequential and has w-bit data registers and random-access memory. Unit-cost operations are reads and writes, comparisons, branches, addition and subtraction modulo 2ʷ, multiplication of two words with the product returned in two words, quotient and remainder of two words with a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and left or right shifts by a word-specified amount. Shifted-out bits are discarded, and shifts by at least w return zero. Addresses may use a constant number of words to index polynomially many memory cells; all address computation is charged. An operation can generate one fresh independent uniform w-bit random word. These are the only primitive operations; arbitrary-length arithmetic, a built-in sorting operation and free tables are unavailable. All preprocessing, memory initialization performed by the algorithm, and output writes count. A fixed finite program receives n and w; it may select methods according to their values but has no advice depending on them. Las Vegas means every terminating computation is correct and the algorithm terminates with probability one. Expectation is over the internal random choices for each fixed input. C must be independent of both n and w, including when w grows with n.

context_blocks.text: Integer sorting asks how much of the cost of comparison sorting comes from treating keys as indivisible objects. If only comparisons are allowed, identifying one of n! possible orders needs \(\Omega (n \log  n)\) comparisons in the worst case. Word operations can inspect several bits at once, compute bucket addresses and manipulate packed fields. The comparison decision-tree lower bound therefore does not rule out a linear number of word operations.

The relevant input size is n words, not nw individual bits. Reading one entire word is a unit operation regardless of w, but reading a whole list is still n operations. Conversely, the machine cannot concatenate all n keys into an nw-bit integer and then treat that enormous object as one register. Fixing the register width and the permitted instructions is essential; unrestricted unit-cost arithmetic would answer a different question.

Simple radix sorting already handles \(w=O(\log  n)\). Divide each key into digits of about \(\log _{2}n\) bits, and sort stably by one digit at a time using counting arrays of size \(O(n)\). There are \(O(1+w/\log  n)\) passes, giving \(O(n(1+w/\log  n))\) time. For any fixed polynomial-size universe this is linear. If \(w=(\log  n)^{3/2}\), however, that same argument takes about \(\sqrt{\log  n}\) passes and does not prove the desired bound.

Surprisingly, very large words also admit linear expected time. Belazzougui, Brodal and Nielsen achieve this for \(w=\Omega ((\log  n)^{2} \log  \log  n)\), improving an earlier sufficiently-large-word regime. Their construction replaces full keys by shorter signatures and processes many packed fields with a single word operation. Larger keys bring more possible values, but the larger machine words simultaneously provide more internal parallelism. The difficult range sits between the easy radix regime and the proven large-word regime.

The best general expected upper bound retained in the sources is Han and Thorup’\(s O(n\sqrt{\log  \log  n})\), independent of word length. It is substantially below n log n, but the square-root iterated-log factor still grows without bound. The problem asks whether this remaining overhead can be removed completely. An upper bound with any unbounded overhead factor does not imply the stated linear bound.

Han also gives deterministic \(O(n \log  \log  n)\) sorting with linear space. This is a different guarantee: it bounds every computation without random choices. The present question allows randomization and asks only for an expected linear bound on every input. A deterministic linear-time algorithm would answer it affirmatively, while a lower bound confined to deterministic algorithms would not answer it negatively.

Zero error is explicit because sorting has a convenient final check but not every failure mode is detected by checking adjacent comparisons alone. A proposed randomized procedure must preserve the input multiset as well as produce a sorted sequence. The large-word construction uses a verifiable randomized sorting procedure and repeats when needed to obtain a Las Vegas guarantee. This is different from relying on a typical distribution of input keys: adversarially selected keys are permitted here.

Uniformity also prevents the missing work from being hidden in preprocessing. An enormous lookup table listing answers for all possible word patterns cannot be supplied for free. Any table needed for a particular n and w must be constructed within the expected time budget. Likewise, treating a concrete machine’s 64-bit width as an immutable constant does not address the asymptotic problem, where n and w vary together.

The question is fundamental because sorting supplies order to many other algorithmic tasks: grouping equal identifiers, scanning consecutive values, merging collections and organizing events. An affirmative answer would give a clean linear-time primitive across the whole word-RAM range. A negative answer would explain a basic limitation of word arithmetic that is invisible to ordinary comparison-counting arguments. The 2025 teaching source still explicitly presents the unrestricted linear-time target as open.

cards.title: Sorting \(X + Y\)
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform deterministic real-RAM algorithm A and a constant C such that, for every integer \(n\ge 2\) and every \(X=(x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}), Y=(y_{1},\ldots ,y_{n})\in \mathbb{R} ^{n}, A\) outputs a permutation \(((i_{1},j_{1}),\ldots ,(i_{n^{2}},j_{n^{2}}))\) of \([n]\times [n]\) satisfying \(x_{i_{r}}+y_{j_{r}}\le x_{i_{r+1}}+y_{j_{r+1}}\) for \(1\le r<n^{2}\), in at most \(Cn^{2}\) unit-cost operations?
cards.why: This is a basic test of whether algebraic dependence among many sortable objects can be exploited with no overhead beyond writing them down. It also makes the distinction between short comparison decision trees and fast uniform algorithms unusually concrete.
cards.status_note: TOPP Problem 41, primary comparison and real-RAM sources, and subsequent-result searches were checked on 11 September 2026. No uniform quadratic-time algorithm or matching impossibility result for the stated real-valued problem was found. The \(2017/2018\) decision-tree result does not settle total time. This is a source review, not an independent proof audit.

progress.text: Fredman proves an \(O(n^{2})\) comparison bound for sorting \(X+Y\); this does not provide quadratic total running time.
Lambert and Steiger–Streinu give algorithms combining \(O(n^{2})\) comparisons with \(O(n^{2} \log  n)\) total time.
The necklace/convolution paper explicitly retains quadratic-time sorting on the real RAM as open while proving faster algorithms for more limited convolution outputs.
Kane–Lovett–Moran obtain \(O(n \log ^{2} n)\) depth using 8-sparse linear tests. The bound concerns decision-tree queries and excludes output and general computational costs.

cards.definitions: The input consists of n and the 2n exact real numbers in random-access arrays; no sortedness, distinctness, integrality or magnitude bound is promised. All \(n^{2}\) index pairs must occur once in the output, including pairs with equal sums. Ties may appear in any order. A real RAM has exact real registers and cells, supporting copy, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by nonzero reals and comparisons at unit cost. A fixed finite program may use rational constants, with no advice depending on n. It also has integer registers and cells of \(b=d\lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) bits for some fixed integer \(d\ge 3\) chosen with the algorithm. Integer instructions are copy, comparison, branching, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{b}\), quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and logical shifts; shifts by at least b return zero. Integer addresses access individual real or integer cells, and each read or write costs one operation. Integer-to-real conversion is permitted, but real-to-integer conversion, floor on reals, extraction of their bits and arbitrary-precision integer operations are not primitives. Memory starts empty apart from the input and fixed program constants; all preprocessing, table construction, address computation and output writes are charged. The algorithm must halt correctly on every input and uses no randomness. Constants C and d are independent of n and of the real values. This is the quadratic-time real-RAM version explicitly asked in the cited necklace paper and identified as the main target in TOPP. Indexed multiset output resolves possible equal sums; allowing repeated input entries does not change the target, since repetitions can be grouped by \(O(n \log  n)\) comparison sorting and expanded within the output budget.
cards.answer_criterion: Give one uniform deterministic program with a proof of exact output correctness and the \(O(n^{2})\) worst-case total-time bound for every real input, or prove that no such program exists in the specified model. Equivalently, a negative answer shows that every correct program has unbounded worst-case running-time/\(n^{2}\) ratio. Neither a bound only on the number of comparisons nor an algorithm restricted to bounded integers resolves this claim.

context_blocks.text: The input is small compared with the output. For \(X=(0,3)\) and \(Y=(1,4)\), the four indexed sums are 1,4,4,7. Both occurrences of 4 remain in the sorted output because they come from different pairs. In general there are \(n^{2}\) output entries, but only 2n independent input numbers. This strong dependence is the reason ordinary sorting bounds for \(n^{2}\) unrelated numbers may be wasteful.

If the two input lists are already sorted, the matrix \(M_{ij}=x_{i}+y_{j}\) increases along every row and every column. That information alone does not determine the relative order of every two cells: a later row may contain an entry smaller than an entry in an earlier row. Moreover, sum matrices satisfy additional equalities such as \(M_{ij}+M_{kl}=M_{il}+M_{kj}\). The question concerns the full algebraic structure, not just arbitrary matrices with sorted rows and columns.

Explicitly generating and comparison-sorting all \(n^{2}\) sums takes \(O(n^{2} \log  n)\) time. Writing the required output already takes \(\Omega (n^{2})\) operations, so quadratic time would match the output-size lower bound. TOPP identifies removal of the logarithmic factor as the main question. The real-valued input convention avoids assuming a small integer universe, where different operations can change the complexity.

Fredman proved that \(O(n^{2})\) comparisons suffice. A decision tree specifies the next comparison after every possible history of answers and places the sorted order at its leaves. Its depth counts comparisons, but it does not charge for constructing the tree or determining the next comparison from a succinct program. Consequently, a short decision tree does not automatically become an equally fast uniform algorithm.

Lambert and Steiger–Streinu made the comparison savings algorithmic while retaining \(O(n^{2} \log  n)\) total running time. This is a concrete separation between counting tests and charging the bookkeeping that organizes them. The target includes both costs, as well as all preprocessing and output writes.

Kane, Lovett and Moran later obtained \(O(n \log ^{2} n)\) decision-tree depth by allowing tests involving differences of sums; each such linear test uses at most eight input coordinates. Those tests are more expressive than simply comparing two entries of \(X+Y\). The subquadratic depth does not conflict with the quadratic output-size lower bound, because decision-tree depth does not charge for writing the output.

Related convolution problems ask only for a minimum, maximum or median on each antidiagonal of the sum matrix. These requests can have subquadratic algorithms without supplying a complete sorted list of all entries. The necklace-alignment paper explicitly records this distinction and the unresolved quadratic-time real-RAM question.

The importance of the question extends beyond sorting. Pairwise sums describe many ordered geometric events, and TOPP records reductions from this sorting task to polygon-containment and arrangement-ordering problems. A resolution would clarify how much algorithmic work can be saved when a large output is generated from a much smaller collection of numerical parameters.

For bounded-integer inputs on a word RAM, a linear-time algorithm for sorting arbitrary word-sized integers would also sort the explicitly generated pairwise sums in quadratic time, allowing a constant-factor increase in word length for the sums. The present target instead allows arbitrary exact real inputs, without floor or bit extraction. An integer-sorting result therefore does not automatically answer this real-RAM question.

cards.title: Hypergraph cut sparsifiers with \(O(n/\varepsilon ^{2})\) hyperedges
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal constant \(C>0\) such that every nonnegatively weighted hypergraph \(H\) on \(V=[n]\), \(n\ge2\), and every real \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\) admit a nonnegatively weighted hypergraph \(H'\) on the same vertices with \(|E'|\le Cn/\varepsilon^2\) and \((1-\varepsilon)\operatorname{cut}_H(S)\le\operatorname{cut}_{H'}(S)\le(1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{cut}_H(S)\) for every \(S\subseteq V\)?
cards.why: Tests whether preserving all cuts of a multiway interaction system requires any more hyperedges than the graph sparsification upper bound. It separates the number of retained interactions from their incidence storage and from the cost of computing them.
cards.status_note: The original source permits arbitrary weighted replacement hyperedges on the same vertex set. The reviewed general upper bound has a logarithmic factor; later sketching and streaming-space results do not themselves remove it. A bounded 13 September 2026 later-work search did not locate a matching existence theorem or refutation. Cited proofs were not independently verified.

The size measure counts hyperedges rather than their total incidence size, making the project specifically about how many distinct multiway interactions must be retained.

cards.definitions: For \(n\ge2\), write \(V=[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A weighted hypergraph \(H=(V,E,w)\) has a set \(E\subseteq\{e\subseteq V:|e|\ge2\}\) and finite nonnegative real weights \(w:E\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\). For every \(S\subseteq V\), set \(\operatorname{cut}_H(S)=\sum_{\substack{e\in E:\ e\cap S\ne\varnothing,\\e\cap(V\setminus S)\ne\varnothing}}w(e)\). Thus each crossing hyperedge contributes its weight exactly once, regardless of the number of vertices on either side. Empty and singleton edges are omitted because they cross no cut; repeated edges can be merged by summing weights. The approximating hypergraph \(H'=(V,E',w')\) follows the same rules. Its edge set may contain any subsets of the original vertex set, not necessarily original edges; additional vertices are forbidden. Size is \(|E'|\), rather than the sum of edge cardinalities or a bit-encoding length. The same approximation must hold for all cuts simultaneously, and a zero-valued original cut must remain exactly zero. The empty edge set is allowed. This is an existence question with no construction-time, randomness or rational-weight restriction. The constant \(C\) is independent of dimension, accuracy, hyperedge count, maximum edge size and weights.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of this universal existence theorem with one constant \(C\), or prove its logical negation in Lean: for every \(C>0\), some permitted \(n,H,\varepsilon\) has no same-vertex weighted hypergraph meeting both the size and all-cut guarantees. A refutation must allow arbitrary nonnegative replacement hyperedges, not just sampled original edges. A size bound retaining an unbounded logarithmic factor does not establish the stated theorem.

context_blocks.text: A sparsifier replaces a large interaction structure by a smaller one while preserving the values needed for later cut computations. The guarantee holds for every partition at once, including a partition chosen after seeing the sparsifier. A separate approximation for one predetermined cut would be much weaker. A hypergraph can contain exponentially many distinct hyperedges on n vertices, so reducing their number to near linear can be a large compression.

The cut convention is important for multiway interactions. A hyperedge \(\{1,2,3,4\}\) of weight one contributes one to both the partition \(\{1\}|\{2,3,4\}\) and the partition \(\{1,2\}|\{3,4\}\). Replacing it by a uniformly weighted clique gives contributions proportional to three and four respectively. Thus the ordinary graph representation does not automatically preserve the hypergraph’s cut function.

The formulation follows the broad source question: the approximating hypergraph may introduce different hyperedges on the same vertices. Requiring only reweighting and deleting original edges is an additional restriction. A construction satisfying that stronger condition also answers the stated existence question, but a lower bound restricted to that condition would not by itself refute it.

Ordinary graphs already admit \(O(n/\varepsilon ^{2})\)-edge sparsifiers. Batson, Spielman and Srivastava prove a spectral guarantee, which implies the required cut inequalities by substituting zero-one indicator vectors. This gives the benchmark without a logarithmic overhead. For hypergraphs, preserving an associated energy on all real vectors is also stronger than preserving cut indicators, and the particular energy definition must be specified before importing a spectral result.

The quadratic-in-n bound quoted in the 2018 problem entry is outdated. Chen, Khanna and Nagda give a randomized polynomial-time construction using \(O(n \log  n/\varepsilon ^{2})\) reweighted original hyperedges. Their result removes the extra dependence on maximum hyperedge size. The remaining log n is unbounded, so it cannot be absorbed into the universal C in this card.

Subsequent sketching and streaming results address how a sparsifier can be represented or maintained with limited memory. A rank-r hyperedge can require r vertex identifiers, so near-linear hyperedge count does not mean near-linear bit storage independent of r. The FOCS 2024 sketch bounds retain logarithmic factors in their near-linear output guarantee.
The ICLR 2026 insertion-only work further improves memory use, but its guarantees also retain logarithmic factors. Its space theorem does not establish the \(Cn/\varepsilon ^{2}\) hyperedge count.

Resolving the target would determine whether hypergraph cuts admit the same upper bound on the number of interactions as graph cuts at each accuracy. It would not automatically remove the cost of describing large hyperedges or reading the original input. Those separate costs explain why stronger data-access and streaming results can coexist with an unresolved existence question.

cards.title: Near-linear-time approximation of reachability diameter
cards.formal:
Is there an integer constant \(C\ge1\) and a single uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm that, on every finite unweighted directed graph \(G\), returns an integer \(\widehat D\) satisfying
\[
\Pr\!\left[D(G)/C\le\widehat D\le D(G)\right]\ge 2/3
\]
and always halts in near-linear time? Here
\[
D(G)=\max\{d_G(u,v):u,v\in V(G),\ d_G(u,v)<\infty\}
\]
is the reachability diameter. The graph representation, machine and worst-case time bound are specified below. This retains the card's near-linear constant-factor specialization of the source's broader approximation-versus-time question; it does not ask to determine that entire tradeoff.
cards.why: This asks whether a basic distance statistic of an arbitrary directed network can be estimated without computing distances from every vertex. It captures information that conventional directed diameter loses when directions are disconnected, and appears in assessing diameter reduction by reachability-preserving shortcut edges. A resolution would establish a general algorithmic principle or limitation for directed reachability and distance estimation.
cards.definitions:
The input is a graph \(G=([n],E)\), where \(n\ge1\), \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and \(E\subseteq[n]\times[n]\) is a set of directed edges. Loops are allowed, repeated edges are not, and every edge has length one. Write \(m=|E|\). A directed walk is a sequence \(v_0,\ldots,v_\ell\) with \((v_{j-1},v_j)\in E\) for \(1\le j\le\ell\), and has length \(\ell\). The distance \(d_G(u,v)\) is the minimum length of such a walk from \(u\) to \(v\), or \(\infty\) if no walk exists. Walks of length zero are permitted, so \(d_G(v,v)=0\), the displayed maximum is nonempty, and \(0\le D(G)\le n-1\). In particular, an edgeless graph has diameter zero. No connectivity, acyclicity or sparsity promise is imposed.

The input occupies \(O(n+m)\) read-only words: \(n,m\), an array of \(n+1\) offsets beginning with zero and ending with \(m\), and an array of \(m\) head labels. For each tail \(u\), the head labels between its two consecutive offsets list its outgoing neighbors without repetition, in arbitrary order. Correctness and cost bounds hold for every ordering of every valid list; there is no succinct encoding or separately supplied reachability information.

The algorithm is one finite program, independent of \(n,m,G\), with a fixed finite set of registers and random-access memory. For some fixed integer \(d\ge3\), a word has \(w=d\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits, represents an integer in \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\), and can hold a memory address. Work cells are initially zero; only addresses in that range can be used. The program has the word width available but no advice, oracle, input-dependent program or precomputed table. In one step it may read or write one addressed word, copy a word, compare two words, branch, or perform one of addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer quotient, remainder, Boolean bitwise operations or a shift. Arithmetic results other than comparison are reduced modulo \(2^w\); quotient and remainder on divisor zero return zero; shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Each instruction has fixed bounded arity. Reading one fresh independent fair random bit also costs one step. Input access, memory operations, random bits, preprocessing and writing the output all count.

Near-linear worst-case time means that there are fixed integers \(K\ge1\) and \(k\ge0\) such that, on every valid input and every sequence of random bits, the program halts with an integer output in \(\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\) after at most
\[
K(n+m)\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil^k
\]
steps. The probability in the target is over these independent random bits for each fixed input. Both underestimates outside the allowed interval and overestimates count as failure; no correctness requirement is imposed on the failure event beyond the output range. The constants \(C,d,K,k\) and program are chosen once before the universal quantification over inputs. There is no separate input approximation parameter and no restriction to combinatorial algorithms.

progress.text: The first arXiv version introduces the approximation/time landscape and leaves the best tradeoff for general unweighted directed graphs open. It distinguishes that question from reducing general graphs to acyclic ones.

The ESA version states in Theorem 7 a randomized additive-\(k\) approximation and in Theorem 9 a randomized near-linear-time \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\)-approximation. Allowing logarithmic factors, the additive guarantee has time \(\widetilde O(nm/k)\) with high probability. The deterministic bound in Theorem 8 has an additional multiplicative factor and is restricted to acyclic graphs.

Corollary 5 conditionally rules out better-than-two approximation in time \(O(n^{\omega-\varepsilon})\), where \(\omega\) is the infimum exponent of arithmetic matrix multiplication and \(\varepsilon>0\) is fixed. Its separate combinatorial version rules out truly subcubic combinatorial algorithms. Theorem 6 gives a conditional better-than-\(3/2\) barrier on sparse instances. These results concern bounded approximation factors and do not settle existence of some absolute constant factor in near-linear time.

This card retains the previously disclosed near-linear constant-factor part of that question, with an explicit randomized word-RAM and worst-case clock. context_blocks.text: Reachability diameter measures the longest shortest route that actually exists. Unreachable ordered pairs are omitted, so a one-way path on five vertices has reachability diameter four. This differs both from ordinary directed diameter, which becomes infinite if any ordered pair is unreachable, and from min-diameter, which uses the smaller of the two directional distances.

The source studies general directed graphs and separately asks whether the reachability-diameter problem can be reduced to directed acyclic graphs. Its hardness instances can already be acyclic, but this does not make an algorithm for acyclic inputs a solution for arbitrary inputs. Strong connectivity makes reachability diameter coincide with ordinary directed diameter and removes an essential part of the general question.

The card retains the specialization recorded in September 2026: a constant approximation in time \(\widetilde O(n+m)\), where the tilde permits a fixed power of \(\log n\). Open Problem 1 asks more broadly for the best approximation/time tradeoff. The explicit word operations, finite program, \(2/3\) success convention, integer output and worst-case clock make the inherited algorithmic model precise; the source does not itself spell out this complete RAM instruction set.

Theorem 7 gives additive approximation, and Theorem 9 gives a randomized near-linear-time \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\)-approximation. Neither supplies a constant multiplicative factor on every input. Additive error can dominate the diameter on small-diameter graphs, even when it is useful on graphs with long routes. The source also gives conditional barriers for sufficiently small approximation factors; those barriers do not rule out all constant factors.

cards.title: Near-linear output-sensitive Subset Sum
cards.formal: Do there exist a uniform bounded-error randomized word-RAM algorithm and constants \(C>0\), \(b\ge0\) that, given \(n\ge1\) positive integers \(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\le t\) and an integer \(t\ge1\), output exactly the distinct values in \(S(X,t)=\{\sum_{i\in I}x_{i}:I\subseteq[n]\}\cap\{0,\ldots,t\}\) in at most \(C(n+|S(X,t)|)(\log(n+t+2))^{b}\) operations?
cards.definitions: The input is an explicitly listed multiset; repeated values are allowed and each index can be selected at most once. The empty subset contributes zero. Output every attainable value once, in any order, with no requirement to list subsets or witnesses. Inputs exceeding the threshold can be discarded when represented in the same word model. Use a uniform word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_{2}(n+t+2)\rceil\), for a fixed positive integer \(d\) chosen with the algorithm and large enough for its addresses and input values. Unit-cost instructions are word reads/writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), and integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword computation is charged by its component instructions. The fixed finite program receives no advice or precomputed tables; all initialization, preprocessing and output writes count. Randomness consists of independent uniform random words, each generated at unit cost. On every input, the whole output must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\). The time bound holds for every random execution, including unsuccessful ones. The word-size constant and all time constants are independent of both \(n\) and \(t\). The target permits polylogarithmic dependence on the numerical threshold, but no linear scan of its universe unless covered by the stated output bound.

cards.title: Maximum reset threshold of synchronizing automata
cards.formal: For every integer \(n\ge 1\), determine \(T(n)=\max\){\(rt(A): A\) is a synchronizing complete deterministic finite automaton with n states and any finite nonempty alphabet}, where \(rt(A)\) is its shortest reset-word length.
cards.definitions: An automaton here is a finite transition system \(A=(Q,\Sigma ,\delta )\), with |\(Q|=n, a\) finite nonempty alphabet \(\Sigma\), and a total function \(\delta :Q\times \Sigma \to Q\). Extend \(\delta\) to words by \(\delta (q,\varepsilon )=q\) and \(\delta (q,wa)=\delta (\delta (q,w),a)\). A word w is a reset word when |\(\{\delta (q,w):q\in Q\}|=1\). The automaton is synchronizing if at least one such word exists; its reset threshold \(rt(A)\) is the minimum number of letters in a reset word. The quantification ranges over every n and every finite alphabet and total transition function satisfying this promise. The common final state need not be specified beforehand. Initial states and accepting states play no role. The empty word handles \(n=1\). No strong-connectivity, binary-alphabet, permutation-letter, or other structural restriction is imposed. Partial automata, nondeterministic transitions, and synchronizing only a prescribed proper subset of Q are different models. The maximum is well-defined: on n labeled states there are only \(n^{n}\) different letter transformations, and duplicate transformations may be removed without changing shortest reset lengths. Thus finitely many transition alphabets suffice. \(T(1)=0\). The target is the integer-valued function of n, not the running time of testing synchronization.
cards.answer_criterion: Specify a real-valued approximation g on the positive integers and prove in Lean that |\(g(n)- (T(n) : \mathbb{R} )|\le 1/100\) for every integer \(n\ge 1\), using the model and target defined here. Certified lower and upper functions \(\ell\)\((n)\le T(n)\le u(n)\) with \(u(n)- \ell (n)\le 1/50\) also qualify via their midpoint. The answer may use unambiguous mathematical expressions or certified bounds; g need not be integer-valued, and no simple exact formula for \(T(n)\) is required. An exact determination also qualifies. A one-sided bound, agreement at finitely many n, or an asymptotic estimate without the stated pointwise error guarantee does not meet this criterion.

context_blocks.text: This card asks for the worst-case reset-length function with absolute approximation error at most 0.01 for every n. The Černý conjecture predicts \(T(n)=(n- 1)^{2}\). Determining a different function would also answer this card, but merely refuting the conjectured formula would not.

Synchronization asks how to restore a finite system to a known state when its current state is unknown. A fixed input sequence must work simultaneously from every possible starting state; it cannot observe the intermediate state and adapt its next letter. The length bound therefore measures the cost of an open-loop reset, rather than ordinary shortest-path navigation from a known vertex.

The proposed constant is forced by a concrete family. On states \(0,\ldots ,n- 1\), let a cyclically increment the state and let b send \(n- 1\) to 0 while fixing the other states. For \(n\ge 2\), the word \(b(a^{n- 1}b)^{n- 2}\) has length \((n- 1)^{2}\) and resets this automaton. Černý’s construction also proves that no shorter reset word works. This is the known lower bound for \(T(n)\); the Černý conjecture predicts equality for every n.

Knowing that a reset exists is much easier than establishing its sharp maximum length. Pairwise merging gives polynomial criteria for synchronizability, and successive compression of subsets gives general polynomial length bounds. The bottleneck is how much progress one can force as the current set of possible states shrinks. Adding separate worst-case bounds for these stages gives a cubic estimate and can lose information about how the stages interact.

The August 2026 open-problems survey records a general upper bound of approximately \(0.1654n^{3}+o(n^{3})\), due to Shitov’s refinement of Szykuła’s result. The gap is therefore in the exponent as well as the leading constant: the conjecture asks for the exact quadratic bound \((n- 1)^{2}\). Results for restricted transition systems do not establish that bound for all synchronizing automata.

A July 2026 preprint reports the conjectured bound for one-cluster automata: systems having a letter whose functional graph has exactly one directed cycle. Its sharper positive-level estimate uses the cycle length and the distance of off-cycle states from that cycle. This is a claim for a restricted class, and the later general survey still states the unrestricted conjecture as open.

cards.title: Sakoda–Sipser problem
cards.formal: Do universal constants \(C,k\ge 1\) exist such that, for every \(n\ge 1\), every finite nonempty input alphabet \(\Sigma\) and every two-way nondeterministic finite automaton A over \(\Sigma\) with at most n states, there is a two-way deterministic finite automaton D over the same alphabet with at most \(C(n+1)^{k}\) states satisfying \(\mathrm{L}(D)=\mathrm{L}(A)\)? Equivalence must hold on all finite input words, without a length bound.
cards.definitions: The read-only input tape contains a left endmarker, a word \(w\in \Sigma\)*, and a right endmarker. Each automaton has one head, initially on the left endmarker, a finite set Q of states with a designated initial state and designated halting accepting states. In each nonhalting configuration it uses its current state and the scanned symbol to choose a new state and a head displacement in \(\{- 1,0,+1\}\); moves outside the endmarkers are forbidden. A missing transition rejects that branch. A word is accepted if some finite computation reaches an accepting state. Infinite nonaccepting branches do not count as acceptance. For a deterministic automaton there is at most one available transition in each state-symbol pair, and its unique infinite run, if any, rejects. There is no work tape, rewritable input, second head, stack, counter, randomness or advice. State count includes all control and halting states, but the bound is independent of word length and alphabet size. The target is existence of D for each A; computing D from A is not required to take polynomial time. Standard endmarker and stay-put conventions change these state bounds only by polynomial factors.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of universal constants C,k giving an equivalent 2DFA with at most \(C(n+1)^{k}\) states for every n-state 2NFA, or prove that no such constants exist. In the negative direction, every proposed polynomial bound must fail on some source automaton; all language comparisons concern words of every length.
cards.why: A principal unresolved measure of the succinctness provided by nondeterminism. It isolates the issue in finite-state machines, connects to nonuniform space complexity, and asks whether revisiting read-only data can replace a large internal record of possible computations.

importance.reason: The flagship state-complexity problem for two-way finite automata, open since 1978, with unusually direct connections between finite-state descriptions and logarithmic-space complexity.

progress.text: Sakoda and Sipser formulate the polynomial-state simulation questions and conjecture that nondeterminism cannot always be removed with polynomial cost.
The Geffert–Mereghetti–Pighizzini simulation gives \(n^{O(\log  n)}\) states for unary two-way NFAs. It leaves a polynomial-versus-superpolynomial gap.
Kapoutsis characterizes polynomial-state simulation on short inputs by \(\mathrm{NL}\subseteq \mathrm{L}\)/poly, carefully distinguishing input-length restrictions and advice.
Clerici Lorenzini and coauthors obtain a polynomial-size normal form for two-way NFAs accepting letter-bounded languages.
Guillon and coauthors give polynomial-size complementation using self-verifying 1-limited automata, with rewritable annotations; the unrestricted read-only determinization question remains open.

Adeogun and Kapoutsis’ revised preprint establishes a quadratic 2DFA state lower bound for one-way liveness and the resulting NFA-to-2DFA conversion. This does not exclude a polynomial determinization bound.

cards.status_note: Checked on 11 September 2026. The STACS 2026 paper explicitly retains ordinary two-way determinization as open. Adeogun and Kapoutsis’ July 2026 revision supplies a quadratic lower bound, still compatible with polynomial determinization. Writable-annotation complementation and bounded-input-length simulations are separate results.

context_blocks.text: All four basic finite-automaton models—one-way or two-way, deterministic or nondeterministic—recognize exactly the regular languages. Their descriptions can nevertheless have very different sizes. The familiar subset construction gives an exponential conversion from a one-way NFA to a one-way DFA. The open issue is whether the deterministic machine can avoid that cost by repeatedly revisiting the original input instead of remembering all possible nondeterministic states at once.

A simple example shows why a one-way lower bound is insufficient. Over \(\{0,1\}\), consider words whose r-th symbol from the right is 1. A one-way deterministic automaton must distinguish all binary suffixes of length r and therefore needs at least \(2^{r}\) states. A two-way deterministic automaton can scan to the right endmarker, walk left r positions while counting in its finite control, and inspect the symbol. It uses \(O(r)\) states. Rereading changes the representation cost even though the accepted language is unchanged.

Known unrestricted upper bounds still pass through a one-way representation and are exponential in a polynomial of the number of states. At the opposite end, exponential separations are known if the deterministic target has restricted head motion, such as reversing only at endmarkers. Those restrictions can themselves make deterministic automata exponentially larger. A lower bound using them therefore cannot be transferred to an unrestricted 2DFA without another argument.

The unary case remains meaningful: the input then consists of repetitions of one letter, and only its length can carry information. Unary two-way NFAs can be simulated by two-way DFAs with \(n^{O(\log  n)}\) states. This is far smaller than an exponential bound but still exceeds every fixed polynomial. It demonstrates that even removing almost all input syntax does not make the remaining determinization question routine.

Connections to logarithmic-space computation require careful quantifiers. Kapoutsis proves that polynomial-state deterministic simulation on inputs of length at most the source state count is equivalent to \(\mathrm{NL}\subseteq \mathrm{L}\)/poly. Here L/poly allows a deterministic logarithmic-space machine polynomially long advice depending only on input length. That theorem concerns bounded-length agreement, whereas this card requires agreement on every word. It should not be restated as an unconditional equivalence of the full Sakoda–Sipser question with \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{NL}\).

Clerici Lorenzini, Pighizzini, and Prigioniero study letter-bounded languages in 2025: languages contained in \(a_{1}*\cdots a_{t}\)* for fixed letters. They obtain a polynomial-cost normal form in which nondeterministic choices and head reversals occur at endmarkers. The source language restriction is crucial; the theorem does not put every two-way NFA into that normal form.

Guillon, Prigioniero, and Taheri’s STACS 2026 theorem complements arbitrary two-way NFAs with a polynomial-size self-verifying 1-limited automaton. Such a machine can annotate input cells on their first visit; the construction uses a shared guessed annotation that subsequent traversals can inspect. It remains a recognizer of regular languages, but its ability to retain those annotations is absent from a 2DFA. Their introduction explicitly leaves ordinary determinization and ordinary two-way-NFA complementation open.

Adeogun and Kapoutsis’ July 2026 revision proves a quadratic state lower bound for deterministic two-way automata solving one-way liveness. The problem encodes paths through successive layers of a graph; a small nondeterministic automaton can guess a path, whereas a deterministic one must use more control states. The lower bound also applies to conversion from one-way NFAs. Quadratic growth is compatible with the polynomial simulation asked here, so this strengthens the documented lower-bound picture without resolving the conjecture.

cards.title: Generalized star-height problem
cards.formal: Does there exist a finite nonempty alphabet \(\Sigma\) and a regular language \(\mathrm{L}\subseteq \Sigma\)* such that every generalized regular expression denoting L has Kleene-star nesting depth at least two, when complement is allowed without increasing that depth?
cards.definitions: \(\Sigma\)* is the set of all finite words over \(\Sigma\), including the empty word \(\varepsilon\). A regular language is one accepted by a finite deterministic automaton. Generalized expressions are finite expressions built from \(\varnothing , \varepsilon\), and the letters \(a\in \Sigma\) using binary union \(E\cup F\), concatenation EF, complement \(E^{c}\), and Kleene star E*. Their meanings are respectively the empty language, \(\{\varepsilon\}, \{a\}\), language union, all concatenations uv with \(u\in \mathrm{L}(E)\) and \(v\in \mathrm{L}(F), \Sigma *\setminus \mathrm{L}(E)\), and the union of all finite concatenation powers of \(\mathrm{L}(E)\), including power zero \(\{\varepsilon\}\). Set \(h(\varnothing )=h(\varepsilon )=h(a)=0, h(E\cup F)=h(\mathrm{EF})=\max \{h(E),h(F)\}, h(E^{c})=h(E)\), and \(h(E*)=h(E)+1\). Define \(h_{g}(\mathrm{L})=\min \{h(E):\mathrm{L}(E)=\mathrm{L}\}\), which exists because every regular language has an ordinary regular expression. The question is whether \(h_{g}(\mathrm{L})>1\) for at least one such L. There is no bound on expression size, number of complements, union or concatenation depth, automaton size, or alphabet size. Intersection is permitted as the abbreviation \((E^{c}\cup F^{c})^{c}\) and does not add star depth. Backreferences, infinite words, additional predicates and auxiliary alphabets in the final expression are not part of the syntax.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that some regular language has generalized star height at least two, including a lower bound over all generalized expressions for that language, or prove that every regular language over every finite nonempty alphabet has a generalized expression of star height at most one. Expression size is unrestricted in both alternatives.
cards.why: A basic unresolved expressive-depth question for regular languages: determine whether Boolean operations eliminate every need for nested iteration, or whether a genuine second level exists.

importance.reason: A longstanding foundational problem connecting regular expressions, finite automata, algebraic language theory and logical descriptions.

cards.status_note: The checked author sources distinguish the open generalized question from the solved ordinary star-height problem. A later-work search on 11 September 2026 found no verified height-two example or universal height-one theorem. The inspected factor-counting results establish additional height-one subclasses only.

context_blocks.text: Kleene star represents arbitrary finite repetition. Nested stars arise naturally when repetitions occur inside other repeated blocks. The question is whether such nesting expresses a real hierarchy once a language can also be complemented at no cost to the height measure. Complement preserves regularity, so it does not enlarge the class recognized by finite automata. It may nevertheless radically change the shape of the shortest-depth expression for the same language.

Even elementary examples demonstrate that syntax and language height must be separated. Over \(\Sigma =\{a,b\}\), the language of all words has the ordinary expression \((a\cup b)\)*, with a star. With complement, it is simply \(\varnothing ^{c}\) and has height zero. The language avoiding the factor ab is \((\Sigma *ab\Sigma *)^{c}\); replacing each displayed \(\Sigma\)* by \(\varnothing ^{c}\) makes this a star-free expression. Infinitely many words can therefore belong to a language of generalized height zero.

Height zero does not capture all regular languages. Over the unary alphabet \(\{a\}\), the even-length language \((aa)\)* has generalized height exactly one. Its two-state automaton remembers length modulo two. Schützenberger’s theorem characterizes height zero through an aperiodic syntactic monoid, and this parity language has a nontrivial two-element group. Thus the first separation, between zero and one, is known; the question asks for the next separation.

The syntactic monoid packages how words behave inside arbitrary contexts: u and v are equivalent when puq belongs to L exactly when pvq does, for every pair of words p,q. Concatenation induces multiplication on the finitely many equivalence classes. A finite monoid is aperiodic when some exponent N makes \(x^{N}=x^{N+1}\) for every element x. Schützenberger’s characterization gives an effective algebraic test for star-freeness, but no corresponding complete height-one criterion is known.
