references.title: Research reference · arXiv 1705.04840
Research reference · arXiv 2502.11690

context_blocks.text: The Lovász Local Lemma concerns many individually unlikely failures that share only limited dependencies. In a variable instance, a bad event is a condition on some independent random variables. The goal is to choose the variables so that none of these conditions holds. The distributed question asks how quickly processors located at the events can agree on such choices when communication follows the dependency graph.

For an illustrative instance, independently color the vertices of a hypergraph red or blue, and let each hyperedge define the bad event that all its vertices receive the same color. A hyperedge containing k vertices is monochromatic with probability \(2^{1- k}\). Events are adjacent when their hyperedges share a vertex. A successful assignment is a two-coloring with no monochromatic hyperedge. This example explains the objects; the card allows arbitrary finite event tables, rather than only coloring events.

Small individual probabilities do not mean that one simultaneous random assignment succeeds with high probability globally. Even n mutually independent events of probability p are all avoided with probability \((1- p)^{n}\), which can be tiny. The LLL guarantees existence in a suitable probability-and-dependency regime. A distributed algorithm must obtain a globally valid assignment with the much stronger success guarantee stated on the card.

The slack condition \(p\cdot d^{c}<1/2\) is deliberately stronger than the usual existence threshold. One universal constant c must work before the degree bound d is chosen; choosing an exponent that grows with n would answer a different question. Each d is fixed while n grows, so constants in the round bound may depend on d. This bounded-degree convention is essential to interpreting the conjecture.

In LOCAL, messages have no bandwidth limit, but information still crosses only one dependency edge per round. After r rounds a node can depend only on information and random choices within its r-hop neighborhood. Shared variables also require agreement: two neighboring event processors cannot assign different colors to the same underlying variable and count that as a solution.

Fischer and Ghaffari gave a sublogarithmic algorithm under polynomially strengthened criteria. Subsequent derandomization tools and Davies’s algorithm yield bounds of the form \(O(d/\log  d + (\log  \log  n)^{O(1)})\) in the relevant regime. For fixed d this is polynomial in log log n, but it does not give a bound linear in log log n. The conjecture targets that remaining distinction.

The 2025 locality paper gives an \(O(\log  \log _{1/p} n)\) node-averaged guarantee while retaining a larger worst-case round bound. The average measures how long a typical node remains active; it can be small while a few nodes keep working. This card requires every node to finish within the same \(O(\log  \log  n)\) budget. Results for local-computation queries, MPC or the congested clique also have different access and communication rules.

The 2026 resilient-LLL paper broadens the coloring applications with polynomial-log-log round algorithms. It also distinguishes those applications from unrestricted dependency degree. Its broader general-LLL question must not erase the bounded-degree upper bounds already known here. Lower bounds from sinkless orientation explain why log log n is a central scale, with the precise LLL criterion relevant when transferring such a bound.

The question has broad consequences because distributed conflict-resolution tasks can be expressed as avoiding overlapping bad events. Chang and Pettie’s connection to locally checkable labeling problems gives the LLL a structural role in distributed complexity, beyond its use in any one coloring algorithm.

cards.title: Optimal exact single-source shortest paths in CONGEST
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(b\ge 1\), do there exist constants \(K,c>0\) and a uniform randomized CONGEST algorithm which, on every connected simple undirected graph with \(n\ge 2\) vertices, integer edge weights in \([0,n^{b}]\) and a designated source s, makes every vertex output its exact weighted distance from s in at most \(K(\sqrt{n}+D)(\log _{2}(n+2))^{c}\) rounds on every execution, with simultaneous correctness probability at least \(1- n^{- 3}\)? Here D is the diameter of the unweighted graph.
cards.why: This asks whether exact weighted shortest distances can be computed as quickly as the general communication lower bound permits, up to logarithmic factors. It separates the cost of exact optimization from the costs of network diameter and limited link bandwidth.
cards.status_note: Primary exact CONGEST bounds, randomized distance lower bounds, the approximation result and later-result searches were checked on 11 September 2026. No algorithm or impossibility theorem settling the full stated polylogarithmic-overhead target was found. The inherited 2026 paper is retained as related-work provenance, rather than used alone as evidence of the current best bound.

cards.definitions: A path length is the sum of its edge weights; the distance is the minimum path length, and the source distance is zero. D is the maximum over vertex pairs of the minimum number of edges on a path between them. The graph itself is the network. In each synchronous round, each endpoint of each edge can send at most \(B\lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) bits to the other endpoint, for a constant B depending only on b. Nodes initially know n,b, the source identifier, their own identifiers, and the identifiers and weights of incident neighbours. Identifiers are distinct integers in \([n^{2}]\). Local computation and memory are unrestricted, but each local computation between rounds terminates. Nodes use independent private fair random bits. One finite program, allowed to depend on b, runs at all nodes; no global graph description, advice, routing tables or preprocessing is supplied. The graph, weights, source and identifiers are fixed before randomness is drawn. Output at v is an ordinary binary integer for \(\operatorname{dist}(s,v)\), stored locally. The guarantee concerns all vertices together, over all coins. All communication, including finding termination and any preprocessing, counts in the round bound. K,c,B are independent of n,D and the instance; no value of D is initially supplied.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that for every fixed weight exponent b there is a single uniform algorithm meeting the stated \(O((\sqrt{n}+D)\operatorname{polylog} n)\) round bound on every execution and the simultaneous \(1- n^{- 3}\) correctness probability on every eligible network. Alternatively, prove that this is impossible for at least one fixed b, for every choice of algorithm and fixed constants K,c,B. An approximation guarantee, an \(n^{o(1)}\) overhead not bounded by a fixed power of log n, or a result for only one diameter regime is not the stated affirmative answer.

context_blocks.text: Every vertex must learn its distance from one designated source, measured by the sum of edge weights. The processors sit at the vertices and can communicate only along the graph’s edges. The question is about the number of synchronous communication rounds, rather than the time a single processor would spend on an adjacency-list representation.

There are two different notions of distance. If s is joined directly to v by an edge of weight 10, but a two-edge route has weights 2 and 2, the weighted distance is 4 even though v is one communication hop from s. The parameter D ignores weights and measures the largest hop distance between vertices. A minimum-weight path can contain many more edges than a minimum-hop path.

Each edge transports only \(O(\log  n)\) bits per direction in one round, while different edges can communicate simultaneously. A distance fits in \(O(\log  n)\) bits because weights are polynomially bounded, but many different pieces of information may need the same link. The \(\sqrt{n}\) term in the benchmark reflects a bandwidth obstacle in worst-case networks; the D term reflects how far information has to travel.

The requested output is distributed: vertex v stores \(\operatorname{dist}(s,v)\). Collecting all distances at s, printing full paths, or making every vertex learn the whole distance table would impose additional communication requirements. Conversely, a local estimate that is merely close to the shortest distance is not the exact output required here.

Chechik and Mukhtar give an exact randomized bound \(\tilde\{O\}(\sqrt{n} D^{1/4}+D)\), where the tilde hides factors polynomial in log n. Their theorem also handles directed weighted graph inputs over an undirected communication network, so it covers the undirected case retained on this card. The extra \(D^{1/4}\) factor is not absorbed by the logarithmic allowance when D grows polynomially with n.

Cao and Fineman’s 2023 theorem supplies another bound, \(\tilde\{O\}(n^{2/5+o(1)}D^{2/5}+\sqrt{n}+D)\), for polynomially bounded weights. This improves the comparison in part of the diameter range. For \(D\approx n^{1/2}\), its displayed terms give \(n^{3/5+o(1)}\), while the target is \(\tilde\{O\}(n^{1/2})\). This comparison of proven bounds displays a remaining gap; it does not prove that any particular graph requires \(n^{3/5}\) rounds.

The notation \(n^{o(1)}\) allows factors larger than every fixed power of log n. Such a factor cannot automatically be treated as the polylogarithmic overhead specified in the statement. Similarly, a theorem for one fixed diameter regime does not supply the single bound required for all connected networks.

Near-optimal algorithms for \((1+\varepsilon )\)-approximate undirected distances provide an important contrast. For fixed \(\varepsilon\) they may return a nonzero relative error. Since integer distances can be as large as \(n^{b+1}\), forcing exactness by taking \(\varepsilon\) extremely small can increase the algorithm’s complexity through its \(\varepsilon\) dependence. A fixed-accuracy approximation theorem therefore does not imply this exact result.

The inherited 2026 reference studies programmable matter with reconfigurable circuits that transmit signals in a different way. Its related-work section is useful background for CONGEST, but its own polylogarithmic algorithm is not a solution in the present model. The card now cites the original CONGEST results as well, including the 2023 bound missing from that summary.

Resolving the question would determine whether exact numerical optimization has an additional distributed cost beyond the familiar bandwidth-and-diameter benchmark. Shortest distances are also a primitive in other distributed constructions, so a faster exact computation would affect more than routing from one source.

cards.title: Strongly polynomial linear programming
cards.formal:
Does there exist one deterministic algorithm and fixed positive integers \(C,d,C',e\) with the following guarantee for every \(m,n\ge1\), \(A\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb Q^m\) and \(c\in\mathbb Q^n\)? For the linear program
\[\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x: x\in\mathbb R^n,\ Ax=b,\ x\ge0\},\]
the algorithm returns an exact rational optimal vector, or correctly reports infeasibility or an objective unbounded below. It uses at most \(C(m+n+1)^d\) elementary operations in the rational arithmetic model below, and every numerical value during the computation has binary encoding length at most \(C'(N+1)^e\), where \(N\) is the full input bit length. The same program and constants must work for all dimensions and coefficient values.
cards.definitions:
The input contains the dimensions and the complete dense lists of entries of \(A,b,c\), including zeros. Each rational is supplied as a signed binary integer numerator and a positive binary integer denominator. Their lengths, the dimensions and the delimiters all contribute to \(N\). No rank, nondegeneracy, strict-feasibility, boundedness, coefficient-size or conditioning promise is imposed. The variables range over the real numbers; rational input guarantees that a finite optimum, when the feasible set is nonempty and the objective bounded below, has a rational optimal vector.

Computation uses one fixed finite arithmetic-RAM program with rational registers, integer addresses and finite control. One scalar addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero rational, exact comparison, register read/write or copy costs one operation. Conditional branches, elementary integer index arithmetic and comparisons, and data transfers also count. Index operations are integer addition and subtraction; indirect addressing accesses one location at a time. Indices start from dimensions or fixed integer constants and are manipulated by these index operations. A rational coefficient or computed rational cannot be reinterpreted as an address. Each scalar entry of a vector or matrix operation must be charged separately. All preprocessing, memory access, feasibility testing and production of the output count. A scalar rational input read or output write counts once at this arithmetic level; transferring its individual binary digits is accounted for by the bit implementation.

The program may contain finitely many fixed rational constants. It has no oracle, advice, randomness, floor or integer-part primitive, square-root primitive, or instruction inspecting the binary digits, numerator, denominator or encoding length of a rational register. Comparisons and arithmetic act on exact rational values, not floating-point approximations. Here the binary size of a rational is the combined length of its signed numerator and positive denominator in lowest terms. The bound also covers integer indices and the output. Reduction to lowest terms specifies representation and exact bit simulation; it supplies no additional operation with which the arithmetic program can extract numerator or denominator data. The elementary rational operations must admit an exact implementation on a binary multitape Turing machine in time polynomial in their operand lengths. Thus the dimension-only operation bound together with the polynomial numerical-size bound yields total bit time polynomial in \(N\); the bit-time bound is not required to be independent of \(N\).

Let \(F=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\). An infeasibility answer is correct exactly when \(F=\varnothing\). An unbounded-below answer is correct exactly when \(F\ne\varnothing\) and
\[\forall M\in\mathbb R\ \exists x\in F,\qquad c^{\mathsf T}x<M.\]
Otherwise the algorithm must return \(x^*\in F\cap\mathbb Q^n\) with
\[\forall y\in F,\qquad c^{\mathsf T}x^*\le c^{\mathsf T}y.\]
Any optimal vector is allowed when several exist; an optimal basis is not required. An unbounded feasible region can still have a finite minimum, and must then receive an optimal-vector output. Infeasibility and unboundedness outputs are distinct tags, not an approximate numerical infinity. The operation bound depends only on \(m+n\); neither coefficient magnitudes, their bit lengths, numerical conditioning nor a requested accuracy may enter it.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of this algorithm-existence statement or of its logical negation. A positive answer must specify a finite deterministic program, prove its correct exact output in all three cases for every rational input, and prove both a single dimension-only polynomial operation bound and a single polynomial bound on numerical encoding lengths, with an exact polynomial-time bit implementation.

A negative answer must prove that no program with any fixed constants \(C,d,C',e\) satisfies all these requirements on every input. An exponential example for one pivot rule or a restricted class of interior-point methods does not exclude every algorithm in the specified model. A guarantee restricted to special matrices, fixed dimension, well-conditioned or strictly feasible inputs, or an approximate optimum does not settle the question. This is a yes/no existence target; the benchmark's numerical approximation tolerance does not replace exact optimization or either complexity bound.
cards.why: Linear programming is a basic language for optimization across combinatorics, algorithms and applications. The question asks whether exact optimization needs a number of arithmetic decisions that grows with numerical precision, or whether the dimensions alone suffice. A positive answer would extend a central efficiency property of several combinatorial optimization problems to every rational linear program.

importance.reason: A leading open question in optimization, separating ordinary polynomial-time solvability from a dimension-only arithmetic bound. Its reach includes general linear programming and many combinatorial optimization problems.

context_blocks.text: Linear programming already has algorithms polynomial in the full binary input length. That length can increase while the numbers of variables and constraints stay fixed. Strong polynomiality asks for a dimension-only arithmetic operation count while retaining polynomially bounded numerical representations. It does not promise that writing an arbitrarily long exact output takes a constant number of bit operations.

The three output cases refer to the objective as well as the feasible set. For example, \(x_1=1\), \(x_2\ge0\), with objective \(x_1\), has an unbounded feasible region and finite minimum \(1\). The algorithm must return an optimal vector in this case. Failure to find a feasible point is not by itself a certificate that none exists.

Tardos’s 1986 theorem removes the dependence of the arithmetic operation count on the right-hand side and objective coefficients, while retaining dependence on the constraint matrix. This gives strong polynomiality for important small-coefficient matrix classes. Dadush, Koh, Natura, Olver and Végh’s STOC 2024 theorem covers minimum-cost generalized flow and linear programs with at most two nonzero entries per row or per column, including controlled bit complexity. An unrestricted dense matrix need not belong to these classes.

Allamigeon, Gaubert and Vandame prove exponential iteration lower bounds for interior-point trajectories confined to the specified neighborhoods of self-concordant-barrier central paths. A central path is the curve of minimizers of the barrier-penalized objective as its parameter varies. Their theorem restricts which trajectories the method follows; it is not a lower bound for every arithmetic algorithm for linear programming.

The STOC 2026 trust-region paper gives guarantees relative to the straight-line complexity of an appropriate central-path neighborhood: the number of line segments needed to traverse it. Instance optimality within this path-following framework does not supply a dimension-only polynomial bound on that quantity for every LP. The paper also distinguishes its real-RAM running times from the additional work needed to control bit complexity. Its approximate trust-region subproblems retain accuracy parameters and are not exact general LP solvers.

cards.title: Exact semidefinite feasibility in polynomial time
cards.formal:
Does exact semidefinite feasibility belong to \(\mathrm P\) in the ordinary Turing model? The input is an explicitly listed tuple of symmetric rational matrices
\[A_0,A_1,\ldots,A_m\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n},\qquad n\ge1,\ m\ge0,
\]
and the required output is \(1\) if and only if
\[\exists x\in\mathbb R^m\quad A_0+\sum_{i=1}^{m}x_iA_i\succeq0.\]
More precisely, do there exist one deterministic finite-program Turing machine \(M\) and positive integers \(a,d\) such that, for every input string of total binary encoding length \(N\), \(M\) halts within \(a(N+1)^d\) steps and correctly decides the language defined below? Both matrix dimension and number of variables are unbounded input parameters. No numerical promise or approximation tolerance is supplied.
cards.definitions:
The input lists \(n,m\) in binary and then all \((m+1)n^2\) entries of the matrices in row order. An entry is a signed binary integer numerator and a positive binary integer denominator, with fixed separators; separators and sign symbols have fixed binary encodings and count toward \(N\). Numerators and denominators need not be relatively prime. All entries, including zeroes and both symmetric halves, are explicitly written; the input is not a circuit, oracle or abbreviated prescription for larger matrices. The language contains exactly the valid encodings with \(n\ge1\), \(m\ge0\), matching dimensions, symmetric matrices and a feasible real vector. Malformed strings, zero denominators and nonsymmetric matrix lists are rejected. Equivalent conventional explicit integer/list encodings differ only by polynomial overhead.

A real symmetric matrix \(B\) is positive semidefinite, written \(B\succeq0\), when \(z^{\mathsf T}Bz\ge0\) for every \(z\in\mathbb R^n\). Zero eigenvalues are allowed. The variable \(x\) ranges over all real vectors, not only rational ones. For \(m=0\), the sum is zero and the unique vector in \(\mathbb R^0\) is feasible precisely when \(A_0\succeq0\). For a valid general input, output \(0\) means that no real feasible vector exists.

The computation model is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with fixed finite tape alphabets and one transition charged per time step. Input access, arithmetic on binary strings, intermediate computations, memory access and output are all charged. The algorithm has no oracle, advice, randomness or unit-cost operations on arbitrary exact real numbers. Its time constants are fixed independently of the matrices, their dimensions and their entries. The only output is the decision bit; it need not write a feasible point, an algebraic representation of one, an optimum value or an infeasibility certificate.

The domain includes feasible sets with empty interior, singular feasible matrices, unbounded feasible sets and infeasible affine matrix families at distance zero from the positive semidefinite cone. In particular, there is no positive-definite-feasibility promise, no known containing radius or interior ball, and no lower bound on conditioning or distance to feasibility. Strict feasibility would require a vector producing a positive definite matrix, meaning \(z^{\mathsf T}Bz>0\) for every nonzero \(z\); it is not assumed here. 'Exact' refers to the correct membership bit on every input, including these boundary cases, rather than to numerically accurate matrix entries.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of membership of this language in \(\mathrm P\), or of its negation. An affirmative proof must give one deterministic algorithm and one universal polynomial bit-time bound, and prove that its decision agrees with real feasibility for every valid input, with rejection of invalid encodings. A negative proof must rule out every deterministic polynomial-time decider in this model. Failure of one numerical method, exponential size of an explicit witness, or a conditional hardness reduction with an unproved assumption is insufficient. A decision procedure may use arbitrary internal methods, but a guarantee for approximate feasibility, strictly feasible inputs, bounded regions or fixed dimensions does not establish the complete target.
cards.why: Semidefinite constraints underlie many successful optimization relaxations, yet their unrestricted exact decision complexity is still unsettled. This problem isolates whether finite rational input admits a polynomial-time decision even when numerical separation and small explicit witnesses are unavailable.

importance.reason: A foundational complexity gap in a widely used convex optimization model; exact decision remains open despite powerful approximation algorithms, exact duality and symbolic decidability.

The card remains source_open; this pass does not independently certify all cited proofs.

context_blocks.text: A semidefinite constraint requires a quadratic form to be nonnegative in every direction. Diagonal matrix inequalities include ordinary linear inequalities. Exact decision asks whether the feasible region is empty, which is different from obtaining a useful approximate optimizer on well-conditioned instances.

De Klerk–Vallentin’s inspected approximation theorem is supplied with a rational feasible center and quantitative inner and outer radius information. Its runtime also depends on requested accuracy. This is a polynomial bit-complexity result under explicit geometric assumptions, not an unrestricted exact emptiness test.

Approximate feasibility need not imply exact feasibility. For example,
\[B(t)=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&t\end{pmatrix}\]
has determinant \(-1\), so it is never positive semidefinite. Nevertheless its negative eigenvalue \((t-\sqrt{t^2+4})/2\) tends to zero as \(t\) tends to positive infinity. This infeasible affine family has distance zero from the positive semidefinite cone in the Frobenius norm, the square root of the sum of squared matrix entries.

A rational input can also have only irrational feasible parameters. The rational affine block-diagonal matrix
\[\operatorname{diag}\!\left(\begin{pmatrix}x&2\\2&2x\end{pmatrix},\begin{pmatrix}2&x\\x&1\end{pmatrix}\right)\]
is positive semidefinite exactly when \(x=\sqrt2\). Replacing the real domain by rational substitutions would change the answer to this instance.

Even when rational feasible points exist, all of them can require exponentially many bits relative to the number of variables. Pataki–Touzov study the structural occurrence of such examples and questions about compact representations. This explains an obstacle to algorithms that must explicitly output a point; it does not itself lower-bound the complexity of the decision bit requested here.

General exact decision is possible through real-algebraic methods. Henrion–Naldi–Safey El Din develop symbolic algorithms accommodating degenerate feasible sets. Their optimization analysis retains generic auxiliary choices and objectives, and its displayed bounds count arithmetic operations. Bounds polynomial when one dimension is fixed do not establish one polynomial bit bound when both dimensions and coefficient lengths vary.

Ramana’s exact alternative replaces infeasibility by feasibility of another semidefinite system of polynomial description size. In the Turing model it implies that the problem lies in NP if and only if it lies in coNP; neither membership is thereby established on its own. The separate NP-intersect-coNP result over exact real-number machines uses a different model of computation.

Pataki’s October 2025 treatment retains this complexity distinction and gives a fuller description of the exact dual’s feasible set. A polynomial-size dual system is not automatically a polynomial-size binary certificate: its real variables still have to satisfy semidefinite constraints.

Slot–Steurer–Wiedmer obtain effective solution bounds and polynomial-time approximate minimization of convex polynomials over polyhedra. The constraints in that result are linear, and the authors explicitly contrast their result with general semidefinite programming. It does not make arbitrary linear matrix inequalities decidable in polynomial bit time.

The September 2026 higher-order Newton paper of ter Voert–de Klerk explicitly retains the unknown exact SDP complexity. Its iteration analysis uses a derivative oracle and real-number computation, and fixed-accuracy SDP subproblems require stated regularity. A reduction of an iteration to an SDP is therefore not a solution of this unrestricted Turing-model decision question.

cards.title: Conforti–Cornuéjols conjecture
cards.formal: Does every finite clutter with the packing property have the max-flow min-cut property? Equivalently, if every deletion/contraction minor satisfies unweighted integral packing–covering equality, must weighted integral packing–covering equality hold for every nonnegative integer weight vector?
cards.definitions:
A clutter \(\mathcal C\) on a finite ground set \(E\) is a family of subsets of \(E\), no one properly containing another. Its original members are nonempty; the empty family is allowed. A cover is a set \(T\subseteq E\) meeting every member, and \(	au(\mathcal C)\) is its minimum cardinality. A packing is a family of pairwise disjoint members; \(
u(\mathcal C)\) is its maximum cardinality. Deleting an element removes it from the ground set and discards all members containing it. Contracting an element removes it from the ground set and from every member, then keeps only inclusion-minimal members. A minor is obtained by any finite sequence of these operations, including the empty sequence. The packing property is \(	au(\mathcal D)=
u(\mathcal D)\) for every minor \(\mathcal D\). For the empty family both numbers are zero. For the degenerate minor \(\{\varnothing\}\), set both numbers to \(+\infty\): no cover exists and arbitrarily many copies of the empty member can be packed. These conventions give no obstruction from degenerate minors. For an original clutter and capacities \(w\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{E}\), define \[	au_w(\mathcal C)=\min\left\{\sum_{e\in T}w_e:T\subseteq E	ext{ is a cover}ight\},\qquad 
u_w(\mathcal C)=\max\left\{\sum_{F\in\mathcal C}y_F:y\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{\mathcal C},\ \sum_{F
i e}y_F\le w_e	ext{ for every }e\in Eight\}.\] Multiplicities \(y_F\) allow repeated packed members, and every copy consumes one unit of capacity at each of its elements. Both optima are finite because original members are nonempty. The max-flow min-cut (MFMC) property is equality of these optima for every nonnegative integer capacity vector; the weights and ground-set size have no fixed upper bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal implication, or of its logical negation. An affirmative answer must establish \(\tau_w(\mathcal C)=\nu_w(\mathcal C)\) for every clutter with the packing property and every nonnegative integer vector \(w\). A negative answer must exhibit a finite clutter and such a vector with \(\tau_w(\mathcal C)>\nu_w(\mathcal C)\), and verify the packing property for every minor. A finite census, a proper subclass theorem, or fractional duality alone is insufficient.

context_blocks.text: Packing and covering often give two descriptions of the same combinatorial optimum. In a clutter, the unweighted equality can fail. Requiring equality after every deletion and contraction removes many such obstructions. The Conforti–Cornuéjols conjecture asks whether this local robustness already guarantees equality for every integer capacity vector.

For a concrete example, take E as the vertices of a bipartite graph and the clutter members as its edges. Covers are vertex covers and packings are matchings. This illustrates the familiar kind of min–max equality that the general conjecture seeks to characterize, without restricting its input to graph edge families.

For the member-by-element incidence matrix \(A\), whose entry \(A_{F,e}\) is one precisely when \(e\in F\), the corresponding fractional problems are \(\min\{w^{\mathsf T}z:Az\ge\mathbf1,\ z\ge0\}\) and \(\max\{\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y\le w,\ y\ge0\}\). The conjectured equality concerns integer solutions, and hence is stronger than ordinary linear-programming duality. It asks for integral optima on both sides for every integer weight.

Schrijver’s Survey Question 68 calls the target the assertion that every packing hypergraph is Mengerian. The terminology differs, but its packing property includes all minors and its conclusion includes arbitrary nonnegative integer weights. Checking only the all-ones weight on the original instance would yield a much weaker, insufficient hypothesis.

Abdi and Schwarcz’s July 2026 manuscript calls the statement the replication conjecture and explicitly retains it as open. It reports verification for clutters on at most ten elements and for a specified bounded-degree family of cuboids. These are finite or restricted confirmations, not a proof for arbitrary ground-set size.

The same work gives a finite set of weight vectors sufficient to test the MFMC property of a fixed clutter, with an improved bound on their entries. This makes checking individual instances more effective. The number and size of possible clutters still grow without bound, so instance-wise testability does not prove the universal implication.

Roy and Saha report a proof for \((n-2)\)-uniform clutters: every member has size exactly \(n-2\) when the ground set has \(n\) elements. Arbitrary clutters can have unrelated member sizes, so this subclass result leaves the stated universal implication unchanged.

cards.why: Identify whether all obstructions to weighted integral packing–covering duality are already visible as unweighted failures in minors, a central issue in integer programming and combinatorial optimization.

importance.reason: A central conjecture connecting minor obstructions, integral linear programming and packing–covering duality. Schrijver treats it as a major survey question, and a July 2026 primary paper develops both theoretical and computational methods around it.

cards.title: Nearly linear-time solution of general sparse linear systems
cards.formal:
For every fixed integer \(c\ge1\), do there exist a uniform randomized classical algorithm \(A_c\) and constants \(C_c,K_c\ge1\), \(d_c\ge0\), all integers, with the following guarantee? Every promised input consists of \(n\ge2\), a nonsingular rational matrix \(A\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n}\) with \(m\) nonzero entries, a nonzero vector \(b\in\mathbb Q^n\), and an integer \(1\le p\le c\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\). Every input numerator magnitude and positive denominator has at most \(c\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\) binary digits, and
\[\kappa_2(A)\le n^c.\]
On every run, \(A_c\) must halt within
\[C_c m\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil^{d_c}\]
word operations in the model below, with word length \(w=K_c\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\). With probability at least \(2/3\), its explicit rational output \(\widehat x\in\mathbb Q^n\) must satisfy
\[\|A\widehat x-b\|_2\le2^{-p}\|b\|_2.\]
The constants and the finite program may depend on \(c\), but must work for all promised dimensions, matrices, right-hand sides and accuracies. Matrices may be nonsymmetric and indefinite.
cards.definitions:
The input explicitly gives \(n,m,p\) in binary, followed by an unordered list of \(m\) triples consisting of a row index, a column index and a nonzero rational value, with distinct positions in \(\{1,\ldots,n\}^2\), and then all \(n\) entries of \(b\). Unlisted matrix entries are zero. Rational numbers are signed binary integer numerators and positive binary integer denominators; reduced fractions are not required. The binary length of zero is one, and a sign is stored separately. Fixed separators specify the list boundaries and integer lengths. Nonsingularity implies \(n\le m\le n^2\), so the total encoding has \(O_c(m\log n)\) bits. The parameter \(c\) specifies the family of promises, rather than an additional runtime input. The algorithm need not verify the promises; guarantees are required only on inputs satisfying them.

For a real vector \(z\), \(\|z\|_2=(\sum_i z_i^2)^{1/2}\). Define \(\sigma_{\max}(A)=\max_{\|z\|_2=1}\|Az\|_2\), \(\sigma_{\min}(A)=\min_{\|z\|_2=1}\|Az\|_2\), and \(\kappa_2(A)=\sigma_{\max}(A)/\sigma_{\min}(A)\). The minimum is positive for nonsingular \(A\). The requested error is relative residual error for this exact rational input, with \(\varepsilon=2^{-p}\). It is not a promise that the approximate vector has the same relative forward error as the residual.

The word RAM has a fixed finite program and a fixed finite number of registers, each holding an unsigned \(w\)-bit word. Input is stored as an explicit binary string packed into a read-only word array. Working memory consists of \(w\)-bit cells addressed by \(w\)-bit words and initially zero; no input-dependent advice or precomputed table is supplied. A step performs one read or write, comparison, conditional branch, addition, subtraction or multiplication modulo \(2^w\), unsigned quotient or remainder with a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operation, or logical shift of a word. A shift by at least \(w\) positions returns zero. Address computations use the same instructions. One fresh independent uniform \(w\)-bit word costs one step. Longer integers occupy multiple cells and use multiple operations. No instruction acts on an arbitrary real number or arbitrary-length integer at unit cost.

The output is a length-delimited explicit list of \(n\) signed binary numerators and positive binary denominators. Every output word must be written, and all its bits occupy the output encoding. Input processing, preprocessing, any auxiliary matrices, numerical precision, randomness and output cost are included in the stated time bound. The clock is a worst-case bound on every choice of random words, not an expected bound. Probability refers only to the algorithm's independent randomness for each fixed input. An invalid output counts as failure. Uniformity means one program for each fixed \(c\), without dependence on \(n\) or on the particular input; no extra effective procedure generating programs from \(c\) is requested.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition, or of its full logical negation, in this word-RAM model. An affirmative proof must establish the algorithm, its worst-case clock and its success guarantee for every fixed \(c\) and every input in the associated promise family. A negative proof must establish that for some fixed \(c\), no finite program and constants satisfy all these guarantees. It must exclude all algorithms in the stated model, rather than only a chosen iterative method or preconditioner. A result restricted to one structured matrix family, a different output representation or an uncharged real-arithmetic model does not meet the target.

context_blocks.text: Sparse linear equations are a basic subroutine in optimization and scientific computation. A matrix with \(m\) nonzeros can be stored without its \(n^2-m\) zero entries, and multiplying it by a vector requires only a small amount of arithmetic per stored coefficient. Whether solving the system can have comparable worst-case cost is a stronger question. Moderate conditioning controls numerical sensitivity, but does not itself supply an efficient solver.

Residual error and solution error are different. With \(x^*=A^{-1}b\),
\[\frac{\|\widehat x-x^*\|_2}{\|x^*\|_2}\le\kappa_2(A)\frac{\|A\widehat x-b\|_2}{\|b\|_2}.\]
For example, \(A=\operatorname{diag}(1,\delta)\), \(b=(1,\delta)\) and \(\widehat x=(1,0)\), for \(0<\delta<1\), have absolute residual \(\delta\) even though the second solution coordinate is wrong by one. The card fixes the norm, conditioning and requested tolerance so that these distinct accuracy notions are not conflated.

Spielman and Teng obtain nearly linear expected-time algorithms for symmetric diagonally dominant matrices, whose diagonal entries satisfy \(A_{ii}\ge\sum_{j\ne i}|A_{ij}|\). Their error guarantee uses the energy norm \(\|z\|_A=(z^{\mathsf T}Az)^{1/2}\). Their paper also analyzes finite precision. For positive-definite inputs, comparison with the Euclidean residual depends on conditioning. These results establish the importance of structural assumptions; their stated norm and expected-time convention are not identical to this card's general guarantee.

Peng and Vempala's SODA 2021 theorem gives a general finite-precision solver that beats matrix-multiplication time for sufficiently sparse, polynomially conditioned systems. The theorem measures residual relative to the projection of the right-hand side onto the column space; for the nonsingular square inputs here, that projection is simply \(b\). The work later appears in JACM in 2025. Asking only to beat the matrix-multiplication barrier would therefore miss the remaining near-linear question.

Nie's 2022 result improves the general bound to
\[\widetilde O\!\left(m^{(\omega-2)/(\omega-1)}n^2\right)\]
in the polynomial-conditioning and precision regime. Here \(\omega\) denotes the matrix-multiplication exponent and \(\widetilde O\) suppresses polylogarithmic factors. For \(m=\widetilde O(n)\), the displayed bound becomes \(\widetilde O(n^{(3\omega-4)/(\omega-1)})\). This remains well above near-linear time; the historical numerical exponent printed in the paper is tied to the matrix-multiplication bound then available.

Ding, Kyng, Probst Gutenberg and Zhang show that linear equations in Laplacians of two-dimensional simplicial complexes are sparse-linear-equation complete. Their reduction preserves sparsity up to logarithmic factors and has polynomial effects on coefficient sizes, conditioning and requested accuracy for the stated integer-input family. Thus apparently structured higher-dimensional systems already capture substantial general difficulty. This is a reduction between solver tasks, not an unconditional lower bound ruling out a near-linear algorithm.

The August 2026 Simons workshop report discusses scalable solvers for parameterized partial-differential-equation benchmarks, preconditioning, and finite-precision iterative methods. Those questions distinguish guarantees for a selected family from a universal guarantee over sparse inputs. They also distinguish iteration counts from a full cost accounting. The report supplies contemporary context rather than a theorem settling the editorial target here.

The output is part of the computational task. Writing \(n\) approximate coordinates is compatible with near-linear sparse-input time because \(m\ge n\). Returning selected observables, oracle access to an implicit vector, or a quantum state changes that requirement. Requiring the exact rational solution instead would also change the question by introducing potentially much larger coordinate encodings. The stated word model charges storage and processing of all precision actually used.

cards.title: Smale’s seventh problem
cards.formal: Do there exist real constants \(C,K>0\), an integer \(k\ge1\), and one deterministic real-number algorithm \(A\) in the model below such that, for every integer \(N\ge2\), \(A(N)\) outputs distinct points \(x_1,\ldots,x_N\in S^2\) in at most \(KN^k\) operations and satisfies \(E_N(x_1,\ldots,x_N)\le E_N^{\ast}+C\ln N\)?
cards.why: Connects the complexity of constructing global near-minimizers with discrete potential theory and the conditioning of polynomial-root problems. Its logarithmic total-energy tolerance is much sharper than leading-order equidistribution.
cards.status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. No general deterministic polynomial-time construction with logarithmic total-energy excess was located. The March 2026 finite-cardinality classification and existing distributional energy guarantees do not establish the uniform algorithmic target. This source review did not independently verify the cited proofs.

cards.definitions: Let \(S^2=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2=1\}\). For distinct points define \(E_N(x_1,\ldots,x_N)=-\sum_{i\ne j}\ln\|x_i-x_j\|_2\), counting ordered pairs; configurations with collisions have energy \(+\infty\). Let \(E_N^{\ast}\) be the infimum over all \(N\)-tuples on \(S^2\). Here \(\ln\) is the natural logarithm and \(\|\cdot\|_2\) is Euclidean distance. Use one deterministic finite real-arithmetic program with a fixed finite list of real constants independent of \(N\). The machine has exact real registers, finite control and tapes; each scalar copy, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero register, sign test, or tape movement costs one operation. It may allocate storage, charging the operations that use it, and has no primitive logarithm, square root, floor, randomness or optimization oracle. The input integer \(N\) is supplied as one exact real value. Output is the explicit list of \(3N\) coordinates, all required to lie exactly on the sphere. Time is polynomial in \(N\), not in \(\log N\); this is a real-number computation model, not a bit-cost model. The energy inequality is a mathematical condition on the output, and the machine need not evaluate that energy.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of one permitted real-arithmetic program and constants \(C,K,k\), independent of \(N\), satisfying both the time and energy guarantees for every integer \(N\ge2\), or prove in Lean that no such program and constants exist. The output must lie exactly on the sphere. Expected energy under a distribution, finitely many solved cardinalities, or a larger asymptotic additive error does not meet this criterion.

references.title: Research reference · www.lebesgue.fr
Mathematical Problems for the Next Century
references.locator: Problem 7; real-number computation model and logarithmic excess energy.

context_blocks.text: Imagine placing mutually repelling particles on a sphere. For this problem, a pair contributes minus the logarithm of its straight-line distance through three-dimensional space. Bringing two points together sends their contribution to positive infinity. Spreading points lowers the energy, but the question asks for a guarantee against the best configuration of the entire collection, rather than against a locally stable arrangement. Exact minimizers are called elliptic Fekete configurations.

For two points the answer is concrete: opposite poles have distance 2, the largest possible distance on the unit sphere, and ordered-pair energy −2 ln 2. For general N an optimum still exists: the sphere is compact, collisions have infinite energy, and some distinct configuration has finite energy. Existence therefore is not the open part. The unresolved requirement is one fixed algorithm with a polynomial operation bound for every N.

The tolerance \(C\ln N\) is an additive error in the total energy. The minimum has leading terms \(E_N^{\ast}=(1/2-\ln2)N^2-(N/2)\ln N+O(N)\). An approximation that only matches these leading terms may still have error proportional to \(N\), much larger than the requested logarithmic excess.

Smale’s original statement counts each unordered pair once. This card counts each pair twice, as in much subsequent literature. Both the optimum and excess energy are doubled, so the existence of a universal logarithmic-error constant is unchanged. The real-arithmetic model also comes from Smale’s formulation: a step manipulates an exact real value. A polynomial number of such steps does not assert polynomial bit complexity, and the output inequality does not give the program a free logarithm or minimization instruction.

The generalized Diamond ensemble supplies configurations for every N with a precisely analyzed expected energy: the two leading terms above plus a specified linear term and an \(O(\sqrt{N} \ln  N)\) remainder. These constructions quantify how well a structured distribution spreads points. That estimate is not a deterministic C ln N excess guarantee relative to the unknown optimum.

Beltrán and Hardy obtain the required logarithmic excess for a low-temperature Coulomb-gas distribution: at inverse temperature N, the mean excess is at most 9 ln N, and excess at most 10 ln N holds with probability at least \(1- \exp (- N \ln  N)\). The theorem analyzes the distribution, while polynomial-time sampling from it remains an additional computational issue. A probabilistic existence statement also differs from the deterministic algorithm asked for here.

Michelen and Yakir prove a central limit theorem for the energy of zeros of a rotationally invariant random polynomial, with fluctuations on the \(\sqrt{N}\) scale. This measures variation around that ensemble’s mean, not error from the global minimum.

Recent exact algebraic work by Armentano and coauthors classifies critical configurations with at most six points, and treats seven points under an antipodal-pair restriction. Such finite classifications do not supply a uniform algorithm for arbitrary N.

The original motivation connects low-energy spherical points, through stereographic projection, to well-conditioned polynomials and the complexity of finding polynomial roots. The energy question has its own stronger output guarantee; progress on polynomial conditioning or on a different Smale problem does not automatically resolve it. It also asks a basic algorithmic question in discrete potential theory: how cheaply can globally near-equilibrium configurations be constructed?

Recent exact algebraic work by Armentano and coauthors classifies critical configurations with at most six points, and treats seven points under an antipodal-pair restriction. Such finite classifications do not supply a uniform algorithm for arbitrary N.

The original motivation connects low-energy spherical points, through stereographic projection, to well-conditioned polynomials and the complexity of finding polynomial roots. The energy question has its own stronger output guarantee; progress on polynomial conditioning or on a different Smale problem does not automatically resolve it. It also asks a basic algorithmic question in discrete potential theory: how cheaply can globally near-equilibrium configurations be constructed?

cards.title: Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits conjecture
cards.formal: Does there exist a real constant \(C>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), every isotropic log-concave probability measure \(\mu\) on \(\mathbb R^n\), and every locally Lipschitz function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) with \(\int f^2\,d\mu<\infty\) and \(\int\|\nabla f\|_2^2\,d\mu<\infty\), \[\operatorname{Var}_{\mu}(f)\le C\int_{\mathbb R^n}\|\nabla f(x)\|_2^2\,d\mu(x)?\] The same constant must work for all dimensions, measures and admissible functions. This is the Poincaré formulation of the Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits conjecture.
cards.definitions: All norms and derivatives are Euclidean, with \(\|x\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2)^{1/2}\). Here a log-concave probability measure has a Lebesgue density \(\rho(x)=e^{-V(x)}\) of integral one, where \(V:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is measurable and convex; \(e^{-\infty}=0\). Convexity means \(V((1-s)x+sy)\le(1-s)V(x)+sV(y)\) for all \(x,y\) and \(0<s<1\), using the extended-real convention on the right. Thus \(d\mu(x)=\rho(x)\,dx\). Isotropy means finite second moments and \(\int x_i\,d\mu=0\), \(\int x_i x_j\,d\mu=\delta_{ij}\) for every \(i,j\), where \(\delta_{ij}=1\) if \(i=j\) and zero otherwise. Equivalently, the mean vector is zero and the covariance matrix is the identity. Isotropy excludes measures supported on a proper affine subspace, so no lower-dimensional singular case is omitted by using a density. Locally Lipschitz means that every point has a neighborhood on which \(|f(y)-f(z)|\le L\|y-z\|_2\) for some finite \(L\); the neighborhood and constant may depend on the point. Such a function has a Euclidean derivative outside a Lebesgue-null set, and \(\nabla f\) is the vector of its partial derivatives there; set it to zero where the derivative does not exist. This choice on the null set does not affect integration against \(\mu\). Write \(\bar f=\int f\,d\mu\), which is finite by the second-moment assumption, and \(\operatorname{Var}_{\mu}(f)=\int(f-\bar f)^2\,d\mu\). The gradient energy is the integral of \(\|\nabla f\|_2^2\). Define \(C_{\mathrm P}(\mu)\) as the infimum of all \(a\ge0\) for which the displayed inequality holds with \(a\) for every admissible function, with infimum of the empty set interpreted as \(+\infty\). The question asks whether these constants are uniformly bounded; it does not ask for their optimal universal value. No symmetry, product structure, differentiability of \(V\), bounded support or positive lower bound on its curvature is assumed. Uniform laws on full-dimensional convex bodies are included after isotropic normalization; a convex body is a compact convex set with nonempty interior. The problem is an analytic existence statement, with no oracle, encoding or algorithmic-time requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal Poincaré inequality with some finite real \(C>0\), or a Lean-checked proof of its logical negation: for every real \(C>0\), there exist an integer \(n\ge1\), a measure \(\mu\) satisfying all stated log-concavity and isotropy conditions, and an admissible locally Lipschitz \(f\) of finite second moment and finite gradient energy such that \(\operatorname{Var}_{\mu}(f)>C\int\|\nabla f\|_2^2\,d\mu\). The dimension, measure and function may depend on \(C\). A single violation for one proposed numerical constant does not refute existence of some larger universal constant. A dimension-dependent bound, or a theorem restricted to linear, radial or quadratic functions or a narrower class of measures, is insufficient unless the proof also establishes the entire stated target. No optimal value of \(C\) is required. An equivalent geometric statement can qualify only with a Lean-checked implication proving this proposition or its negation; cited but unproved conjectural dependencies do not complete acceptance.
cards.why: KLS asks whether covariance normalization alone controls the relation between global variation and local change for every log-concave distribution. Its equivalent geometric expansion principle is central to concentration inequalities and the analysis of random walks used for sampling, integration and convex optimization.

importance.reason: A foundational high-dimensional geometry conjecture with substantial consequences for sampling, integration, optimization, and concentration inequalities.

context_blocks.text: Isotropy fixes scale in every linear direction. For a unit vector \(\theta\), the function \(f(x)=\sum_i\theta_i x_i\) has variance one and gradient energy one, so every admissible universal constant is at least one. The conjecture asks whether nonlinear observables can have an arbitrarily greater variance relative to their average squared local change. Log-concavity is much weaker than independence of coordinates or a uniformly curved smooth potential.

The geometric formulation compares the boundary size of a set with the probability mass it separates. For a Borel set \(S\), let \(S_\varepsilon=\{x:\operatorname{dist}(x,S)<\varepsilon\}\), where distance is the infimum of \(\|x-y\|_2\) over \(y\in S\), and define \(\mu^+(S)=\liminf_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}(\mu(S_\varepsilon)-\mu(S))/\varepsilon\). The Cheeger expansion constant is \(h_\mu=\inf_{0<\mu(S)<1}\mu^+(S)/\min\{\mu(S),1-\mu(S)\}\). KLS asserts a positive universal lower bound on this expansion after isotropic normalization. A small value describes a separator with little boundary relative to the masses on its sides.

Notation changes across sources: Lee and Vempala’s survey uses its isoperimetric symbol for expansion itself, while Klartag and Letwin use \(\psi_\mu=1/h_\mu\), the reciprocal. With the latter convention, \(\psi_\mu^2\) and \(C_{\mathrm P}(\mu)\) differ by at most universal factors for log-concave measures, as recalled in Klartag’s equation (1.4). Thus an upper bound \(O((\log n)^{1/4})\) on the reciprocal expansion means an upper bound \(O(\sqrt{\log n})\) on the Poincaré constant, rather than the same exponent.

The original algorithmic motivation was sampling by random walks: poor expansion can slow movement between substantial parts of a convex body. The Lee–Vempala survey explains how sampling supports volume estimation, integration and optimization. These algorithmic consequences also depend on access to the input body or density, initialization and the chosen walk; the analytic inequality alone is not a complete computational-cost statement.

Klartag and Lehec’s 2022 Theorem 1.1 gives a polylogarithmic upper bound on reciprocal expansion, with exponent five in that paper. This broke the earlier subpolynomial dimension dependence. It is a historical bound, not a dimension-free resolution.

Klartag’s 2023 Theorem 1.2 improves reciprocal expansion to \(O(\sqrt{\log n})\), hence \(C_{\mathrm P}(\mu)=O(\log n)\). These logarithmic estimates are stated for \(n\ge2\); no formula involving \(\log1=0\) is asserted for the one-dimensional case.

Klartag and Lehec’s thin-shell paper, first posted in 2025 and revised in February 2026, proves \(\operatorname{Var}(\|X\|_2^2)\le a n\) and consequently \(\mathbb E(\|X\|_2-\sqrt n)^2\le a\) for a universal \(a\) and isotropic log-concave \(X\). These results control particular radial observables. Their relation to the now resolved slicing problem does not turn them into the full inequality for every locally Lipschitz function.

Chen and Klartag’s July 2026 preprint states the sharp radial bound \(\operatorname{Var}(\|X\|_2^2)\le8n\), with equality for independent centered exponential coordinates. The statement of Theorem 1.1 was inspected, but its complete new proof was not independently verified here. This optimizes the thin-shell constant, not the universal Poincaré constant over all test functions.

Letwin’s preprint of 27 July 2026 states \(\operatorname{Var}(X^{\mathsf T}MX)\le2\mathbb E\|\nabla(X^{\mathsf T}MX)\|_2^2\) for every real symmetric matrix \(M\), where \(X\) is isotropic and log-concave. It derives \(\psi_n=O((\log n)^{1/4})\) for \(n\ge2\), where \(\psi_n=\sup_\mu\psi_\mu\) over the measures in dimension \(n\). Its general-function consequence is \(C_{\mathrm P}(\mu)=O(\sqrt{\log n})\), which still grows. The paper’s new proof was not independently verified in this review.

Zhang’s sampling preprint, revised on 5 September 2026, still explicitly calls KLS open. It claims an improved mixing theorem for hit-and-run, the walk that chooses a random line through its current point and then a uniform point on the chord inside the body. The result requires a warm initial distribution, whose density is bounded by a finite multiple of the uniform target density, and retains dependence on the KLS constant. Resolving that mixing-time question is therefore distinct from proving a universal Poincaré bound.

cards.title: Gupta–Newman–Rabinovich–Sinclair conjecture
cards.formal: For every fixed finite simple graph H, is there a finite constant \(C_{H}\ge 1\) such that, for every finite connected simple undirected H-minor-free graph G with strictly positive real edge lengths, its shortest-path metric \(d_{G}\) admits a map \(f:V(G)\to \mathbb{R} ^{m}\) into some finite-dimensional \(\ell\)\(_{1}\) space satisfying \(d_{G}(u,v)\le \Vert f(u)- f(v)\Vert _{1}\le C_{H} d_{G}(u,v)\) for all vertices u,v?
cards.definitions: H-minor-free means that deleting vertices and edges and contracting edges of G cannot produce a graph isomorphic to H, after removing loops and duplicate edges. The length of a path is the sum of its edge lengths, and \(d_{G}(u,v)\) is the minimum path length. In \(\mathbb{R} ^{m}, \Vert x- y\Vert _{1}=\sum_{j=1}^{m} |x_{j}- y_{j}|\). The displayed inequalities normalize the embedding to be noncontracting; permitting a common scaling factor gives the same distortion notion. The constant \(C_{H}\) may depend on the excluded graph H, but must be independent of |\(V(G)|\), the edge lengths and their ratio. The target dimension m and the map f may depend on the entire weighted graph and have no computational or dimension bound. This is an existence question for all vertex pairs simultaneously. It concerns undirected shortest-path distances themselves, without a snowflake transformation, average-pair guarantee or restriction to selected terminals.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: Determine whether excluded graph minors exactly prevent unbounded \(\ell\)\(_{1}\) distortion and multicommodity flow–cut gaps in proper minor-closed graph families.

importance.reason: A central link between graph minor structure, metric embeddings and the quality of the basic sparsest-cut relaxation, already open in the planar case.

cards.status_note: The planar constant-distortion case remains explicitly open in the checked May 2026 notes. Restricted-family and face-cover results, including February 2026 exact values for \(K_{2},_{n}\), do not settle arbitrary fixed-minor-free metrics. The inherited fixed-treewidth approximation theorem uses a stronger relaxation and expressly does not prove a flow–cut-gap bound. No general settlement found through 11 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: The conjecture asks whether excluding a fixed graph minor removes every large-scale obstruction to representing graph distances as sums of coordinate differences. The graph can have arbitrarily many vertices and very unequal edge lengths. Its topology supplies the restriction, while the conclusion concerns the metric generated by all those lengths. Gupta, Newman, Rabinovich and Sinclair formulate this connection in their work on cuts, trees and \(\ell\)\(_{1}\) embeddings.

The target \(\ell\)\(_{1}\) space is useful because its finite metrics are nonnegative combinations of cut metrics. A cut metric assigns distance one to pairs separated by a chosen vertex subset and zero to other pairs. Coordinates can be decomposed by thresholding their values, producing precisely such cuts. Thus an \(\ell\)\(_{1}\) embedding replaces a complicated distance function by weighted separation tests that are closely connected to graph partitioning.

Trees give a concrete exact example. Root a weighted tree and assign one coordinate to each edge. For that coordinate, give a vertex the edge’s length if it lies below the edge and zero otherwise. Two vertices differ in exactly the coordinates corresponding to their unique connecting path. Their \(\ell\)\(_{1}\) distance therefore equals their original tree distance. Cycles allow competing shortest paths, which makes a common coordinate representation much harder.

The equivalent flow formulation compares two bounds on simultaneous routing. A concurrent flow routes the same fraction of every specified pair’s demand through a capacitated graph, splitting traffic among paths when useful. Every cut bounds that fraction by its available capacity divided by the demand it separates. GNRS predicts that, on any fixed-minor-free family, the best cut bound exceeds the achievable concurrent-flow value by at most a family-dependent constant, for arbitrary nonnegative demands.

Arbitrary demands are essential. Restricting to uniform demand between all vertex pairs gives an easier problem with stronger known results. Likewise, the capacity graph can be minor-free while demand pairs connect vertices in any pattern. Requiring the demands themselves to form a planar graph would change the target. The geometric formulation avoids these auxiliary conventions by requiring distance preservation for every vertex pair.

The planar case remains a central unresolved test. Rao’s general guarantee is \(O(\sqrt{\log  n})\) distortion for n-vertex planar metrics, and Chekuri’s May 2026 lecture notes still list a constant bound as open. No growing lower bound for planar metrics is known in that account. Both a constant upper bound and a superconstant counterexample would therefore represent a substantial change in understanding.

Several restricted families do satisfy constant distortion bounds. The original work handles series-parallel graphs. Lee and Sidiropoulos prove a stronger random-tree embedding result for graphs of any fixed pathwidth k, with distortion depending only on k. Their theorem establishes GNRS for minor-closed families that exclude a tree. Fixed pathwidth is a substantial additional restriction and does not include all graphs of fixed treewidth.

This last distinction exposes a common pitfall in reading algorithmic progress. Chlamtac, Krauthgamer and Raghavendra obtain constant-factor sparsest-cut approximation on every fixed-treewidth class using the Sherali–Adams hierarchy. They explicitly explain that their stronger relaxation does not establish a constant gap for the ordinary concurrent-flow LP. Thus the inherited paper is important context and an algorithmic success, but it is not a proof of the bounded-treewidth case of GNRS.

Filtser improves a terminal-sensitive planar bound: when the terminals can be covered by \(\gamma\) faces of a planar drawing, their metric embeds with distortion \(O(\sqrt{\log (\gamma +1)})\). The added one simply handles the single-face case in asymptotic notation. This is constant for fixed \(\gamma\) and recovers the familiar n-dependent bound when all vertices require many faces. The 2024 journal-online publication refines which geometric parameter creates the loss.

There is also recent exact progress inside small planar families. Mori’s February 2026 preprint calculates the worst-over-edge-lengths distortion of \(K_{2},_{n}\) as \((3k- 2)/(2k- 1)\), where \(k=\lceil n/2\rceil\). The values approach \(3/2\). This demonstrates a nontrivial bounded loss in an infinite family, rather than a counterexample with distortion growing without bound. Such examples help test the sharpness and limitations of proposed embedding mechanisms.

A solution would connect a qualitative structural restriction—excluding one fixed minor—to a uniform quantitative statement about all distances and all concurrent-routing instances. It would explain whether the logarithmic losses in current general embedding arguments are unavoidable on these graph families. The question remains meaningful independently of how efficiently the embedding can be constructed.

sentences: The GNRS conjecture asks how faithfully shortest-path distances in graphs excluding a fixed minor can be represented in \(\ell\)\(_{1}\).
The graph may have arbitrary positive edge lengths, and every pair of vertices must be preserved within a constant factor.
This constant may depend on the excluded minor but cannot grow with the graph.
Because \(\ell\)\(_{1}\) metrics decompose into weighted cuts, the question also governs multicommodity flow–cut gaps.
Even the planar case tests whether a strong topological restriction is enough to remove all growing distortion.

cards.context:
The conjecture asks whether excluding a fixed graph minor removes every large-scale obstruction to representing graph distances as sums of coordinate differences. The graph can have arbitrarily many vertices and very unequal edge lengths. Its topology supplies the restriction, while the conclusion concerns the metric generated by all those lengths. Gupta, Newman, Rabinovich and Sinclair formulate this connection in their work on cuts, trees and \(\ell\)\(_{1}\) embeddings.

The target \(\ell\)\(_{1}\) space is useful because its finite metrics are nonnegative combinations of cut metrics. A cut metric assigns distance one to pairs separated by a chosen vertex subset and zero to other pairs. Coordinates can be decomposed by thresholding their values, producing precisely such cuts. Thus an \(\ell\)\(_{1}\) embedding replaces a complicated distance function by weighted separation tests that are closely connected to graph partitioning.

Trees give a concrete exact example. Root a weighted tree and assign one coordinate to each edge. For that coordinate, give a vertex the edge’s length if it lies below the edge and zero otherwise. Two vertices differ in exactly the coordinates corresponding to their unique connecting path. Their \(\ell\)\(_{1}\) distance therefore equals their original tree distance. Cycles allow competing shortest paths, which makes a common coordinate representation much harder.

The equivalent flow formulation compares two bounds on simultaneous routing. A concurrent flow routes the same fraction of every specified pair’s demand through a capacitated graph, splitting traffic among paths when useful. Every cut bounds that fraction by its available capacity divided by the demand it separates. GNRS predicts that, on any fixed-minor-free family, the best cut bound exceeds the achievable concurrent-flow value by at most a family-dependent constant, for arbitrary nonnegative demands.

Arbitrary demands are essential. Restricting to uniform demand between all vertex pairs gives an easier problem with stronger known results. Likewise, the capacity graph can be minor-free while demand pairs connect vertices in any pattern. Requiring the demands themselves to form a planar graph would change the target. The geometric formulation avoids these auxiliary conventions by requiring distance preservation for every vertex pair.

The planar case remains a central unresolved test. Rao’s general guarantee is \(O(\sqrt{\log  n})\) distortion for n-vertex planar metrics, and Chekuri’s May 2026 lecture notes still list a constant bound as open. No growing lower bound for planar metrics is known in that account. Both a constant upper bound and a superconstant counterexample would therefore represent a substantial change in understanding.

Several restricted families do satisfy constant distortion bounds. The original work handles series-parallel graphs. Lee and Sidiropoulos prove a stronger random-tree embedding result for graphs of any fixed pathwidth k, with distortion depending only on k. Their theorem establishes GNRS for minor-closed families that exclude a tree. Fixed pathwidth is a substantial additional restriction and does not include all graphs of fixed treewidth.

This last distinction exposes a common pitfall in reading algorithmic progress. Chlamtac, Krauthgamer and Raghavendra obtain constant-factor sparsest-cut approximation on every fixed-treewidth class using the Sherali–Adams hierarchy. They explicitly explain that their stronger relaxation does not establish a constant gap for the ordinary concurrent-flow LP. Thus the inherited paper is important context and an algorithmic success, but it is not a proof of the bounded-treewidth case of GNRS.

Filtser improves a terminal-sensitive planar bound: when the terminals can be covered by \(\gamma\) faces of a planar drawing, their metric embeds with distortion \(O(\sqrt{\log (\gamma +1)})\). The added one simply handles the single-face case in asymptotic notation. This is constant for fixed \(\gamma\) and recovers the familiar n-dependent bound when all vertices require many faces. The 2024 journal-online publication refines which geometric parameter creates the loss.

There is also recent exact progress inside small planar families. Mori’s February 2026 preprint calculates the worst-over-edge-lengths distortion of \(K_{2},_{n}\) as \((3k- 2)/(2k- 1)\), where \(k=\lceil n/2\rceil\). The values approach \(3/2\). This demonstrates a nontrivial bounded loss in an infinite family, rather than a counterexample with distortion growing without bound. Such examples help test the sharpness and limitations of proposed embedding mechanisms.

A solution would connect a qualitative structural restriction—excluding one fixed minor—to a uniform quantitative statement about all distances and all concurrent-routing instances. It would explain whether the logarithmic losses in current general embedding arguments are unavoidable on these graph families. The question remains meaningful independently of how efficiently the embedding can be constructed.

cards.title: Unknot recognition in polynomial time
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic Turing algorithm and a constant c such that, on every explicit combinatorial knot diagram D of encoding length N, the algorithm decides in \(O((N+1)^{c})\) bit operations whether the represented knot in the 3-sphere is ambient isotopic to the unknot?
cards.definitions: A knot is a tame embedding of one circle into \(S^{3}\); the unknot is the isotopy class of a round circle. Ambient isotopy means a continuous family of homeomorphisms of \(S^{3}\) starting at the identity and carrying one embedded circle to the other at its endpoint. A diagram is a generic projection with transverse double crossings and specified over/under information. Encode it by an explicitly listed connected 4-regular planar multigraph, including loops when needed, its cyclic orders of half-edges at vertices, a distinguished outer face and the overpassing pair of opposite half-edges at each crossing. Tracing the opposite pairs must give one component. A separate constant-size encoding represents the crossing-free circle. The embedding is required to be a valid sphere embedding; malformed encodings may be rejected by polynomial-time combinatorial checks. If the diagram has n crossings, a standard such encoding has \(O(n \log (n+1))\) bits. The complexity parameter is the supplied encoding length N, not the minimum crossing number among equivalent diagrams. The input is explicit rather than a compressed description of an exponentially larger diagram. No disk, simplification sequence, knot invariant, auxiliary advice or promise of triviality is supplied. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: Determine whether triviality of an explicitly given knot can be decided efficiently, a foundational test of the gap between topological certificates and algorithms.

importance.reason: A central algorithmic topology problem in NP∩coNP; a fresh claimed polynomial-time solution makes precise formulation and validation especially valuable.

cards.status_note: Musick’s 6 September 2026 preprint claims a polynomial-time solution. Its correctness has not been independently established in this review, so the card is not labelled either a settled theorem or an unqualified open problem. Established certificates and earlier algorithmic results are distinguished from this new claim. Checked through 11 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: Status requires special care: Chad Musick’s preprint of 6 September 2026 claims a positive answer in Corollary 1. Its route is a polynomial-time construction of a locally minimal bridge presentation using compressed descriptions, followed by an existing characterization of bridge presentations of the unknot. I checked the claim and its main proof dependencies, but have not independently verified the local-minimality argument or compressed-update complexity. The card is therefore marked uncertain pending validation of this fresh claimed resolution.

The underlying task is deceptively simple: determine whether a closed loop can be untangled without cutting it or passing one strand through another. A diagram can contain many crossings that are artifacts of its projection. Looking complicated does not prove knottedness, while repeatedly removing visible twists can get stuck on a diagram that still represents the unknot. The input can be deliberately chosen to frustrate familiar simplification strategies.

The chosen representation makes the computational question independent of numerical geometry. Coordinates, thickness, physical forces and drawing quality do not enter the running time. Cyclic orders record the planar embedding, and the crossing data tell us which strand passes over the other. The task concerns the topology represented by those finite combinatorial data, not the visual complexity of a particular rendering.

Hass, Lagarias and Pippenger prove that unknot recognition belongs to NP using normal-surface techniques. Informally, an unknot bounds an embedded disk, and a suitable disk can be encoded compactly through its intersections with tetrahedra in a triangulation. Large counts are stored in binary. The existence of a polynomial-size verifiable certificate gives an upper bound on nondeterministic complexity, while finding such a certificate may still require substantial search.

Lackenby proves that knottedness also belongs to NP, so unknot recognition lies in coNP as well. This is an unconditional theorem, unlike earlier approaches that required the generalized Riemann hypothesis. It places the problem in \(\mathrm{NP}\cap \mathrm{coNP}\) and makes ordinary NP-completeness unlikely: an NP-hard language in coNP would imply \(\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}\). Membership in both classes does not itself give a polynomial-time decision algorithm.

There is another strong certificate theorem. Lackenby proves that any n-crossing unknot diagram can be reduced to a crossing-free circle using at most \((236n)^{11}\) Reidemeister moves. These are local diagram changes preserving the knot type. The result bounds the length of a successful route; it does not identify which route to choose efficiently. Enumerating a branching collection of polynomial-length routes can still take exponential time.

In 2021, Lackenby announced an algorithm with quasipolynomial running time. The SoCG 2025 source still describes this as an announcement, and the checked author webpage lists talks on it. I retain that attribution rather than presenting a fully checked published proof. Quasipolynomial time, of the form \(\exp ((\log  N)^{O(1)})\), can be much smaller than exponential time while remaining above a fixed polynomial bound.

Practical algorithms illustrate a different kind of progress. He, Sedgwick and Spreer’s SoCG 2025 paper builds knot factorisation machinery around edge-ideal triangulations and normal-surface crushing. Their introduction notes that Regina’s unknot-recognition implementation behaves polynomially in experiments but has an exponential worst-case bound. Strong performance on a census or on difficult examples is useful evidence for implementation design, without controlling every possible input diagram.

Lackenby’s July 2026 preprint gives a new algorithm through incompressible surfaces and hierarchies. For a nontrivial knot, the boundary of its exterior is incompressible; for the unknot it is compressible. This turns knot recognition into a question about surfaces in a 3-manifold. The paper’s Section 9 explicitly leaves key hierarchy-length and surface-complexity parameters unbounded in terms of the input, so it does not establish polynomial running time.

The central challenge is algorithmic control over global topology. A small diagram may hide the disk or decomposition that makes its type evident. Good certificates show that concise explanations exist; an efficient recognizer would show how to decide without searching an uncontrolled space of explanations. Any verified polynomial-time solution, including the new claimed one, would resolve a basic benchmark of computational topology and change how we understand this gap.
