cards.context:
A Fourier coefficient records correlation with a parity of selected input bits. Squaring these correlations gives a probability distribution on subsets of the coordinates. Its Shannon entropy measures dispersion among subsets; total influence is the expected cardinality of a subset from that distribution. The conjecture asks whether being the spectrum of a Boolean-valued function forces a universal linear relation between these two quantities.

This is not a generic fact about probability distributions on subsets. A distribution uniform on the n singleton sets has entropy \(\log _{2} n\) but expected set size one. It is the squared Fourier spectrum of the normalized real function \(g(x)=(x_{1}+\cdots +x_{n})/\sqrt{n}\), which is generally not Boolean. Conversely, a parity of all n inputs has entropy zero and total influence n. These examples explain both why Boolean-valuedness matters and why the proposed inequality has only one direction.

If FEI holds with constant \(C\), then for every \(0<\delta<1\), some family \(\mathcal T\) of at most \(2^{CI(f)/\delta}\) subsets satisfies \(\sum_{S\notin\mathcal T}q_S\le\delta\). Equivalently, retaining those Fourier coefficients approximates \(f\) with mean squared error at most \(\delta\) under the uniform measure. The support bound depends on the accuracy parameter; a guarantee independent of accuracy is not being asserted.

O’Donnell, Wright and Zhou prove FEI for symmetric Boolean functions, which are invariant under every permutation of coordinates, and for read-once decision trees, where the variables used in the two branches at each query are disjoint. The read-once condition is stronger than merely avoiding a repeated query along each path. Their application to a disjunction of \(m\ge2\) conjunctions of literals uses \(I(f)=O(\log m)\): FEI would give concentration on \(m^{O(1/\delta)}\) Fourier coefficients for each fixed error \(\delta\). This is a version of Mansour’s conjecture, not its stronger proposed logarithmic dependence on inverse error. It concerns uniform-measure spectral concentration and the associated query-learning setting.

Han’s Theorem 1 bounds \(H(f)\) by an absolute constant times \(I(f)+\sum_i I_i(f)\log_2(1/I_i(f))\), with zero terms when \(I_i(f)=0\). The journal version appeared online on 20 December 2024 in Combinatorica volume 45 (2025). The 10 December 2025 arXiv revision adds an acknowledgement of related prior work by Keller, Mossel and Schlank. The extra coordinate-entropy term can exceed a constant times total influence, so this bound leaves FEI open.

The earlier Keller–Mossel–Schlank paper already gives \(H(f)\le\sum_i h_2(I_i(f))\) in Claim 4.1, where \(h_2(t)=-t\log_2 t-(1-t)\log_2(1-t)\) with zero endpoint terms. The claim supplies the same general kind of coordinate-entropy control and applies beyond Boolean-valued spectra after normalization. This is why a later proof or refinement of that weaker bound must be distinguished from resolving FEI. Min-entropy, \(-\log_2\max_S q_S\), concerns just the largest coefficient and is a different, weaker target than Shannon entropy.

González, MacManus and Pereyra’s revision of 9 June 2026 reports FEI for the defined \(\delta\)-tribes class and for classes with recursive separation properties. The separation theorems retain hypotheses on their terminal functions and constants; they are not assertions for all monotone functions or unrestricted decision trees. The paper also exhibits failure of a stronger inequality involving a prescribed splitting coordinate. Those examples satisfy FEI, so that failure is not a counterexample to this card’s target.

Slote’s 2 August 2026 preprint reports a counterexample to the quantum extension, whose inputs are Hermitian unitary operators and whose coefficients come from tensor products of Pauli matrices. Theorems 1 and 5 give operators supported on degree-\(d\) Pauli terms with entropy \(\Theta(d^2)\) and influence \(d\). Classical Boolean functions form a restricted diagonal case of that operator setting. The operators constructed in the theorem therefore do not supply scalar Boolean counterexamples. The full new construction was not independently verified in this review.

A follow-up by Slote, Volberg and Zhang, revised 6 August 2026, also treats quantum counterexamples. Its §6.6 reports Hermitian involutions with total influence below two and spectral entropy \(\log_2 n+O(1)\) in its family parameter. The underlying auxiliary scalar functions take complex values of modulus one, rather than only the real values \(-1\) and \(1\). That domain change is essential, and §6 still describes classical FEI as open. These theorem scopes were checked without independently certifying the full proofs.

A positive solution would expose a strong restriction on the spectra of every Boolean computation, independently of how that computation is represented. A negative solution would identify Boolean functions whose spectral information greatly exceeds their sensitivity to input changes. Either outcome would clarify a basic link between combinatorial stability, harmonic analysis and the possibility of learning from sparse spectral descriptions.

benchmark_focus.reason: A longstanding, broadly consequential conjecture in Boolean function analysis, with direct learning-theory implications and active 2026 progress that still leaves the universal classical inequality open.

cards.title: Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis
cards.formal: For every real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), does there exist an integer \(q\ge3\) such that no q-SAT decider A has a bound \(t_A(F)\le C\,2^{(1-\varepsilon)n(F)}(L(F)+1)^d\) for every valid q-CNF formula F, for any fixed integers \(C\ge1,d\ge0\)? The width q may depend on epsilon but is fixed independently of the input. Equivalently, is \(\lim_{q\to\infty}s_q=1\)? This is the deterministic Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis.
cards.definitions: Fix an integer clause-width bound \(q\ge 3\). A q-CNF formula is a finite list of clauses, each a finite list of at most q literals. A literal is a variable \(x_i\) or its negation \(\neg x_i\), with \(1\le i\le n\). The variables that occur are exactly \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), so n counts distinct variables, not clauses or input bits. Repeated literals, repeated clauses and clauses containing both signs of a variable are allowed. A Boolean assignment satisfies the formula if every clause has at least one true literal. An empty clause is false; the empty conjunction is true and has n=0. For a completely specified binary encoding, let \(\operatorname{code}(a)\), for a nonnegative integer a, be \(1^b0\) followed by the b-bit binary expansion of a+1, where \(b=\lfloor\log_2(a+1)\rfloor+1\). Encode n and the number m of clauses with this code, then each clause by its coded length followed by its literals. Each literal is a sign bit (0 for positive, 1 for negated) and the code of its variable index. All indicated lists must be fully present, with no trailing bits, valid indices and every declared variable occurring. Let L be the complete bit length. Ill-formed strings, including clauses wider than q, are rejected. No density, satisfiability-count, occurrence or input-distribution promise is imposed. A q-SAT decider A is one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program and fixed finite tape alphabets, a read-only input tape and initially blank work tapes. Each transition reads or writes only the cells at the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. The total transition count includes parsing, input access and all internal work. A must halt on all inputs, decide satisfiability exactly on valid q-CNF formulas, and reject malformed strings in polynomial time in their length. It receives no advice, random bits, quantum operations, oracle or precomputed instance information. The machine may depend on the fixed q. For a valid formula F, let \(t_A(F)\) be its runtime and \(n(F),L(F)\) its variable count and bit length. An exponent \(\alpha\ge 0\) is attainable at width q if there exist such a decider A and fixed integers \(C\ge1,d\ge0\) with \(t_A(F)\le C\,2^{\alpha n(F)}(L(F)+1)^d\) for every valid q-CNF formula F. The constants are independent of F. Define \(s_q\) as the infimum of all attainable exponents. This set is nonempty because exhaustive assignment testing gives an attainable exponent 1, so \(0\le s_q\le1\). The infimum need not itself be attainable. Polynomial factors in L remain explicit, including when clauses are repeated many times. The chosen explicit syntax and malformed-input normalization do not impose a new satisfiability promise; they fix the bit model for the source’s exponential-rate question. The sequence \(s_q\) is nondecreasing: a decider for width q+1 also decides the width-q restriction after checking its syntax. Since every \(s_q\le1\), its limit exists. The quantified statement says that no fixed positive saving from the exponent 1 works for all fixed widths. Its negation is that there exists one real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) such that for each integer \(q\ge3\) there are a q-SAT decider \(A_q\) and constants \(C_q,d_q\) with \(t_{A_q}(F)\le C_q2^{(1-\varepsilon)n(F)}(L(F)+1)^{d_q}\) for every q-CNF formula F. The algorithm and polynomial factor may depend on q and the selected epsilon. There is no added requirement of one algorithm receiving q as an input, nor of an effective procedure generating \(A_q\) from q. Each individual machine is uniform over its formula inputs. Infima need not be attained; the equivalence uses the available slack between a limit below 1 and 1.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed deterministic all-width proposition, equivalently a proof that \(\lim_{q\to\infty}s_q=1\) or that this limit is strictly below 1. A refutation must establish one positive exponential saving valid at every fixed width, with the algorithm and polynomial factors allowed to depend on that width. A positive answer must exclude such a shared saving. Improvement at finitely many widths, a randomized algorithm, or a lower bound only under another unproved hypothesis does not by itself meet this criterion. The target is a yes/no assertion about the limit, not its numerical approximation.
cards.why: SETH is one of the main assumptions used to explain why specific polynomial running-time exponents resist improvement. Settling it would test the foundation of a broad network of tight conditional bounds in strings, graphs, data structures, and exact exponential-time algorithms.

importance.reason: A principal organizing hypothesis of fine-grained complexity, connecting exact SAT complexity to tight running-time barriers across many algorithmic areas.

progress.text: Impagliazzo and Paturi study the optimal exponential rates of fixed-width satisfiability and their limiting rate, proving relations among widths under ETH. They do not prove the limiting rate equals one.
The textbook states deterministic SETH as Conjecture 14.2, distinguishes separate fixed-width algorithms from a single unrestricted CNF-SAT algorithm, and proves that SETH implies ETH.
Vassilevska Williams surveys fine-grained reductions from satisfiability hypotheses to polynomial-time problems, explicitly tracking the relevant models and forms of hypotheses.

Jiang and Cai report the randomized general-3-SAT bound \(O^*(1.307031578^n)\) and a separate stronger Unique-3-SAT bound. Their Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2 concern fixed width; these preprint claims do not settle the deterministic all-width hypothesis.

context_blocks.text: Exhaustive search tries all \(2^{n}\) assignments and checks the formula each time. Restricting clause width supports much faster algorithms, particularly for small k. SETH accommodates these speedups: it says that no positive constant saving in the exponent survives uniformly across arbitrarily large fixed widths. It does not assert that 3-SAT needs essentially \(2^{n}\) time.

The order of quantifiers separates this statement from several nearby claims. A \(2^{0.9n}\)-time algorithm for every fixed k would refute SETH even if the polynomial factors and implementations depended on k. A family of bounds \(2^{(1- 1/k)n}\) would be compatible with it. A fast algorithm for unrestricted CNF-SAT would also refute it, but the failure of such an unrestricted algorithm is not the definition being used here.

ETH asks for a positive optimal exponential rate already at width three; SETH additionally asks that the rates approach one as width grows. Sparsification relates bounded-width formulas to bounded-density formulas and helps transfer these hypotheses through reductions. It does not make the two hypotheses equivalent. Proving either would go beyond \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\), which by itself allows intermediate running times such as \(2^{\sqrt{n}}\).

Fine-grained reductions turn this hypothesis into precise conditional barriers for familiar polynomial-time problems, including Orthogonal Vectors, edit distance, and graph-distance questions. The reduction must preserve the intended exponential saving, not merely be polynomial-time as in an NP-hardness reduction. When a reduction or resulting algorithm uses randomness, the corresponding randomized hypothesis must be tracked separately.

Jiang and Cai’s July 2026 preprint reports randomized bounds \(O^*(1.306969598^n)\) for Unique-3-SAT and \(O^*(1.307031578^n)\) for general 3-SAT, where \(O^*\) suppresses polynomial input factors. These are stated preprint results whose proof and numerical certification have not been independently verified here. In either case, fixed width three and internal randomness differ from a deterministic saving that holds at every fixed width.

The 2015 textbook explicitly cautions that its limiting-rate definition is more precise than the informal question about one unrestricted CNF-SAT algorithm. A negative answer may consist of separate algorithms for all fixed widths, sharing one positive saving in the exponential rate but not necessarily a uniform generator or a common polynomial input factor.

sentences: SETH asks whether the optimal deterministic exponential rates for fixed-width satisfiability approach one as the allowed width grows.
Every proposed constant saving from exhaustive search must fail at some fixed width.

Faster algorithms for width three, including recent randomized ones, do not meet that requirement.
The hypothesis underlies many precise conditional lower bounds, including problems whose algorithms already run in polynomial time.

cards.title: Truly subcubic APSP
cards.formal: Is there a uniform randomized algorithm \(A\), a fixed rational constant \(0<\varepsilon\le1\), and a fixed constant \(C>0\) such that, on every directed \(n\)-vertex graph with arbitrary real edge weights and no negative-weight cycle, \(A\) outputs the entire exact shortest-distance matrix with probability at least \(2/3\), while every run takes at most \(Cn^{3-\varepsilon}\) steps? Here \(n\ge2\), and steps are measured in the comparison-addition real RAM with logarithmic-size index words defined below. The same program, exponent improvement and time constant must work for every graph size and every real weight assignment.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated algorithm-existence proposition or its full logical negation in this exact machine model. A positive proof must exhibit one finite uniform program and fixed constants, prove the promised-graph distance semantics and joint correctness probability, and charge every operation to the worst-case \(Cn^{3-\varepsilon}\) bound. A negative proof must rule out every such program and every fixed positive exponent saving, including randomized programs.

A result for bounded integer weights, a restricted graph family, approximate distances, a single source, or additional accurate predictions does not settle this target. Neither does a lower bound restricted to one reduction method or to machines lacking the permitted word operations. An unproved APSP hardness hypothesis cannot serve as the proof of its own consequence here. A bound \(n^3/f(n)\) with only a subpolynomial saving \(f(n)=n^{o(1)}\) does not establish a fixed exponent saving; expected running time alone does not establish the specified worst-case bound. There is no additive or multiplicative error allowance in the distance output.
cards.why: All-pairs distances are a basic graph primitive. A fixed improvement over the cubic exponent would also change the complexity of several equivalent path, matrix and weighted-triangle problems. Their reductions make the exact weight and machine assumptions essential to interpreting claimed improvements.
cards.definitions:
The vertex set is \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The input gives \(n\) and an \(n\times n\) adjacency matrix in vertex order. Each entry has a presence flag and, when present, one exact finite real weight. Thus there is at most one edge for each ordered pair; self-loops are allowed. Missing edges have no weight and are represented by the flag, not by a large finite number. There is no bound on the magnitude, sign or precision of a real weight. The graph is promised to have no directed cycle of negative total weight, including negative self-loops.

A finite directed walk \((v_0,\ldots,v_k)\) has weight \(\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}w(v_i,v_{i+1})\). The empty walk from a vertex to itself has weight zero. For each ordered pair \((u,v)\), the distance \(d_G(u,v)\) is the minimum weight of a walk from \(u\) to \(v\), or the separate symbol \(+\infty\) if none exists. The no-negative-cycle promise ensures that every reachable minimum is finite and attained; nonnegative cycles can be removed, so a simple path suffices for distinct endpoints. In particular \(d_G(u,u)=0\). Zero-weight cycles and equal shortest distances are allowed. Output consists of all \(n^2\) exact distances in vertex-pair order, each a real value or an unreachable flag. Printing the vertices of every shortest path is not required.

The machine has one fixed finite program and two kinds of random-access memory cell: exact real cells and finite index-word cells. One real-cell load, store or copy, addition, subtraction, or comparison costs one step; comparison returns its trichotomy result as a word. These are the only operations inspecting real values. Real constants built into the finite program are restricted to \(0\) and \(1\); there are no arbitrary advice constants. A real value cannot be converted to its digits, an integer address, or its floor. Multiplication or division of real cells and operations packing several arbitrary reals into one word are not available.

For some fixed integer \(a\ge4\) chosen as part of the program's model, an index word has \(b(n)=\lceil a\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits. Word loads, stores, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, shifts, and addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{b(n)}\) cost one step. Unsigned integer quotient and remainder by a nonzero word also cost one step; division by zero is an invalid computation. A shift of at least \(b(n)\) positions returns zero. Addresses are words. All accessed cells must fit in this address range; a new work cell starts at zero and each access is charged. Word operations can process indices, counters and comparison results; they do not reveal the representation of a real edge weight. The input matrix and initially empty work memory are the only input-dependent initial state.

The randomized instruction obtains one fresh independent fair bit per step. All preprocessing, table construction, memory access, random-bit generation, input reading and output writing are charged to the same runtime. There is no nonuniform table supplied for free, extra prediction, oracle, parallel work unit or quantum operation. The bound is worst case over the input and every coin sequence. For each fixed promised graph, the probability that the whole output matrix is correct must be at least \(2/3\); separate success probabilities for individual entries are insufficient. A deterministic algorithm is included by ignoring the coins.

The bound depends on \(n\), not the bit length or magnitude of weights, because the real operations are exact primitives. This is a classical real-operation question, not an ordinary bit-time algorithm for arbitrary real encodings. Restricting \(\varepsilon\) to rational values in \((0,1]\) preserves existence of a fixed positive exponent saving; any positive saving implies a smaller such rational saving. No behavior is required on graphs violating the no-negative-cycle promise.

progress.text: Subcubic equivalences connect APSP to min-plus products, negative triangles and several other tasks; the full manuscript distinguishes integer-range reductions from its strongly polynomial randomized reduction.
Williams obtains randomized time \(n^3/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}\) on the real RAM; STOC publishes the result in 2014 and an expanded journal version appears in 2018.
The few-weights manuscript gives deterministic improvements under restrictions on the number of outgoing weights per vertex, with explicit weight-model conventions.
ICALP publishes the matrix-multiplication-time node-weighted zero-triangle result; independently weighted edges remain a different target.
The prediction-assisted APSP preprint gives a fixed exponent saving when its supplied certificate has sufficiently few erroneous or unverifiable pairs.
The black-box-reduction preprint establishes barriers for reductions uniform over arbitrary triangle relations; it does not establish an unrestricted APSP lower bound.

cards.status_note: Source-open evidence checked on 15 September 2026. The published July 2026 node-weighted-triangle introduction and July prediction-assisted APSP preprint explicitly retain the general fixed-exponent challenge. The inspected few-weight algorithms, extra-prediction bounds and August black-box reduction barriers do not resolve the uniform randomized comparison-addition real-RAM question stated here. Bounded current searches located no full matching solution claim. This is an individual formulation and source-scope review, not exhaustive certification of every cited proof or all later literature.

context_blocks.text: If the edges from u to v, u to z and z to v have weights 8, 5 and −2, and there are no other edges, then the shortest u-to-v distance is 3. Negative edges are compatible with a finite exact answer. By contrast, a negative cycle reachable on a u-to-v walk would make its weights unbounded below; the input promise excludes that case. An unreachable ordered pair is reported separately from every finite distance.

The corresponding min-plus matrix operation is \((X\star Y)_{ij}=\min_k(X_{ik}+Y_{kj})\). This uses minimum and addition, whereas ordinary matrix multiplication uses addition and multiplication. Vassilevska Williams and Williams establish subcubic equivalences among APSP, min-plus products, negative edge-weighted triangles and related tasks. Their integer-range theorem carries weight-length factors; Section 4.3 separately gives a randomized strongly polynomial reduction whose overhead depends on the matrix dimension instead. These equivalences preserve existence of some positive saving, not necessarily its exact exponent.

Williams gives a randomized real-RAM bound \(n^3/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}\), and a deterministic subpolynomial improvement with a different exponent in the denominator. These are substantial savings over cubic time. Nevertheless, for each fixed \(c>0\), the expression \(n^3/2^{c\sqrt{\log_2 n}}=n^{3-c/\sqrt{\log_2 n}}\) has an exponent tending to three. That bound alone does not establish \(O(n^{3-\varepsilon})\) for any fixed \(\varepsilon>0\). The algorithms permit ordinary computation on finite words as well as comparisons and additions of weights.

Abboud and coauthors study graphs with at most \(d\) distinct weights on the outgoing edges of each vertex. Their Theorem 1.4 gives a fixed exponent saving when \(d\le n^{3-\omega-\delta}\) for a fixed \(\delta>0\), where \(\omega\) is the ordinary matrix-multiplication exponent. This theorem is stated in their bounded-integer word-RAM setting. Theorem 1.2 for one outgoing weight per vertex also has an explicitly stated real-weight extension in Section 4.4. Neither statement covers unrestricted arbitrary real edge weights with up to \(n\) different outgoing weights per vertex.

Akmal and Fischer’s ICALP 2026 Theorem 1 solves zero-sum node-weighted triangle detection in \(O(\mathrm{MM}(n))\) time. Here a triangle’s value is the sum of three vertex weights, and \(\mathrm{MM}(n)\) denotes an admissible running-time bound for ordinary matrix multiplication, with the paper’s monotonicity convention. This is different from independently weighting every edge. The introduction explicitly retains the unresolved fixed-exponent improvement for minimum edge-weighted triangles. The paper uses \(\mathrm{MM}(n)\), rather than asserting that the infimum exponent \(\omega\) must be attained.

Polak and Schmidt’s July 2026 preprint gives an exact APSP algorithm with supplied prediction certificates and running time \(O(n^{2.83}+\eta n)\) for its chosen parameters. The error measure \(\eta\) counts vertex pairs whose induced distance estimates are incorrect or fail the paper’s verification condition. It can be as large as \(n^2\), so this guarantee can still be cubic. Obtaining a sufficiently accurate certificate at no charged cost is an additional input assumption, not a uniform worst-case solution of this card.

Sheffield, Vassilevska Williams and Xi’s August 2026 preprint proves limits on reductions that treat a triangle relation as a black box and must work for every such relation. Its Definition 1 makes this uniformity across relations essential. These limits concern the strength of a particular reduction model, not a lower bound excluding every algorithm for the fixed shortest-path problem.

cards.title: P versus BPP
cards.formal:
Does \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{BPP}\)? Equivalently, is the following statement true?
\[\forall L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad L\in\mathrm{BPP}\ \Longrightarrow\ L\in\mathrm P.\]
Here \(\mathrm{BPP}\) requires one randomized polynomial-time machine whose probability of a correct answer is at least \(2/3\) separately on every input, including both members and nonmembers of \(L\). The proposed deterministic machine must decide the same total language correctly on every input in polynomial time.
cards.definitions:
A language \(L\) is a set of finite binary strings; its membership bit is \(\mathbf1_L(x)\in\{0,1\}\). Put \(n=|x|\), allowing \(n=0\). Computation uses finite multitape Turing-machine programs over fixed finite tape alphabets. Each ordinary tape transition costs one step. A randomized transition may read at most one fresh independent unbiased bit. There is no oracle, advice, quantum operation, input distribution or promise excluding some inputs.

The condition \(L\in\mathrm{BPP}\) means that there exist one randomized program \(R\) and fixed positive integers \(C,d\) such that, with \(p(n)=C(n+1)^d\), both of the following hold for every \(x\):
\[\begin{gathered}
 R(x)\text{ halts within }p(n)\text{ steps on every random tape and outputs a bit},\\
 \Pr[R(x)=\mathbf1_L(x)]\ge 2/3.
\end{gathered}\]
The probability is only over the internal fair bits. An exact finite interpretation is to supply a uniformly distributed string \(z\in\{0,1\}^{p(n)}\), ignoring its unused suffix. The probability condition is then the integer inequality
\[3\bigl|\{z\in\{0,1\}^{p(n)}:R(x;z)=\mathbf1_L(x)\}\bigr|\ \ge\ 2\cdot 2^{p(n)}.\]
The time bound is worst case over both the input and every random tape, rather than an expectation. The error bound is pointwise: success on almost all inputs of a length does not suffice. The same constants apply at every length; an input-dependent exponent is not polynomial time in this definition.

The condition \(L\in\mathrm P\) means that there exist one deterministic program \(A\) and fixed positive integers \(C',d'\) such that for every binary string \(x\), the program halts within \(C'(|x|+1)^{d'}\) steps and outputs \(\mathbf1_L(x)\). Reading, writing, arithmetic and tape access all count toward time. The deterministic program and its constants may depend on the language and its randomized decider, but not on the particular input or its length.

The requested deterministic computation may use a different algorithm and a different polynomial exponent. The target does not require an effective compiler taking descriptions of randomized machines to deterministic ones. It asks for existence of a polynomial-time deterministic decider for each language in the class. Deterministic programs are also randomized programs that ignore their coins, so \(\mathrm P\subseteq\mathrm{BPP}\) holds directly. Sampling a distribution, returning a valid witness, and answering only promised inputs are different tasks from deciding this total membership bit.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated inclusion, or of its logical negation
\[\exists L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad L\in\mathrm{BPP}\ \land\ L\notin\mathrm P.\]
A positive proof must establish existence, correctness and a uniform polynomial time bound for a deterministic decider of every language satisfying the randomized definition. A negative proof must give one fixed language with a single randomized decider meeting the full pointwise error and worst-case polynomial time guarantees, and prove that no deterministic program with any fixed polynomial time bound decides that language.

A result conditional on an unproved hardness assumption, a nonuniform circuit simulation, an oracle separation, a promise-problem separation, or a simulation valid only at some lengths does not settle the target. A lower bound for one simulation rule or one generator family does not exclude every deterministic decider. The probability threshold is exact; this is a yes/no question with no numerical approximation tolerance.
cards.why: This asks whether independent random bits increase the set of total decision problems solvable efficiently. An equality would identify deterministic and randomized polynomial-time decision power; a separation would exhibit an inherent benefit of randomness even when a different deterministic algorithm is allowed.

importance.reason: The main general derandomization question for polynomial-time decision algorithms, with broad consequences for the role of randomness and for hardness-versus-randomness techniques.

The inspected 2019 book poses the total-language equality; the May 2026 primary derandomization results retain explicit hardness and structural assumptions. context_blocks.text: A randomized answer is allowed to be wrong with probability at most one third on any specified input. For example, correctness on 99% of all strings of each length would still fail this definition if a remaining string were always answered incorrectly. The uncertainty belongs to the machine’s internal choices, not to which inputs the user may supply.

Adleman’s theorem gives \(\mathrm{BPP}\subseteq\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{poly}\). Here \(\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{poly}\) allows a separate polynomial-size Boolean circuit at each input length, without requiring one efficient procedure that constructs these circuits. This is a nonuniform existence statement; the target requires one finite deterministic program for all lengths.

Impagliazzo and Wigderson prove a conditional equality: if a Boolean function computable in deterministic time \(2^{O(n)}\) has worst-case circuit complexity at least \(2^{\varepsilon n}\), for some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) and all sufficiently large \(n\), then \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{BPP}\). Circuit complexity here counts gates of unrestricted nonuniform Boolean circuits over a fixed complete finite basis that compute the function correctly on every input of that length. The exponential lower-bound hypothesis is part of the theorem; this is not an unconditional equality or a theorem assuming only \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\).

Doron, Moshkovitz, Oh and Zuckerman’s May 2026 preprint obtains finer conditional derandomization bounds for algorithms with a specified insensitivity property. For each fixed input, changing one uniformly chosen coin coordinate of a correct tape must rarely make the answer incorrect. Their two-sided version additionally constrains incorrect tapes that have a correct neighbor. Theorem 9.10 retains explicit circuit-hardness, insensitivity and error assumptions; these structural conditions are not properties required of every BPP program. The paper distinguishes hitting-set and pseudoentropy generators from general pseudorandom generators.

Tianrong Lin’s July 2026 revision states a direct claim of \(\mathrm P\subsetneq\mathrm{BPP}\) in Theorem 1.1, with additional claimed separations. That would answer this card negatively if its proof were valid. This review read the claimed theorem and checked its version history, but has not certified its proof or located independent primary validation in the bounded searches. It is therefore recorded as an unverified claim, and the card retains uncertain status.

cards.title: Optimal explicit pseudorandom generators for read-once branching programs
cards.formal:
Does there exist one deterministic finite-program algorithm \(A\) and absolute integers \(C,D\ge1\) with the following property? For every \(n,w\ge2\) and \(p\ge1\), all integers, the algorithm specifies an integer seed length \(s=s(n,w,p)\ge0\) and a function
\[G_{n,w,p}:\{0,1\}^{s}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{n}\]
with \(s\le Cq\), where \(q=\lceil\log _2 n\rceil+\lceil\log _2 w\rceil+p\), such that every length-\(n\), width-at-most-\(w\) ordered binary read-once branching program \(B\) satisfies
\[\left|\Pr_{u\sim U_s}[B(G_{n,w,p}(u))=1]-\Pr_{z\sim U_n}[B(z)=1]\right|\le 2^{-p}?\]
Here \(U_k\) is the uniform distribution on the \(2^k\) binary strings of length \(k\). Require \(A\) to compute both \(s(n,w,p)\) and any requested bit \(G_{n,w,p}(u)_i\), \(1\le i\le n\), in at most \(Dq\) work bits and \((nw2^p)^D\) steps per call, in the model below. The same algorithm, constants and generator family must work for every parameter triple and every permitted program.
cards.definitions:
A length-\(n\), width-at-most-\(w\) ordered binary read-once branching program consists of nonempty finite layers \(V_0,\ldots,V_n\), each of size at most \(w\), a start state in \(V_0\), an accepting subset of \(V_n\), and functions \(\delta_{i,b}:V_{i-1}\to V_i\) for \(1\le i\le n\), \(b\in\{0,1\}\). On input \(z\), the state is updated by \(\delta_{i,z_i}\) at step \(i\); \(B(z)=1\) exactly when the final state is accepting. The bit order is \(z_1,\ldots,z_n\). Transitions may merge states, including two equally labeled edges from distinct states; no regularity or permutation promise is imposed. The transition tables, start state and accepting subset are arbitrary finite, possibly nonuniform data. The generator receives none of them.

The algorithm is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program and a mode flag. In the seed-length mode its input is \((n,w,p)\) and its output is \(s(n,w,p)\) in binary. In the bit mode its input is \((n,w,p,u,i)\) and it outputs exactly one bit before halting. Integer parameters use canonical binary notation with separators; the seed is its full binary string, with leading zeroes retained. Inputs occupy read-only tapes whose heads are bounded by endmarkers. There is a fixed finite number of initially blank, semi-infinite work tapes over \(\{0,1,\square\}\), with heads moving by at most one cell per transition. Each distinct work-tape cell visited is charged two work bits, including blank cells. This fixed encoding of tape symbols only fixes a constant in the space bound. All counters, arithmetic, stored history and preprocessing are charged; output is write-only and cannot serve as storage. There is no advice, oracle, external clock or other uncounted memory. Each transition costs one time step. The required bounds hold on every valid call, for every seed and requested index. Only the requested bit must be output in bit mode; there is no requirement to store the whole length-\(n\) string.

Probabilities are exact uniform finite averages. In particular, a seed always has weight \(2^{-s}\), even if several seeds produce the same string; signed weights and externally assigned coefficients are not permitted. The parameter \(p\) controls additive error, not failure probability of a randomized construction: \(A\) itself is deterministic. With \(\varepsilon=2^{-p}\), the target is \(O(\log n+\log w+\log(1/\varepsilon))\) seed length and work space. Ceiling conventions change only constants. Arbitrary \(0<\varepsilon<1\) can be covered by a dyadic tolerance no larger than \(\varepsilon\). No compression requirement \(s<n\) is imposed in parameter regimes where the displayed allowance is already at least \(n\).
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existential proposition above or its full logical negation. An affirmative proof must specify a single finite program and universal constants, formalize its seed-length and bit computations, establish the stated worst-case resource bounds, and prove the additive-error inequality for every permitted program and every parameter triple. A negative proof must rule out every such uniform program and choice of constants; a limitation of one construction, one analysis or one restricted generator class is insufficient. The theorem must use the stated ordinary uniform-seed distribution and arbitrary merging transitions. A result solely for weighted generators, hitting sets or a restricted branching-program subclass does not meet this target.
cards.why: A solution would give a uniform optimal-seed pseudorandom distribution for arbitrary small-memory computations and imply L = BPL. It would close the central gap between the existence of short seeds and their computation in small space, beyond the structural restrictions and weighted approximations covered by current results.

context_blocks.text: A branching program models a stream computation that remembers only its current state. Its width \(w\) permits roughly \(\log_2 w\) memory bits, while its length \(n\) counts inspected input bits. The quantifiers require one distribution that works simultaneously for every allowed transition table. Computing a favorable distribution after seeing a particular table would answer a different question.

Short-seed distributions exist nonconstructively; in particular, seed length \(O(\log(n/\varepsilon))\) is known for width-\(n\), length-\(n\) programs. The unresolved issue is explicit computation with the required space bound. An optimal ordinary generator of the kind requested here would imply \(\mathrm L=\mathrm{BPL}\), the equality of deterministic and bounded-error randomized logarithmic-space decision classes. The card does not assert the converse implication.

The classical general bound is \(O(\log n\cdot\log(nw/\varepsilon))\) seed bits. For polynomial width and constant error, this becomes \(O(\log^2 n)\), whereas the requested bound is \(O(\log n)\). The September 2026 RANDOM paper still identifies this general gap, while distinguishing improvements in special width/length regimes.

Weighted generators approximate the acceptance probability by an average \(\mathbb E_u[\rho(u)B(G(u))]\), where \(\rho\) may take negative values. Hoza’s Theorem 1.5 obtains seed length \(O(\log(wn)\log n+\log(1/\varepsilon))\) for this relaxed object. Such weights are useful for deterministic estimates but do not define the ordinary sampled distribution required in this question.

Cheng–Wu’s July 2026 version improves weighted constructions across several parameter regimes. Its optimal-space simulation theorem concerns regular programs in a short-wide regime, not arbitrary programs. A regular program has equal incoming and outgoing degree at each state of each consecutive-layer graph; general transitions in this question can concentrate many incoming edges at one state.

Chen and coauthors improve weighted error reduction and alphabet dependence in the September 2026 proceedings version. Its separate ordinary-generator implication assumes an ordinary PRG with stronger parameter dependence; the weighted theorem does not supply that assumption. The paper credits the earlier Cheng–Hoza result for this connection.

A hitting set guarantees at least one accepting output whenever the uniform acceptance probability exceeds a specified threshold. It need not approximate that probability. Cheng–Hoza prove that a logarithmic-space hitting set for polynomial-width programs would nevertheless imply \(\mathrm L=\mathrm{BPL}\). Their conclusion about class derandomization does not itself produce the ordinary generator required by this card.

For permutation programs, each symbol acts bijectively between consecutive layers of equal size. Cohen–Doron–Goldgraber’s July 2026 theorem gives an ordinary generator with seed \(O((\log w+\log(1/\varepsilon))\log n)\), including arbitrary accepting subsets. The structural promise and remaining product of logarithms distinguish it from the general target.

Krak’s September 2026 preprint states a hitting-set result with seed \(O(\log(n/\varepsilon))\) for ordered width-three programs. The theorem is both a hitting guarantee and a constant-width result; its definition of explicitness requires polynomial time rather than the logarithmic workspace imposed here. This scope review does not independently certify the new proof.

cards.title: FPT versus \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)
cards.formal: Does there exist one deterministic algorithm A, a total computable function \(f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N_{\ge1}\), and an integer \(c\ge0\), such that A decides whether G contains a k-clique and uses at most \(f(k)(N+2)^c\) steps for every encoded pair (G,k) of total bit length N? The exponent c is independent of both k and G. Equivalently, is \(\mathrm{FPT}=\mathrm{W}[1]\) under parameterized many-one reductions?
cards.definitions: A graph G is finite, simple and undirected, with vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), including n=0. A k-clique is a subset of exactly k vertices with an edge between each pair of distinct vertices. The empty subset is a 0-clique; no k-clique exists when k>n. For a fixed binary encoding, write \(1^n0\), then the n by n adjacency matrix in row order, then the ordinary binary representation of the nonnegative integer k (0 is written as 0, and otherwise there are no leading zeroes). A valid matrix is symmetric with zero diagonal, and the entire remaining suffix is the representation of k. N counts all bits, including k. A rejects any malformed string in time polynomial in its bit length. The bound in the statement applies to every valid pair, including k>n. The parameter is k alone; there is no promise on density, degree, clique number or any other graph property. A is one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program and fixed finite tape alphabets, a read-only input and initially blank work tapes; each transition reads or writes only at the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. The runtime includes parsing, input access and all internal work. Correctness is exact, and no advice, randomness, oracle or quantum operations are supplied. The same A, f and c work for every pair; f must be computable by a machine that halts on every nonnegative integer input, but its growth and the time needed to compute it have no prescribed bound. Constant multiplicative overhead can be absorbed into f. Using full input length rather than n gives the usual FPT question: for k at most n the two lengths are polynomially related, and k>n is rejected after parsing. For completeness, a parameterized language is a set of pairs \((x,k)\in\{0,1\}^*\times\mathbb N\), with both components explicitly encoded. It belongs to FPT if one uniform deterministic machine decides it within \(h(k)(M+2)^a\) steps for a total computable positive h, a fixed nonnegative integer a and complete encoding length M. A parameterized many-one reduction computes a single output pair \((y,k^{\prime})\) in such a time bound, preserves yes versus no membership, and satisfies \(k^{\prime}\le g(k)\) for a total computable function g; writing the output counts toward its runtime. The class W[1] can equivalently be defined as all parameterized languages admitting such a reduction to the Clique problem just specified. This characterization fixes the reduction convention without a change of target. It includes FPT, and Clique belongs to it, so FPT membership of Clique is equivalent to equality of the two classes.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of the single algorithm, computable multiplier and constant exponent in the statement, or prove their joint nonexistence. In the affirmative case, prove correctness and the uniform worst-case bound on all pairs, together with the malformed-input convention. In the negative case, exclude every such algorithm, computable f and exponent c; a conditional lower bound, a bound for a restricted algorithm model, or failure at one proposed multiplier and exponent does not settle this target. An algorithm whose polynomial exponent depends on k also does not satisfy the displayed quantifiers.
cards.why: This is the principal boundary question for algorithms whose exponential difficulty is confined to a small parameter. It determines the force of thousands of parameterized hardness reductions and separates efficient small-solution search from algorithms whose input-size exponent grows with the solution size.

importance.reason: The defining unresolved tractability separation of parameterized complexity, with Clique as a precise and widely used complete problem.

progress.text: The textbook specifies parameterized reductions and proves the completeness framework for Clique, via its complement relation with Independent Set. Theorem 14.21 derives the stronger exclusion of \(f(k)n^{o(k)}\) Clique algorithms assuming ETH.

Bottesch identifies the FPT-versus-W[1] separation as the central conjecture, explains its known implications relative to P versus NP and ETH, and proves structural results with explicitly specified oracle conventions. These do not prove the unrelativized separation.
Lin gives a gap reduction showing that a constant-factor FPT approximation of Clique would imply an exact FPT algorithm. The consequence remains conditional on FPT differing from W[1].

Chen, Feng, Laekhanukit and Liu give a combinatorial proof of the \(k^{o(1)}\) parameterized inapproximability consequence under W[1]-hardness. The checked August 2024 revision precedes the SOSA 2025 publication.

Abboud, Fischer and Shechter improve combinatorial fixed-k Clique bounds by logarithmic factors. Their August 2024 author revision retains a polynomial exponent depending on k; the institutional record lists the Algorithmica publication on 22 May 2026.

cards.status_note: The textbook and Bottesch explicitly state the unresolved separation, and the later approximation papers retain it as an assumption. The checked fixed-k algorithm paper and its 2026 publication metadata provide no FPT algorithm. A bounded primary-source search on 14 September 2026 found no verified resolution; the review does not independently reprove the cited results.

context_blocks.text: For each fixed k, exhaustive search over vertex subsets decides Clique in polynomial time. The exponent grows with k, so this observation gives a different kind of tractability: increasing the target clique size can increase the power of n in the running time. The question asks whether all dependence on k can instead be moved into one multiplicative function. For example, \(2^{2^{k}}n^{3}\) meets the requested form, while \(n^{k/10}\) does not.

The unrestricted Clique problem is NP-complete, but this alone cannot rule out fixed-parameter tractability. The permitted function f can grow much faster than any polynomial when k grows with n. If \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\) then Clique is certainly FPT; the converse implication is not known. Thus \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne \mathrm{W}[1]\) is a stronger separation conjecture than \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) in the direction currently proved.

Parameterized reductions keep the output parameter controlled solely by the original parameter. Since Clique is complete under these reductions, an FPT Clique algorithm would solve every \(\mathrm{W}[1]\) problem in FPT time. This is why a \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)-hardness proof is useful evidence against a parameterized algorithm for another problem. The evidence is conditional on the separation being true, even when the reduction theorem itself is unconditional.

The Exponential Time Hypothesis supplies a stronger quantitative barrier: it rules out \(f(k)n^{o(k)}\) algorithms for Clique. That conclusion excludes FPT, but uses an assumption that is itself open. Matrix-multiplication methods and improved combinatorial methods accelerate Clique for fixed k while leaving an exponent that grows with the parameter. Their progress does not eliminate the central gap.

Approximation has become another way to measure the reach of the conjecture. Lin proves that even fixed-factor parameterized approximation of Clique is \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)-hard. Later constructions strengthen the factor and simplify the reductions. These results enlarge the consequences of a separation; they do not prove \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne \mathrm{W}[1]\).

Uniformity is essential: one finite program must handle every k. Neither a separately chosen algorithm for each fixed k nor a bound with an exponent that increases with k establishes FPT. Conversely, the allowed computable multiplier can be enormous; this is a structural tractability question and does not assert that an affirmative algorithm would be practical.

cards.context:
For each fixed k, exhaustive search over vertex subsets decides Clique in polynomial time. The exponent grows with k, so this observation gives a different kind of tractability: increasing the target clique size can increase the power of n in the running time. The question asks whether all dependence on k can instead be moved into one multiplicative function. For example, \(2^{2^{k}}n^{3}\) meets the requested form, while \(n^{k/10}\) does not.

The unrestricted Clique problem is NP-complete, but this alone cannot rule out fixed-parameter tractability. The permitted function f can grow much faster than any polynomial when k grows with n. If \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\) then Clique is certainly FPT; the converse implication is not known. Thus \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne \mathrm{W}[1]\) is a stronger separation conjecture than \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) in the direction currently proved.

Parameterized reductions keep the output parameter controlled solely by the original parameter. Since Clique is complete under these reductions, an FPT Clique algorithm would solve every \(\mathrm{W}[1]\) problem in FPT time. This is why a \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)-hardness proof is useful evidence against a parameterized algorithm for another problem. The evidence is conditional on the separation being true, even when the reduction theorem itself is unconditional.

The Exponential Time Hypothesis supplies a stronger quantitative barrier: it rules out \(f(k)n^{o(k)}\) algorithms for Clique. That conclusion excludes FPT, but uses an assumption that is itself open. Matrix-multiplication methods and improved combinatorial methods accelerate Clique for fixed k while leaving an exponent that grows with the parameter. Their progress does not eliminate the central gap.

Approximation has become another way to measure the reach of the conjecture. Lin proves that even fixed-factor parameterized approximation of Clique is \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)-hard. Later constructions strengthen the factor and simplify the reductions. These results enlarge the consequences of a separation; they do not prove \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne \mathrm{W}[1]\).

Uniformity is essential: one finite program must handle every k. Neither a separately chosen algorithm for each fixed k nor a bound with an exponent that increases with k establishes FPT. Conversely, the allowed computable multiplier can be enormous; this is a structural tractability question and does not assert that an affirmative algorithm would be practical.

benchmark_focus.reason: The defining unresolved tractability separation of parameterized complexity, with Clique as a precise and widely used complete problem.

cards.title: Exponential Time Hypothesis
cards.formal: Is \(s_3>0\) in the deterministic bit model defined below? Equivalently, does there exist one real \(c>0\) such that no 3-SAT decider A has a runtime bound \(t_A(F)\le C\,2^{c n(F)}(L(F)+1)^d\) on every valid 3-CNF formula F for any fixed integers \(C\ge1,d\ge0\)? The same positive c must exclude all such algorithms. This is the deterministic Exponential Time Hypothesis.
cards.definitions: Fix an integer clause-width bound \(q\ge 3\). A q-CNF formula is a finite list of clauses, each a finite list of at most q literals. A literal is a variable \(x_i\) or its negation \(\neg x_i\), with \(1\le i\le n\). The variables that occur are exactly \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), so n counts distinct variables, not clauses or input bits. Repeated literals, repeated clauses and clauses containing both signs of a variable are allowed. A Boolean assignment satisfies the formula if every clause has at least one true literal. An empty clause is false; the empty conjunction is true and has n=0. For a completely specified binary encoding, let \(\operatorname{code}(a)\), for a nonnegative integer a, be \(1^b0\) followed by the b-bit binary expansion of a+1, where \(b=\lfloor\log_2(a+1)\rfloor+1\). Encode n and the number m of clauses with this code, then each clause by its coded length followed by its literals. Each literal is a sign bit (0 for positive, 1 for negated) and the code of its variable index. All indicated lists must be fully present, with no trailing bits, valid indices and every declared variable occurring. Let L be the complete bit length. Ill-formed strings, including clauses wider than q, are rejected. No density, satisfiability-count, occurrence or input-distribution promise is imposed. A q-SAT decider A is one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program and fixed finite tape alphabets, a read-only input tape and initially blank work tapes. Each transition reads or writes only the cells at the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. The total transition count includes parsing, input access and all internal work. A must halt on all inputs, decide satisfiability exactly on valid q-CNF formulas, and reject malformed strings in polynomial time in their length. It receives no advice, random bits, quantum operations, oracle or precomputed instance information. The machine may depend on the fixed q. For a valid formula F, let \(t_A(F)\) be its runtime and \(n(F),L(F)\) its variable count and bit length. An exponent \(\alpha\ge 0\) is attainable at width q if there exist such a decider A and fixed integers \(C\ge1,d\ge0\) with \(t_A(F)\le C\,2^{\alpha n(F)}(L(F)+1)^d\) for every valid q-CNF formula F. The constants are independent of F. Define \(s_q\) as the infimum of all attainable exponents. This set is nonempty because exhaustive assignment testing gives an attainable exponent 1, so \(0\le s_q\le1\). The infimum need not itself be attainable. Polynomial factors in L remain explicit, including when clauses are repeated many times. The chosen explicit syntax and malformed-input normalization do not impose a new satisfiability promise; they fix the bit model for the source’s exponential-rate question. This card specializes q to 3. Its negation, \(s_3=0\), means that for every real \(\varepsilon>0\) there is a 3-SAT decider \(A_\varepsilon\) with fixed constants \(C_\varepsilon,d_\varepsilon\) satisfying \(t_{A_\varepsilon}(F)\le C_\varepsilon 2^{\varepsilon n(F)}(L(F)+1)^{d_\varepsilon}\) on every valid formula. The machine and constants may depend on epsilon. This statement does not require one machine with a single subexponential runtime bound, nor a computable map from epsilon to a machine.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of \(s_3>0\) or of \(s_3=0\) for the explicitly defined rate. A positive answer requires a positive constant excluding every valid deterministic decider at that exponential rate, with any polynomial input factor. A negative answer must establish arbitrarily small attainable positive exponents with the stated quantifiers. A fixed improved positive exponent, a bound for a restricted algorithm class, or a conditional lower bound does not settle this question. No numerical estimate of \(s_3\) is requested: the target is its strict positivity.
cards.why: ETH is the central hypothesis for ruling out subexponential exact algorithms and many fixed-parameter speedups. It turns the qualitative P versus NP question into a quantitative claim that can be transferred through carefully sized reductions.

importance.reason: A foundational quantitative hardness hypothesis underlying exact, parameterized, graph, and geometric algorithm lower bounds.

progress.text: Impagliazzo and Paturi define the exponential rates of bounded-width satisfiability and relate positive rate at width three to positive rates at other fixed widths. These are structural results about the hypothesis, not a proof of it.
The authors’ IPEC survey explicitly defines ETH by a positive infimum and distinguishes the number of variables from the complete input length.

The parameterized-algorithms textbook retains the positive-infimum definition, explains its distinction from ruling out a single subexponential algorithm, and gives consequences for parameterized complexity.

Liu gives a deterministic \(1.32793^n\) upper bound for 3-SAT up to polynomial factors, recorded in the checked March 2020 revision of the ICALP 2018 work. This leaves the positivity of the optimal rate unresolved.

Aggarwal, Gupta, Morolia and Zhang derive new lattice approximation hardness under ETH or randomized ETH, with different assumptions for their closest-vector and shortest-vector results. The paper still treats these as assumptions and distinguishes Gap-ETH.

The optimal-rate definition and cited algorithmic upper bound were checked against the full relevant source passages. Targeted later-work searches on 14 September 2026 found no verified resolution; bounded searches do not independently verify the cited proofs or exhaust all later literature.

context_blocks.text: NP-completeness describes the possibility of polynomial-time algorithms and does not itself impose a positive exponential rate. Even if P differs from NP, a running time such as \(2^{\sqrt{n}}\) remains possible for 3-SAT. ETH asks for a stronger obstruction: some fixed amount of exponential work must remain unavoidable when complexity is measured by the number of Boolean choices.

That parameter must be preserved carefully by a reduction. An ordinary polynomial-time reduction may turn an n-variable formula into an instance of size \(n^{3}\), which can destroy a claimed exponential lower bound in the new parameter. Sparsification supplies a controlled disjunction of bounded-density formulas, allowing variables and clauses to be related without an arbitrary polynomial blowup. This is a main reason ETH can support sharp bounds across many problems.

The infimum over all algorithms matters. Excluding one \(2^{o(n)}\) algorithm is the common informal wording, but the textbook explicitly keeps the stronger positive-infimum statement because the converse is unclear. ETH would be false if arbitrarily small constant exponents were attainable, even if the known algorithms depended on the desired exponent. A card that omitted this distinction would change the quantified question.

Liu’s deterministic algorithm has runtime \(O(1.32793^n)\) up to polynomial input factors. It therefore supplies an upper bound on \(s_3\); it establishes neither a positive lower bound nor the value of \(s_3\). The existence of one algorithm with a positive exponential rate does not rule out a much faster algorithm. Empirical solver success and promises on the formula are also distinct from this all-input infimum.

ETH is weaker than SETH, whose optimal rates approach one as the fixed clause width grows. It also differs from randomized ETH and from Gap-ETH, which asks for hardness of distinguishing fully satisfiable formulas from formulas with a constant unsatisfied fraction. Recent lattice reductions illustrate the value of tracking these distinctions: some approximation hardness can be obtained from deterministic ETH, while other results use randomized ETH. They extend the consequences of assumptions without proving the assumptions.

A single fixed exponent in ETH must obstruct every algorithm. Refuting one proposed lower-bound constant does not suffice, because another smaller positive constant could still work. Conversely, a refutation may use a different finite algorithm for each desired exponent; no effective procedure generating those algorithms is added to the target.

cards.title: Constant-factor approximation for Densest k-Subgraph
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal:
Does Densest \(k\)-Subgraph have a deterministic polynomial-time constant-factor approximation on all explicitly given finite simple undirected unweighted graphs?

For \(n\ge1\), write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). If \(G=([n],E)\) and \(1\le k\le n\), define
\[e_G(S)=|\{\{u,v\}\in E:u,v\in S\}|,\qquad \operatorname{OPT}(G,k)=\max_{\substack{T\subseteq[n]\\|T|=k}}e_G(T).\]
The proposition is that there exist one real constant \(C\ge1\), positive integer constants \(D,d\), and one deterministic multitape Turing machine \(A\) such that, on every encoded input of length \(L\), \(A\) halts within \(D(L+1)^d\) bit steps, and on every valid \((G,k)\) it outputs an explicitly represented set \(S\subseteq[n]\) satisfying
\[|S|=k\qquad\text{and}\qquad C\,e_G(S)\ge\operatorname{OPT}(G,k).\]
The same algorithm, constants and polynomial clock must work for all \(n,G,k\).
cards.definitions:
The graph has exactly the labelled vertices \([n]\), including isolated vertices. Each edge is an unordered pair of distinct vertices, with no repetitions, loops, weights or directions. Its input is \(U(n)U(k)\) followed by the \(n(n-1)/2\) adjacency bits in lexicographic order of pairs \((u,v)\) with \(u<v\). Here \(U(a)=1^\ell0b\), where \(b\) is the canonical binary expansion of a nonnegative integer \(a\), \(\ell=|b|\), and zero uses \(b=0\). The code must have precisely the indicated number of adjacency bits, with \(n\ge1\) and \(1\le k\le n\). Invalid encodings may be rejected; the clock applies to them too. This dense explicit encoding is polynomially equivalent to an explicit vertex-and-edge list. A succinct circuit or edge oracle is not an input representation for this card.

The output is an \(n\)-bit indicator vector. A one at position \(i\) means vertex \(i\) belongs to \(S\), and exactly \(k\) bits must be one. The objective counts each internal edge once. The maximum exists because the family of \(k\)-subsets is finite and nonempty. An estimate of the optimum without an accompanying vertex set does not satisfy the output requirement.

Running time counts ordinary bounded-symbol Turing-machine steps, including reading input, arithmetic and writing all output bits. The machine has one fixed finite program and a fixed finite number of tapes. The constants cannot depend on graph size, \(k\), edge density or any promise about the input. No advice, randomness, quantum operations or uncharged oracle is supplied. A running time whose polynomial exponent increases with \(k\) does not meet the clock.

The approximation is purely multiplicative and holds on every valid input, with no additive loss, input-distribution exception or probability of failure. When \(\operatorname{OPT}(G,k)=0\), the inequality is automatic but the output must still be a valid \(k\)-set. This includes \(k=1\), edgeless graphs and \(n=1\). The case \(k=n\) is included. The quantifier over \(C\) could equivalently use a positive integer, since rounding an admissible real factor upward preserves the guarantee.

Exactly \(k\) vertices is part of the target. On these feasible sets, maximizing internal edge count, average degree \(2e_G(S)/k\), or edges per vertex \(e_G(S)/k\) gives the same approximation ratio. If the number of selected vertices is allowed to vary, these objectives are no longer interchangeable. A guarantee for at least \(k\) vertices, a special graph class, a planted input distribution or a randomized algorithm is a different statement.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of this proposition or of its full logical negation. A positive answer must specify one deterministic algorithm and universal constants, prove the global polynomial clock, and prove both exact output cardinality and the approximation inequality on every valid graph and parameter. A negative answer must exclude every such constant-factor polynomial-time algorithm. Equivalently, for every deterministic polynomial-time machine that always outputs a valid \(k\)-set and every fixed \(C\ge1\), some valid input must satisfy \(C e_G(A(G,k))<\operatorname{OPT}(G,k)\). A lower bound conditional on an unproved complexity hypothesis, or a limitation of a specified relaxation or algorithm family, does not by itself prove the full negation.
cards.why: Densest k-Subgraph asks whether a prescribed number of vertices can capture a constant fraction of the greatest possible internal connectivity. Its approximation landscape is a central gap between available algorithms, conditional hardness and what follows from the usual P-versus-NP assumption. The answer also matters for several graph optimization objectives linked to its approximability.

importance.reason: A flagship approximation problem with a simple objective, a large algorithmic gap, strong conditional and relaxation barriers, and consequences for several other optimization problems.

cards.status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The deterministic constant-factor question remains source-open in the inspected literature. ETH conditionally excludes such an algorithm, but is unproved; the May 2026 primary source explicitly retains the missing NP-hardness of even 1.001 approximation under the usual P≠NP framework. The March exact-penalty result and August unrestricted/at-least-k density preprint do not claim the specified exactly-k guarantee. The bounded later-work check is not an independent certification of every cited proof or an exhaustive absence-of-results claim.

context_blocks.text: The exact cardinality makes the objective distinctive. A large region of moderate density can be an excellent answer when size is unrestricted or only bounded below, yet it need not contain a k-vertex region with a comparable fraction of the optimum for exactly k. The card asks for the actual selected vertices, so evaluating a continuous objective or estimating an optimum is insufficient.

Bhaskara and coauthors give an \(O(n^{1/4+\varepsilon})\) approximation in \(n^{O(1/\varepsilon)}\) time for each fixed \(\varepsilon>0\). Their paper includes a deterministic combinatorial algorithm. Its title’s \(O(n^{1/4})\) endpoint requires quasipolynomial \(n^{O(\log n)}\) time in that analysis. The 2026 AAAI paper still describes the quarter-power-plus-epsilon bound as the general polynomial-time benchmark; neither bound is a universal constant.

Manurangsi proves that the Exponential Time Hypothesis rules out polynomial-time approximation within \(n^{1/(\log\log n)^c}\) for some universal \(c>0\). The paper states ETH as the absence of a deterministic \(2^{o(m)}\)-time algorithm for 3SAT with \(m\) clauses. Its hard YES instances contain a \(k\)-clique, a property called perfect completeness. The result already excludes every fixed approximation constant if ETH holds, but ETH is an unproved assumption stronger than \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\).

The corresponding conclusion under only P≠NP remains a different issue. The May 2026 at-least-k paper explicitly says that even NP-hardness of a 1.001 approximation for Densest k-Subgraph is not known. This is consistent with the ETH lower bound: different hypotheses support different conclusions. A proof of conditional hardness is significant evidence, but does not establish the unconditional negative answer required by the card.

Chuzhoy and coauthors propose a Low-Degree CSP conjecture. Together with \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\), it would exclude a polynomial-time \(2^{(\log n)^\varepsilon}\)-approximation for some \(0<\varepsilon\le1/2\). Their stated consequence uses Cook-type reductions, which may make multiple oracle queries. The work also connects graph partitioning, dense coloring and other graph objectives, sometimes with quasipolynomial reductions. These are qualified conditional relationships rather than constant-factor polynomial-time equivalences.

The 2012 integrality gaps demonstrate limitations of specified strong semidefinite relaxations. They exhibit a separation between what a relaxation permits and the objective attained by genuine selected vertices. Such a separation constrains approximation arguments based on that relaxation; it does not rule out every polynomial-time algorithm.

Jones and coauthors give further Sum-of-Squares lower bounds in a planted-subgraph distinction model for \(k\le\sqrt n\). Their Theorem 1.1 constructs high-degree pseudoexpectations on random graphs, with approximately correct first-moment cardinality and normalization. These are the theorem’s particular relaxation constraints; they should not be silently replaced by all exact cardinality identities. This adds evidence about a broad algorithmic framework without proving unrestricted constant-factor hardness.

The AAAI 2026 continuous formulation is exact in a different sense. Under a sufficient penalty, its global optima correspond to the combinatorial problem, with an additional local-optimum correspondence. The accompanying convergence result controls a criticality residual under its stated algorithmic conditions. It does not guarantee a global optimum or a fixed approximation ratio on every input. Practical optimization progress can therefore coexist with the unresolved worst-case target.

Laekhanukit, Manurangsi and Trabelsi show that the absence of every constant-factor DkS approximation would rule out a \((3/2-\varepsilon)\)-approximation for the at-least-k density problem, for each \(\varepsilon>0\). Their latter objective is edges per selected vertex and permits more than \(k\) vertices. Its known constant-factor algorithms do not solve the exactly-k problem.

The August 2026 preprint of Grigorescu and Taziki claims a linear-time approximation scheme for the unrestricted density objective. It also gives a near-linear-time at-least-k result with value at least \((1/2-\varepsilon)\) of that objective’s optimum. Both statements permit a different feasible cardinality from this card. They are relevant recent progress, but neither is a claimed resolution of its constant-factor question.

cards.title: Unique Games Conjecture
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: For every pair of rational constants \(\varepsilon ,\delta >0\) with \(\varepsilon +\delta <1\), does there exist an integer \(q\ge 2\) such that it is NP-hard to distinguish Unique Games instances with $\operatorname{val}(G)\ge1-\varepsilon$ from instances with $\operatorname{val}(G)\le\delta$? Here q is the alphabet size, fixed independently of the input graph, and \(\operatorname{val}(G)\) is the largest fraction of constraints simultaneously satisfied by any labeling.
cards.definitions: An instance has finitely many vertices and a nonempty explicit list E of directed edges between distinct vertices; repeated edges are allowed and counted separately. Every vertex receives a label in \([q]=\{1,\ldots ,q\}\). An edge \(e=(u,v)\) carries an explicitly given permutation \(\pi _{e}:[q]\to [q]\) and is satisfied exactly when \(\pi _{e}(\ell (u))=\ell (v)\). Thus \(\operatorname{val}(G)=\max _{\ell} |\){e satisfied by \(\ell\)}|/|E|. There are no graph expansion or degree promises. NP-hardness means a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction from 3SAT mapping every satisfiable formula into the \(\ge 1- \varepsilon\) case and every unsatisfiable formula into the \(\le \delta\) case. The reduction, its running-time exponent, and q may depend on \(\varepsilon ,\delta\). Inputs with value strictly between the thresholds are outside the promise. The question is the NP-hardness proposition itself; \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) is needed when drawing the usual conclusion that no polynomial-time distinguishing algorithm exists. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: UGC would turn many conditional approximation thresholds into NP-hardness theorems and explain the optimality of a general SDP framework. Its very simple permutation constraints isolate a fundamental boundary between exact consistency, approximate consistency, and hardness amplification.

importance.reason: An organizing conjecture for approximation thresholds, with consequences for whole families of constraint satisfaction problems and strong connections to SDP algorithms, PCPs, and analysis.

progress.text: Khot proposes the conjecture. Perfect satisfiability is polynomial-time decidable; the conjectured hard regime has positive completeness error and an alphabet depending on both gap parameters.

Raghavendra gives a general SDP and rounding framework for fixed finite-domain CSPs and transfers SDP integrality gaps to Unique-Games-based hardness. Under UGC, its achievable thresholds are optimal up to any fixed accuracy, unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\).

Arora, Barak, and Steurer give, for an absolute \(\alpha >0\), an \(\exp (q n^{\varepsilon ^{\alpha}})\)-time algorithm finding a \((1- \varepsilon ^{\alpha})\)-satisfying labeling in a \((1- \varepsilon )\)-satisfiable q-label instance on n vertices. In the small fixed-\(\varepsilon\) regime this is subexponential, but not polynomial.

The line of work proving the 2-to-2 Games Theorem yields NP-hardness of Unique Games at completeness \(1/2\) and arbitrarily small soundness. Khot’s exposition states this explicitly as Theorem 2.20; it leaves the near-one completeness of UGC unresolved.

The journal version of Dinur, Khot, Kindler, Minzer, and Safra’s second installment documents its role in the proof sequence, while retaining the full Unique Games statement as Conjecture 1.4. Its publication is not a new proof of full UGC.

context_blocks.text: Each constraint is locally simple: fixing either endpoint label determines exactly one compatible label at the other endpoint. Exact satisfiability of all constraints is decidable in polynomial time. Allowing a small fraction of constraints to fail changes the question sharply.

The conjecture says that an instance admitting an almost perfect assignment can nevertheless be hard to distinguish from one where every assignment fails almost everywhere. These are two promised regimes, rather than a request to compute the exact optimum. The alphabet is allowed to grow as the desired gap becomes more demanding. Indeed, a uniformly random labeling satisfies a \(1/q\) fraction in expectation, so a soundness threshold below \(1/q\) is impossible.

Raghavendra’s theorem connects such reductions to a general semidefinite-programming framework: under UGC, that framework achieves the approximation thresholds of fixed finite-domain constraint satisfaction problems, to arbitrary constant accuracy.

The strongest relevant hardness milestone must be read with its completeness parameter. The 2-to-2 Games Theorem implies hardness for Unique Games with value at least one half versus arbitrarily small value. It does not make the yes instances almost perfectly satisfiable. Raising completeness from one half to arbitrarily close to one is precisely a remaining gap relevant to this card.

Algorithmic progress also matters even when it is slower than polynomial time. Subexponential algorithms exploit spectral decompositions of the constraint graph, limiting what quantitative hardness reductions could establish. Because a polynomial reduction can enlarge the instance by a parameter-dependent power, these algorithms coexist with the NP-hardness conjecture.
