cards.title: Hadwiger’s conjecture
cards.formal: Is the following proposition true? For every integer \(n\ge1\), every simple undirected graph \(G\) on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and every integer \(t\ge1\), if \(\chi(G)\ge t\), then \(G\) contains \(K_t\) as an ordinary graph minor. Equivalently, \(h(G)\ge\chi(G)\) for every such graph, where \(h\) is the Hadwiger number defined below.
cards.definitions: The edge set of \(G\) is any set of unordered pairs of distinct vertices in \([n]\); there are no loops or parallel edges. For an integer \(r\ge1\), a proper \(r\)-coloring is a map \(c:[n]\to\{1,\ldots,r\}\) such that \(c(u)\ne c(v)\) for every edge \(\{u,v\}\). The chromatic number \(\chi(G)\) is the least such \(r\); it exists and lies between \(1\) and \(n\). The graph \(K_t\) has \(t\) vertices and every possible edge. A \(K_t\) minor in \(G\) means that there are \(t\) pairwise disjoint nonempty vertex sets \(B_1,\ldots,B_t\) with both of the following properties: for every \(i\), any two vertices of \(B_i\) are joined by a finite path of edges of \(G\) whose vertices all lie in \(B_i\); and for every \(i<j\), some edge of \(G\) has one endpoint in \(B_i\) and one in \(B_j\). A singleton is connected. The branch sets may have any sizes, need not cover all vertices, and have no restrictions on extra internal edges or on parity. This is equivalent to obtaining \(K_t\) by vertex deletions, edge deletions and edge contractions, discarding loops and merging parallel edges after contraction. It is neither an induced-minor nor an odd-minor requirement. The Hadwiger number \(h(G)\) is the largest \(t\) admitting these branch sets, so \(1\le h(G)\le n\). For \(t\ge2\), the proposition equivalently says that absence of a \(K_t\) minor implies a proper \((t-1)\)-coloring; the \(t=1\) assertion holds automatically for a nonempty graph. Relabeling vertices has no effect. The quantifiers impose no connectedness, degree, order or other restriction on \(G\), and no running-time bound on finding a coloring or a minor.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the proposition for all finite nonempty simple undirected graphs and all integers \(t\ge1\), or a Lean-checked proof of its logical negation: existence of a finite graph \(G\) and integer \(t\ge1\) with \(\chi(G)\ge t\) and no \(t\) branch sets satisfying the definition. A counterexample must certify both the chromatic lower bound and absence of the ordinary clique minor. A proof of \(h(G)\ge\chi(G)\) for every graph is an equivalent positive answer. No efficient algorithm is required. A constant-factor or asymptotic coloring bound, a finite list of established values of \(t\), a restricted graph class, or a counterexample only to the odd-minor variant does not cover the target.
cards.why: Hadwiger’s conjecture proposes an exact relation between two basic graph parameters: the number of colors needed and the size of a complete graph obtainable by contraction. It extends the Four-Color Theorem and would turn exclusion of a complete minor into the sharp universal coloring bound. Its significance comes from this structural connection across all finite graphs, rather than from an algorithmic requirement in the question.

importance.reason: One of the central graph-theoretic conjectures, with an exact extremal target and consequences across coloring and minor structure.

progress.text: Hadwiger’s original conjecture is restated in the introduction of the cited modern paper; the 1943 original was not inspected in this review.
Kostochka and Thomason establish the \(O(t\sqrt{\log t})\) degeneracy bound, summarized in Theorem 1.3 of Delcourt and Postle. Its tightness concerns degeneracy, not the conjectured chromatic bound.

Robertson, Seymour and Thomas establish the structural result that, with the Four-Color Theorem, proves five-colorability of \(K_6\)-minor-free graphs. The institutional abstract and publication metadata were checked.
Delcourt and Postle obtain \(O(t\log\log t)\) colors. The first preprint was submitted on 3 August 2021, the inspected version 5 on 5 March 2024, and the journal article appeared in 2025.

Kühn, Sauermann, Steiner and Wigderson’s Theorem 1.3 disproves the odd Hadwiger conjecture; their ordinary-minor Conjecture 1.1 remains a separate target. The preprint result is also cited in Liu and Luo’s September 2026 introduction.

cards.status_note: The ordinary Hadwiger conjecture is explicitly open in Liu–Luo v2 of 9 September 2026, still its latest arXiv version on 14 September. Its triple-logarithmic coloring theorem is a recent preprint claim, not independently verified here. The December 2025 disproof and its September 2026 citation concern the stronger odd-minor version. Checked source formulations and a bounded later-work search do not certify all cited proofs.

context_blocks.text: A complete minor can be much larger than any complete subgraph: contraction groups connected regions into single vertices. Hadwiger asks whether the resulting complete graph can always have as many vertices as the original graph needs colors. For every \(t\ge2\), the graph \(K_{t-1}\) has no \(K_t\) minor and needs exactly \(t-1\) colors, so the conjectured bound for the excluded-minor class is sharp.

The exact cases through \(t=6\) are known. The \(t=5\) case is equivalent, via Wagner’s theorem, to the Four-Color Theorem for planar graphs. Robertson, Seymour and Thomas established the \(t=6\) case: without assuming four-colorability, their structural result makes a minimal counterexample apex, meaning that deleting one vertex leaves a planar graph. The Four-Color Theorem then gives five colors for that graph. Their paper indexes the conjecture by the allowed number of colors, one less than the clique-minor order used on this card.

Kostochka and Thomason obtained an \(O(t\sqrt{\log t})\) bound on degeneracy, where a graph is \(d\)-degenerate if every nonempty subgraph has a vertex of degree at most \(d\). Such a graph is \((d+1)\)-colorable. The order of this degeneracy bound is tight, but that fact is not a chromatic lower bound of the same order and does not disprove Hadwiger. Delcourt and Postle’s Theorem 1.5 gives \(O(t\log\log t)\) colors for arbitrary \(K_t\)-minor-free graphs; its quantification has no bound on the number of vertices.

Liu and Luo’s version 2, submitted on 9 September 2026, states in Theorem 1.1 that an absolute constant \(C\) satisfies \(\chi(G)\le Ct\log\log\log t\) for every integer \(t\ge16\) and every \(K_t\)-minor-free graph. Their logarithms are natural. This is recorded as a recent preprint claim whose proof has not been independently verified here. It does not establish either the weakening \(\chi(G)=O(t)\) or the exact bound \(t-1\); the introduction still identifies clique-minor orders starting at seven as open.

For the odd-minor variant, the disjoint branch trees must each have a proper two-coloring, with an edge joining vertices of the same color between every pair of trees. Forgetting these extra requirements yields an ordinary minor, so absence of an ordinary minor implies absence of an odd minor; the reverse implication need not hold. Kühn, Sauermann, Steiner and Wigderson’s December 2025 preprint states that for each fixed \(\delta>0\) and every sufficiently large \(t\), some graph has no odd \(K_t\) minor and has \(\chi(G)\ge(3/2-\delta)t\). This refutes the stronger odd-minor conjecture. Odd-minor absence by itself does not certify the ordinary-minor absence required for a negative answer here.

cards.title: Deterministic linear-time minimum spanning tree
cards.formal: Is there one deterministic comparison-based algorithm that, on every connected simple undirected graph with n vertices, m edges and arbitrary real edge weights, outputs a minimum spanning tree in \(O(m+n)\) worst-case time in the comparison RAM model below?
cards.definitions: The graph is explicitly supplied as vertex and edge records, with vertices numbered \(1,\ldots ,n\) and edges given distinct identifiers. An edge record contains its two endpoints and a weight key representing an arbitrary real number. A spanning tree is a set T of \(n- 1\) edges connecting all vertices without a cycle; it is minimum when \(\sum_{e\in T}w(e)\) is smallest among all spanning trees. For \(n=1\) the output is empty. Equal and negative weights are permitted, and any minimum tree is acceptable. Weight keys may be copied and compared, but their bit representations cannot be inspected, and arithmetic on their numerical values is unavailable. Each comparison has unit cost. Nonweight data, addresses and indices use \(O(\log (m+n+2))\)-bit words on a random-access machine, with unit-cost reads, writes, comparisons, standard word arithmetic, bitwise Boolean operations and shifts; arithmetic is restricted to these words. All ordinary operations count in the running time, not just weight comparisons. The algorithm has a fixed finite description and no input-length-dependent advice or free precomputed tables. Any tables it constructs, as well as writing the output, are charged to its time. The hidden linear-time constant must be independent of graph topology, n,m and the weights. This fixes a conventional uniform sequential comparison model. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A central unresolved boundary between deterministic and randomized algorithms for a classical graph optimization problem, and a rare case where a provably optimal algorithm exists before its exact asymptotic complexity is understood.

importance.reason: A foundational graph-algorithm question about the necessity of randomness and the relationship between comparison complexity and actual computation.

cards.status_note: The deterministic linear-time comparison problem remains open in the primary-author material checked through 11 September 2026. Integer-word algorithms, high-girth results and the optimal-decision-tree theorem do not settle this formulation.

context_blocks.text: A minimum spanning tree connects a graph as cheaply as possible without redundant cycles. It is among the basic examples where a local greedy rule produces a global optimum, and it appears in network design and clustering. The optimization objective is well understood; the unsettled issue is how much computation is fundamentally needed to identify the right \(n- 1\) edges when the input already contains m edge records.

Sorting every edge is sufficient for Kruskal’s algorithm, but sorting is a stronger task than the required output. On a graph that is itself a tree, every edge belongs to the answer regardless of their relative weights. On a triangle, only the identity of a largest-weight edge is needed: discard it. Thus the familiar comparison lower bound for sorting all keys does not automatically become a lower bound for finding an MST. A faster algorithm must exploit the graph’s structure to avoid unnecessary ordering information.

The cut and cycle rules make this possible. A lightest edge across a cut can be selected safely, and a strictly heaviest edge on a cycle can be discarded. Equal weights can be handled consistently by comparing pairs consisting of the weight and the edge identifier. These rules avoid numerical arithmetic on weights, so the problem is meaningful for arbitrary real keys even though the objective is expressed as a sum.

Karger, Klein and Tarjan combine random sampling with linear-time MST verification to obtain a Las Vegas algorithm with expected \(O(m+n)\) running time. It always returns a correct tree; randomness controls the work spent on recursive filtering. The target here is a deterministic guarantee for every input, so fixing an arbitrary random seed does not inherit the expected-time theorem.

Chazelle’s deterministic algorithm achieves \(O(m\alpha (m,n))\) time, where \(\alpha\) is a slowly growing inverse-Ackermann function. Its soft-heap machinery deliberately permits a controlled set of key increases inside an auxiliary data structure while the surrounding algorithm preserves the exact MST answer. The extra factor is tiny for practical input sizes, yet unbounded asymptotically. Removing it asks for an exact structural understanding of the problem’s complexity, not merely an implementation improvement.

Pettie and Ramachandran establish a different kind of optimality: total algorithmic running time can match, within a constant factor, the optimal worst-case number of edge comparisons for MST. Their algorithm is uniform; it constructs the small optimal decision trees it needs within the time analysis. But the asymptotic size of that optimum is itself unknown. Consequently a proof that linear-size comparison decision trees always suffice would settle the algorithmic question through their theorem.

The graph family also matters. Eisenstat and coauthors show that it is enough to solve graphs with at most \(3n/2\) edges, and separately relate the general problem to graphs with any fixed lower bound on girth, the length of a shortest cycle. Their available high-girth algorithm requires a lower bound that grows with n. That difference between a fixed girth threshold and a slowly growing threshold leaves the general deterministic question open.

Changing the access model can remove the obstacle. Fredman and Willard give a deterministic linear-time algorithm using integer-word operations on the weights. That theorem can exploit their binary representation, which the real-key comparison model deliberately withholds. Similarly, an algorithm that is fast for a random graph topology has an average-instance guarantee, even if the algorithm itself is deterministic; it does not bound the work on every graph.

The remaining challenge can therefore be stated without ambiguity: retain exactness, arbitrary real-key weights and all graph topologies, and make every part of the computation linear without random choices. A negative answer would be equally significant, by establishing an intrinsic cost for deterministic comparison-based optimization that expected-time random sampling avoids.

cards.title: Dynamic optimality conjecture
cards.formal: Fix n ordered keys and an access sequence X. In the root-BST model, an access is served by rotations until its key is at the root; its cost is one plus the number of rotations. Let \(\operatorname{OPT}(X)\) minimize total cost over offline executions, allowing an optimal initial tree. Is there a universal constant C such that, for every initial splay tree \(T_{0}\) and every X, \(\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{splay}}(X;T_0)\le C(\mathrm{OPT}(X)+n)\)? The additive term allows an arbitrary initial configuration.

context_blocks.text: A balanced search tree guarantees logarithmic time per access, but that worst-case guarantee ignores the sequence. Repeatedly accessing one key, or scanning nearby keys, can be much cheaper if the tree adapts. Dynamic optimality asks for one online rule that exploits every such pattern without being told which pattern will occur.

The benchmark is itself allowed to rotate its tree and knows all future requests. Competing with the best fixed tree only captures access frequencies; competing with a changing tree also captures temporal structure. Splaying uses only local zig, zig-zig, and zig-zag rotations after each access, with no explicit prediction of the future.

For a concrete example, consider a chain on n keys with the requested key at its bottom. The first splay can cost \(\Theta (n)\), whereas an offline comparator can put that key at the root initially. The additive n allowance accounts for this starting discrepancy. Repeating the same request then costs one per access in both trees. A large cost for one badly initialized access therefore does not refute the statement.

The July 2026 preprint bounds splay cost by \(O((\operatorname{OPT}(X)+n) \log  \log  n \cdot  \log ^{2} \log  \log  n)\). Its competitive factor depends only on the number of keys, so the result covers every access pattern; that factor nevertheless grows without bound. A constant bound would be strictly stronger. The theorem is stated asymptotically, with the finitely many small values of n absorbed into constants.

Competitiveness concerns the total cost of a sequence. It does not require every individual access to be cheap, and it does not compare against an arbitrary RAM program with a hash table. Both executions must maintain binary search trees and pay for the specified rotations. Within those rules the offline execution can depend on the complete sequence, while the splay rule reacts only to the current request and tree.

context_blocks.title: Additional source and scope
context_blocks.text: Sublogarithmic competitiveness of splay trees is a weaker quantitative milestone on the way to constant competitiveness. It is preserved as context and is not claimed to imply dynamic optimality.

cards.why: It asks whether a simple local adjustment rule can match every legal strategy with complete knowledge of the future. The issue is fundamental to instance-sensitive data structures: success would replace a growing competitive penalty by a constant for all access patterns. A counterexample would identify a limitation of splaying that its many separate locality guarantees fail to reveal.
cards.definitions: Keys are \([n]=\{1,\ldots ,n\}, n\ge 1\), ordered by their integer values. A binary search tree has one node per key, every key in a left subtree smaller than its root and every key in a right subtree larger. A rotation on a parent-child edge exchanges those two nodes while reattaching the intermediate subtree so that the order is preserved. To splay a requested key x, repeatedly apply the following bottom-up rule until x is root. If its parent is root, rotate the edge from x to its parent (zig). Otherwise let p be its parent and g its grandparent. If x and p are both left children or both right children, first rotate p above g and then x above p (zig-zig). Otherwise rotate x above p and then x above g (zig-zag). Each access costs one plus its number of rotations. The tree after the access is the initial tree for the next access. For a finite sequence \(X\in [n]*, \operatorname{cost}_{\mathrm{splay}}(X;T_{0})\) is the sum of these costs starting from \(T_{0}\). A comparator execution may start with any tree, knows X in full, and serves each request by any finite sequence of parent-child rotations anywhere in the current tree whose final root is the requested key. Its cost is the same one-plus-rotations sum. \(\operatorname{OPT}(X)\) is the minimum cost over all such initial trees and executions; it is zero for the empty sequence. There are no insertions, deletions or additional node operations. This root-BST cost convention is the one used in the saved source, with the additive n term accounting for the initial tree.

progress.text: Splaying has logarithmic amortized access cost and stronger guarantees for useful special patterns. These do not establish competitiveness against an arbitrary changing offline tree.
Tango trees give an online BST with an \(O(\log\log n)\) competitive ratio. This result is for a different data structure and does not settle splaying.
The preprint proves \(O((\mathrm{OPT}(X)+n)\log\log n\,\log^2\log\log n)\) total splay cost. Theorem 1 includes the initialization term explicitly. Constant competitiveness remains the target.

cards.context:
A balanced search tree guarantees logarithmic time per access, but that worst-case guarantee ignores the sequence. Repeatedly accessing one key, or scanning nearby keys, can be much cheaper if the tree adapts. Dynamic optimality asks for one online rule that exploits every such pattern without being told which pattern will occur.

The benchmark is itself allowed to rotate its tree and knows all future requests. Competing with the best fixed tree only captures access frequencies; competing with a changing tree also captures temporal structure. Splaying uses only local zig, zig-zig, and zig-zag rotations after each access, with no explicit prediction of the future.

For a concrete example, consider a chain on n keys with the requested key at its bottom. The first splay can cost \(\Theta (n)\), whereas an offline comparator can put that key at the root initially. The additive n allowance accounts for this starting discrepancy. Repeating the same request then costs one per access in both trees. A large cost for one badly initialized access therefore does not refute the statement.

The July 2026 preprint bounds splay cost by \(O((\operatorname{OPT}(X)+n) \log  \log  n \cdot  \log ^{2} \log  \log  n)\). Its competitive factor depends only on the number of keys, so the result covers every access pattern; that factor nevertheless grows without bound. A constant bound would be strictly stronger. The theorem is stated asymptotically, with the finitely many small values of n absorbed into constants.

Competitiveness concerns the total cost of a sequence. It does not require every individual access to be cheap, and it does not compare against an arbitrary RAM program with a hash table. Both executions must maintain binary search trees and pay for the specified rotations. Within those rules the offline execution can depend on the complete sequence, while the splay rule reacts only to the current request and tree.

Sublogarithmic competitiveness of splay trees is a weaker quantitative milestone on the way to constant competitiveness. It is preserved as context and is not claimed to imply dynamic optimality.

benchmark_focus.reason: Dynamic optimality is a central benchmark for adaptive data structures: one simple online BST would compete with every offline BST on every access sequence.

cards.title: Superlogarithmic static cell-probe lower bounds
cards.formal: Does there exist a fixed integer \(k\ge 2\) and a uniformly polynomial-time computable family of Boolean functions \(F_{n}\) on an n-word database and a \(k\lceil \log _{2} n\rceil\)-bit query such that its optimal deterministic static cell-probe query complexity \(t*F(n)\), with word size \(\lceil 4\log _{2} n\rceil\) bits and \(n\lceil \log _{2} n\rceil ^{2}\) memory cells, satisfies \(t*F(n)/\log _{2} n\to \infty\) as \(n\to \infty\)?
cards.definitions: For each integer \(n\ge 2\) put \(w=\lceil 4\log _{2} n\rceil\) and \(s=n\lceil \log _{2} n\rceil ^{2}\). A database is \(D\in (\{0,1\}^{w})^{n}, a\) query is \(q\in \{0,1\}^{k\lceil \log _{2} n\rceil}\), and \(F_{n}(D,q)\in \{0,1\}\). Explicit means that a single deterministic Turing machine computes \(F_{n}(D,q)\), given \((1^{n},D,q)\), in time polynomial in n; no advice is allowed in this definition. A data structure may preprocess D by any map \(E_{n}\) into s cells of w bits each. Preprocessing time is unrestricted, and this encoding may be nonlinear and nonuniform. For each query, a deterministic adaptive decision tree reads cells, choosing the next address from the query and previously read contents, and must output \(F_{n}(D,q)\) exactly for every database. Computation between probes is free. The trees may depend on n, F and the query, but their only access to D is through \(E_{n}(D)\). Each query starts without free database-dependent private information; memory is static and read-only. Define \(t*F(n)\) as the minimum, over all such encodings and trees, of the maximum number of probes over all D and q. All memory cells count toward s. This card fixes a near-linear-space, short-query, one-bit-answer specialization of the broader static lower-bound challenge; it does not assert equivalence to every space or word-size variant.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that some fixed k and admissible uniform family F satisfy: for every real \(B>0\) there is N such that \(t*F(n)>B \log _{2} n\) for every \(n\ge N\). Alternatively, prove the exact negation: for every fixed k and every admissible family F, there is a finite \(B>0\) such that \(t*F(n)\le B \log _{2} n\) for arbitrarily large n. In particular, the negative answer need not establish an \(O(\log  n)\) bound for all sufficiently large n.
cards.why: A central unconditional lower-bound bottleneck for data structures: establish that a short, explicitly defined static query fundamentally needs more than logarithmically many memory accesses despite unrestricted preprocessing.

cards.status_note: Primary sources and later-result searches checked on 11 September 2026 did not supply a resolution of the stated static specialization. The STOC 2026 paper retains the broader static barrier as Open Problem 1.1. The fixed near-linear space, short-query Boolean output and uniform polynomial-time family are an expressly recorded specialization; conditional proof barriers and bounds for dynamic memory or superpolynomial query sets do not resolve it.

context_blocks.text: A static data structure pays an initial cost to organize a database and then answers queries against that fixed information. In the cell-probe model, only the number of memory cells read during a query matters. The query algorithm has unlimited computational power between reads. Consequently, a lower bound must identify information that cannot be made locally accessible even by an ingenious encoding; showing that a particular search procedure or arithmetic computation is slow is insufficient.

The space allowance is central. With enough space, preprocessing could store every answer in a table, giving constant-probe queries. Here there are at least \(n^{2}\) possible queries, while the stored representation has only \(O(n \log ^{3} n)\) bits. Conversely, the database itself fits in n cells, so reading all n cells always suffices. The target therefore lies strictly between two elementary strategies: an unrestricted table with one entry for every possible query exceeds the budget, but the problem is always solvable without a computational-time obstruction.

The one-bit answer avoids obtaining a large probe bound merely because the output contains many independent bits. The query length is \(O(\log  n)\), with a fixed constant k. Increasing the query length to n bits can create communication lower bounds of an entirely different magnitude. Likewise, allowing only linear combinations in preprocessing or forbidding adaptive reads changes the collection of encodings and algorithms that a lower bound must defeat.

Koucký, Loff, Molli and Saks formulate the broad static challenge explicitly as Open Problem 1.1. Away from storage that is extremely close to the information-theoretic minimum, familiar general lower-bound approaches have not exceeded the logarithm of the number of queries. The present card turns this challenge into one yes/no proposition by fixing the word size, storage overhead, output alphabet and uniform meaning of an explicit problem. Its stricter conventions should be kept in mind when transferring results from a survey.

Korten, Pitassi and Impagliazzo obtain stronger tradeoffs through local pseudorandom generators. Their improvements are especially informative when the number of probes is small and the cells contain few bits. Their general bound includes an explicit dependence on word size. A gain proved for one-bit cells therefore cannot simply be carried over unchanged to \(\Theta (\log  n)\)-bit words. These results advance the tradeoff frontier without proving the superlogarithmic lower bound at the parameters fixed here.

Ko’s 2025 result illustrates another important parameter distinction. For random linear operators with m possible row queries, the lower bound is \(\Omega (\min \{\log (m/s), n/\log  s\})\) in a bit-cell formulation. It can exceed log n when the number m of queries grows sufficiently rapidly. With only polynomially many queries, the first term is at most \(O(\log  n)\). The random choice of an operator also does not by itself supply the uniformly polynomial-time explicit family required in this card.

The STOC 2026 natural-proofs paper supplies conditional obstacles to a broad class of proof methods. Such a proof recognizes a sufficiently large, efficiently testable property of function tables that implies data-structure hardness; conjectured local pseudorandom functions would obstruct that recognition. This is not an unconditional impossibility theorem for stronger lower bounds. The authors’ errata also flag a new sampling method whose coverage had not been checked and explain why a previously cited rigidity consequence no longer constitutes an unachieved barrier.

Static and dynamic memory have different sources of hardness. Larsen, Weinstein and Yu crossed the logarithmic barrier for dynamic Boolean problems, where updates limit how information can be reorganized. Ko’s March 2026 preprint claims a further \(\Omega ((\log  n/\log  \log  n)^{2})\) bound for a dynamic multiphase problem. Those update constraints are absent here: the whole database may be preprocessed without a time bound before any query arrives. Neither dynamic result automatically gives the requested static lower bound.

A positive solution would identify a uniformly computable query whose information cannot be recovered with only logarithmically many reads, even after unrestricted preprocessing. This separates a memory-access bottleneck from the running time of known implementations. The limit in the statement is stronger than an arbitrarily large ratio on an infinite subsequence: the ratio must eventually exceed each fixed constant and remain above it. That distinction also affects the exact negative answer.

cards.title: Deterministic fully dynamic connectivity with polylogarithmic worst-case updates
cards.formal:
Does there exist a finite deterministic word-RAM program \(A\), with fixed positive integer constants \(C,c,d,a\), such that for every integer \(n\ge2\) it maintains an initially empty simple undirected graph on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) under every finite valid online sequence of edge insertions, edge deletions and pairwise connectivity queries, with all the following guarantees?
\[\begin{aligned}
 \text{initialization time}&\le Cn^d,\\
 \text{total stored words at every time}&\le Cn^d,\\
 \text{time of each individual operation}&\le C(\log_2 n)^c.
\end{aligned}\]
Every query must return the exact connectivity bit. Initialization receives only \(n\); the word size is \(w=\lceil a\log_2 n\rceil\), and computation uses the machine conventions below. All constants and the same finite program are chosen before \(n\) or the operation sequence. Give a complete Lean proof of this existence proposition or its logical negation.
cards.definitions:
A graph state is a set \(E\subseteq\{\{u,v\}:u,v\in[n],\ u\ne v\}\), initially empty. An operation has a tag and two vertex labels, each supplied as one word. A valid \(\operatorname{insert}(u,v)\) requires distinct endpoints and an absent edge, and adds that edge. A valid \(\operatorname{delete}(u,v)\) requires a present edge and removes it. A query \(\operatorname{connected}(u,v)\) is valid for any \(u,v\in[n]\) and outputs one bit. Its answer is one exactly when there is a finite sequence \(u=x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_k=v\), with \(k\ge0\), whose consecutive pairs are edges of the current graph. In particular, a vertex is connected to itself. The graph has no additional promise on density, planarity, degree or expansion.

The machine must finish the current operation before the next is supplied. No operation count, future sequence, or complete input graph is available during initialization. The guarantee applies to every finite valid sequence of arbitrary length, including sequences selected using all previously observable states and answers. Persistent memory is bounded in terms of \(n\) alone, independently of the elapsed number of operations. Past output is write-only and cannot serve as free external storage.

Fix a word RAM with a finite instruction list and a fixed finite number of word registers. Words are unsigned integers in \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\); memory addresses are also words. Each indirect load or store, register copy, comparison, conditional branch, Boolean bitwise operation, shift, and arithmetic operation on at most two words costs one step. Arithmetic primitives are addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer quotient and remainder. Addition, subtraction and multiplication return their result modulo \(2^w\); quotient and remainder use unsigned integer division and a zero divisor causes failure. A left shift discards bits outside the word; a right shift fills with zeros; either returns zero when the shift amount is at least \(w\). Reading an input word and writing the query bit also cost one step. The finite program can contain fixed integer constants, interpreted modulo \(2^w\), but has no oracle, random instruction, advice string or input-size-dependent instruction table. Any longer arithmetic computation pays for all constituent instructions.

Mutable registers and allocated memory, including every table and representation of the graph, count toward the stated space bound. Initially they contain only zeros except for the input \(n\); data-dependent initialization, allocation and zeroing of allocated words are charged. Every addressed location must be allocated and have a representable address. The fixed coefficient \(a\) may be chosen sufficiently large for the program's polynomial space; it cannot depend on \(n\) or sequence length. Polynomial preprocessing may depend only on \(n\), and all its computation and stored output count toward the initialization and space bounds. The program and its fixed finite control are independent of \(n\).

Time includes all graph maintenance, rebuilding, memory management, query computation and response output performed during that operation. No background work between operations is free. The operation bound is a worst-case bound for each individual call, not an average over a sequence or an expectation. Using positive integer constants is a normalization of the original polynomial-space and polylogarithmic-time bounds: enlarging constants or exponents absorbs fixed factors and small input sizes. It imposes no graph restriction.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of either
\[\exists A\ \exists C,c,d,a\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n\ge2\ \forall s\in\mathcal S_n,\quad \operatorname{Guarantees}(A,C,c,d,a,n,s),\]
or its logical negation. Here \(A\) ranges over the finite deterministic programs just defined, \(\mathcal S_n\) is the set of all finite valid operation sequences, and \(\operatorname{Guarantees}\) includes initialization, termination, exact answers, memory use and the per-operation bounds in the statement. A positive answer must establish all guarantees for one program and constants that work for every \(n,s\). A negative answer must rule out every such program and every constant choice, equivalently show that each candidate fails a required guarantee for some size and finite valid sequence, with the empty sequence also testing initialization. Failure to terminate is a failure of the applicable time bound.

All memory and running-time statements must refer to the specified machine semantics. A lower bound for a restricted family of implementations, a single counterexample to one proposed algorithm, or a theorem requiring an unproved complexity assumption does not negate the full proposition. An amortized, randomized, expected-time, restricted-graph or offline guarantee does not prove it. This is an existence question, with no numerical tolerance or weaker intermediate target.
cards.why: Exact dynamic connectivity is a basic test of whether a graph data structure can guarantee uniformly low latency without randomness. The question separates efficient processing of a long sequence from a fast response after every individual change, and is relevant to graph algorithms that call connectivity as a subroutine.

cards.status_note: Uncertain after review on 15 September 2026. The inspected October 2025 preprint, published at SODA 2026, explicitly leaves the deterministic polylogarithmic worst-case target open and proves an expected randomized bound plus a conditional deterministic theorem. However, the official FOCS 2026 accepted list and an author page now announce a closely matching new paper by Meierhans, Probst Gutenberg and Yeh. The inspected listings contain no theorem statement or manuscript link; bounded searches did not obtain its full text. Its determinism, error guarantee and exact model therefore remain unchecked. The card stays active with a complete formulation, without treating an announcement title as a matching solution or asserting current openness from the older source.

context_blocks.text: Connectivity asks whether two vertices lie in the same component, not for a shortest path or an explicit list of all vertices in that component. Deleting an edge can change this answer for many pairs simultaneously. The required output is still only the queried bit; the target concerns how much work must be charged to each operation.

Holm, de Lichtenberg and Thorup give a deterministic structure with \(O(\log^2 n)\) amortized update time and \(O(\log n/\log\log n)\) connectivity query time. Their guarantee controls the total work over a sequence, while permitting an expensive individual update. It does not establish the per-operation guarantee asked here.

Kapron, King and Mountjoy give worst-case bounds \(O(\log^4 n)\) for insertion, \(O(\log^5 n)\) for deletion and \(O(\log n/\log\log n)\) for queries. Their randomized structure has one-sided error: a reported connection is valid, but a reported disconnection can be wrong with small probability. This does not give the exact deterministic guarantee.

Chuzhoy and coauthors establish deterministic \(n^{o(1)}\) worst-case update time. This notation permits functions growing more quickly than every fixed power of \(\log n\), for example \(\exp(\sqrt{\log n})\). Consequently a subpolynomial bound alone leaves a gap to the fixed polylogarithm in this card.

Meierhans and Probst Gutenberg’s SODA 2026 Theorem 1.1 is Las Vegas: it maintains a correct spanning forest with polylogarithmic expected worst-case update time. Its guarantee even allows an adaptive adversary observing the internal state and random bits. The expectation is over the algorithm’s randomness for an operation, rather than amortization over operations; it remains different from a deterministic bound on every execution. Theorem 1.3 gives a conditional deterministic result, not an unconditional resolution of this card.

Pătraşcu and Demaine prove \(\max\{t_u,t_q\}=\Omega(\log n)\), together with update–query tradeoffs, in the cell-probe model with \(O(\log n)\)-bit cells. Here \(t_u\) and \(t_q\) measure update and query cost. The bound applies even to disjoint paths and permits amortization and randomization. Cell probes count memory accesses while allowing free computation, so a bound there also constrains a word RAM. A logarithmic lower bound is compatible with the requested polylogarithmic upper bound.

cards.context:
Connectivity asks whether two vertices lie in the same component, not for a shortest path or an explicit list of all vertices in that component. Deleting an edge can change this answer for many pairs simultaneously. The required output is still only the queried bit; the target concerns how much work must be charged to each operation.

Holm, de Lichtenberg and Thorup give a deterministic structure with \(O(\log^2 n)\) amortized update time and \(O(\log n/\log\log n)\) connectivity query time. Their guarantee controls the total work over a sequence, while permitting an expensive individual update. It does not establish the per-operation guarantee asked here.

Kapron, King and Mountjoy give worst-case bounds \(O(\log^4 n)\) for insertion, \(O(\log^5 n)\) for deletion and \(O(\log n/\log\log n)\) for queries. Their randomized structure has one-sided error: a reported connection is valid, but a reported disconnection can be wrong with small probability. This does not give the exact deterministic guarantee.

Chuzhoy and coauthors establish deterministic \(n^{o(1)}\) worst-case update time. This notation permits functions growing more quickly than every fixed power of \(\log n\), for example \(\exp(\sqrt{\log n})\). Consequently a subpolynomial bound alone leaves a gap to the fixed polylogarithm in this card.

Meierhans and Probst Gutenberg’s SODA 2026 Theorem 1.1 is Las Vegas: it maintains a correct spanning forest with polylogarithmic expected worst-case update time. Its guarantee even allows an adaptive adversary observing the internal state and random bits. The expectation is over the algorithm’s randomness for an operation, rather than amortization over operations; it remains different from a deterministic bound on every execution. Theorem 1.3 gives a conditional deterministic result, not an unconditional resolution of this card.

Pătraşcu and Demaine prove \(\max\{t_u,t_q\}=\Omega(\log n)\), together with update–query tradeoffs, in the cell-probe model with \(O(\log n)\)-bit cells. Here \(t_u\) and \(t_q\) measure update and query cost. The bound applies even to disjoint paths and permits amortization and randomization. Cell probes count memory accesses while allowing free computation, so a bound there also constrains a word RAM. A logarithmic lower bound is compatible with the requested polylogarithmic upper bound.

cards.title: Fully dynamic near-optimal matching with polylogarithmic updates
cards.formal: For every fixed rational \(\varepsilon \in (0,1)\), is there a randomized fully dynamic algorithm that maintains an explicit matching M with |\(M|\ge \nu (G)/(1+\varepsilon )\) in every current general graph G using polylogarithmic expected amortized update time against an oblivious adversary?
cards.definitions: The graph is simple, undirected and unweighted, on the fixed vertex set \([n], n\ge 2; \nu (G)\) is its maximum matching cardinality. It starts empty. An update inserts one absent edge or deletes one present edge. Updates arrive online, but the entire valid sequence is fixed independently of the algorithm’s random bits and is not revealed in advance. More precisely, for every fixed \(\varepsilon\) and constant \(a\ge 1\), require constants K,d,B and a uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm \(A_{\varepsilon ,a}\) such that every sequence of \(T\le n^{a}\) updates has expected total initialization-plus-update cost at most \(K[n+T(\log _{2}(n+2))^{d}]\). Words have \(B\lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) bits; standard word operations, memory access and retained random bits are charged. With probability at least \(1- n^{- 3}\), after every update in the sequence an explicit mate array represents a valid matching satisfying the approximation bound. Reading a vertex’s mate or the matching cardinality takes \(O(1)\) time; enumerating all matching edges costs \(O(n)\) and need not occur after every update. Changes to the mate array count toward update cost. Constants may depend on \(\varepsilon\) and a, but not on n, T or the sequence. No polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\), adaptive-adversary guarantee or worst-case per-update bound is required. The word instructions are random-access reads/writes, comparisons, conditional branches, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), integer quotient/remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and shifts of a w-bit word; shifts by at least w yield zero. The constant in word length \(w=\Theta (\log  n)\) (or \(\Theta (\log  N)\) when N is the stated input size) is fixed with the algorithm. Address arithmetic has the same cost, larger integers occupy multiple words, and no instruction performs arbitrary-precision arithmetic in one step. When randomization is allowed, a fresh independent uniform w-bit word costs one operation. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No polylogarithmic-update algorithm meeting the fixed-accuracy, explicit-matching target was found. Matching-size estimators, ordered-RS-dependent bounds and the 2026 maximal-matching improvement do not resolve it.

context_blocks.text: A maximum matching allocates the largest possible number of disjoint pairs. When an edge changes, recomputing it from scratch ignores the substantial information retained from the preceding graph. The dynamic problem asks how much of that information can be reused while keeping a solution within an arbitrarily small fixed relative loss of optimum. Both insertions and deletions are allowed, so previously useful structure can disappear.

The graph’s optimum changes by at most one after a single edge update, but a particular solution may require coordinated replacements. On a long alternating path, gaining one additional matched edge can involve changing many pairs. Approximation creates room to postpone or distribute some repairs. The difficulty is to do so without accumulating a large loss or spending too much time discovering the repairs that are needed.

An explicit solution is part of the target. A number close to \(\nu (G)\) need not identify even one edge that can safely be used with the others. A mate array makes this distinction observable: a query at a vertex must return its current partner or report that it is unmatched. Requiring the whole array to be printed after every update would impose an artificial linear output cost, so the formulation instead charges only actual changes and queries.

Maximality is also weaker than near-optimality. In a four-vertex path, selecting only the middle edge gives a maximal matching of size one, while the two outside edges give a maximum matching of size two. Randomized maximal-matching algorithms already achieve very small update times against oblivious sequences. Chuzhoy–Khanna–Song’s STOC 2026 result improves deterministic maximal matching to \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\) amortized time; its guarantee still concerns maximality.

A separate sequence of breakthroughs beats the factor-two barrier for estimating matching size in polylogarithmic update time. Azarmehr–Behnezhad–Roghani’s SODA 2024 result obtains an estimate corresponding to a \(2- \sqrt{2}- \eta\) fraction of optimum in general graphs, for fixed \(\eta >0\). The paper explicitly studies size estimation. Its title alone can therefore suggest a stronger maintenance result than the theorem actually supplies.

For maintaining actual near-optimal matchings, Assadi–Khanna–Kiss’s SODA 2025 work develops a connection to ordered Ruzsa–Szemerédi graphs. Such a graph has its edges partitioned into matchings, with each matching induced in the union of itself and later matchings. Dense examples quantify how often certain expensive matching searches can recur. Their update bound is expressed through this extremal quantity and works even against adaptive adversaries.

The dependence is roughly \(n^{o(1)}\) times the ordered-RS count for matchings of linear size, with accuracy-dependent parameters. A strong enough combinatorial upper bound would yield subpolynomial update time. This does not currently establish polylogarithmic time: \(n^{o(1)}\) can grow faster than every fixed power of log n, and the required extremal bounds are themselves unresolved. This connection is not an unconditional lower bound.

Pratt’s SOSA 2026 note relates the ordered and ordinary RS notions at the level of polynomial exponents. Dense ordered examples would imply nearly comparably dense ordinary examples. It resolves a structural question about the reduction’s graph families, but does not determine the density needed for a polylogarithmic dynamic algorithm.

Liu’s 2024 work gives a different advance for bipartite graphs: amortized update time \(n/2^{\Omega (\sqrt{\log  n})}\) times a polynomial in \(1/\varepsilon\). It also relates stronger update bounds to online matrix-vector problems. The dependence on accuracy is essential in those statements. In particular, the ordinary-OMv equivalence stated for approximate vertex cover should not be silently transferred to matching, and a barrier using inverse-polynomial accuracy does not settle this card’s fixed-\(\varepsilon\) question.

The adversary convention leaves useful flexibility. An oblivious sequence may be carefully chosen to be difficult, but it cannot react to random decisions or the current matching. The algorithm nevertheless receives updates one at a time; knowing that the sequence was fixed does not give access to future deletions. Similarly, amortization permits occasional expensive repairs as long as their expected total cost satisfies the bound.

The inherited Max Planck report explicitly identifies near-optimal fully dynamic matching with polylogarithmic updates as a long-term target. Its page 123 also distinguishes maintaining matching edges from estimating their number, and describes faster progress in the insertion-only setting. Allowing deletion of a vertex, which removes all its incident edges together, does not automatically supply an algorithm for arbitrary individual edge deletions.

The fundamental issue is whether a changing combinatorial optimum can be tracked almost as cheaply as the graph itself is updated. A positive result would close a major gap between coarse approximation and near-optimal explicit solutions. It would also clarify how much global matching structure must be recomputed when each input change is local.

cards.title: Worst-case sample complexity of trace reconstruction
cards.formal: For every fixed deletion probability \(\delta\in(0,1)\), determine the worst-case sample-complexity function \(N_\delta(n)\) up to multiplicative constant factors as \(n\to\infty\). This is the least number of independent deletion traces from which one estimator can reconstruct every unknown \(n\)-bit string exactly with probability at least \(2/3\). Computation is unrestricted, the original length and deletion probability are known, and constants may depend on \(\delta\).
cards.definitions:
Observation space. Fix \(n\in\mathbb N\) with \(n\ge2\), and a real \(\delta\in(0,1)\). An arbitrary fixed string \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\{0,1\}^n\) is unknown. A deletion trace independently keeps each input bit with probability \(p=1-\delta\) and concatenates the surviving bits in their original order. The output lies in the finite set
\[\mathcal Y_n=\bigcup_{k=0}^{n}\{0,1\}^k,\]
where \(\{0,1\}^0\) consists of the empty string. The length of each received trace is observable. Its original retained indices and deletion mask are not supplied. There are no substitutions, insertions, reversals, cyclic shifts or alignment labels.

Trace law. For \(y\in\{0,1\}^k\), let \(e_x(y)\) be the number of increasing index tuples \(1\le i_1<\cdots<i_k\le n\) with \(x_{i_j}=y_j\) for all \(j\). Define \(e_x(\varnothing)=1\). The trace distribution is
\[\mu_{x,\delta}(y)=e_x(y)(1-\delta)^k\delta^{n-k}.\]
Different deletion masks producing the same observed string all contribute to this probability. For example, for \(x=00\), the one-bit trace \(0\) has probability \(2(1-\delta)\delta\). All \(m\) observations use independent masks on the same original \(x\), so their joint distribution is \(\mu_{x,\delta}^{\otimes m}\).

Estimators. A randomized estimator for fixed \(n,\delta,m\) is a stochastic kernel \(K\) assigning every observed tuple \(\mathbf y\in\mathcal Y_n^m\) a probability distribution on \(\{0,1\}^n\). Thus \(K(\mathbf y,z)\ge0\) and \(\sum_zK(\mathbf y,z)=1\). The kernel may depend on \(n,\delta,m\), but not on the unknown string. It describes all permitted internal randomization; a deterministic estimator assigns probability one to a single output. Its success probability on \(x\) is
\[s_{x,\delta}(K)=\sum_{\mathbf y\in\mathcal Y_n^m}\left(\prod_{j=1}^{m}\mu_{x,\delta}(y_j)\right)K(\mathbf y,x).\]
The output must equal the whole original string, with its original linear order. Small edit distance, a list containing the string, or recovery of only some coordinates does not count as success. There is no prior distribution on \(x\); the success inequality must hold separately for every string.

Sample complexity. With \(\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\), set
\[N_\delta(n)=\min\left\{m\in\mathbb N_0:\exists K\ \forall x\in\{0,1\}^n,\ s_{x,\delta}(K)\ge\frac23\right\}.\]
For \(m=0\), the observation tuple is empty and the product is one. The minimum is finite: a single trace has length \(n\) with probability \((1-\delta)^n>0\), and any such trace equals \(x\). Consequently the probability of receiving at least one complete trace tends to one with the number of independent samples. The cost is the fixed total number of traces, including empty or repeated traces, not their total bit length. Allowing a procedure to use at most \(m\) traces gives the same convention by ignoring unused samples; a bound only on the expected number of observations is not the definition.

Information-theoretic scope. There is no limit on running time, storage, description length or processing between observations, and no computability or uniformity restriction on the kernel family. The real deletion probability is a known mathematical parameter, so no finite encoding or estimation of \(\delta\) is required. These conventions make the question purely statistical. The input string has no codebook, sparsity, separation, random-generation or other promise. The asymptotic limit varies \(n\) while keeping \(\delta\) fixed; a simultaneous guarantee for \(\delta\) depending on \(n\), or uniform constants as \(\delta\) approaches an endpoint, is not required.
cards.answer_criterion:
Supply a positive function \(f_\delta(n)\) and a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that, for every fixed \(\delta\in(0,1)\), there exist \(0<c_\delta\le C_\delta<\infty\) and an integer \(n_\delta\ge2\) such that
\[c_\delta f_\delta(n)\le N_\delta(n)\le C_\delta f_\delta(n)\qquad(n\ge n_\delta).\]
Finite exceptional lengths may equivalently be absorbed into constants for a positive finite representative \(f_\delta\). Give an informative mathematical description of the growth rate, rather than restating the defining minimum or assigning \(f_\delta=N_\delta\) without determining it.

The upper bound must establish estimators with the stated sample budget and success probability for every string. The lower bound must cover all randomized kernels allowed above, not only a named algorithm, local statistics, efficient computation or a restricted family of observations. Worst-case hard strings may depend on the estimator and sample budget; no single string must defeat every estimator.

The requested constant factors multiply the number of traces itself. Matching only the order of \(\log N_\delta(n)\), a polynomial exponent with an unspecified growing factor, or a polynomial-versus-superpolynomial classification is insufficient unless it yields the displayed bounds. This asymptotic criterion has no additive \(1/100\) tolerance. Average-case strings, approximate recovery, circular traces, a chosen codebook, or one special deletion probability do not determine the full target.
cards.why: Determine the intrinsic amount of information needed to recover an arbitrary string when repeated observations lose the positions of deleted symbols. This separates the statistical cost of hidden alignment from the computational cost of processing the observations.

importance.reason: A defining worst-case recovery problem for synchronization noise, linking string algorithms, information theory, statistics and complex-analytic methods.

The inspected July 2026 preprint gives quasipolynomial sample complexity for every fixed retention probability, while the unrestricted lower bound cited by it and the September graph-trace preprint remains polynomial. context_blocks.text: The target asks how the optimal number of observations grows, including its exponent and any unbounded logarithmic factors. Whether some polynomial number of traces suffices is an important unresolved qualitative question within this more precise target.

The input is one unknown string, observed repeatedly through independent losses of symbols. A surviving output bit carries its value but loses its original index. Repetition gives more evidence about the same underlying string, so the question is how many damaged copies contain enough information for exact recovery in the worst case.

A deletion does not mark its former position. Two different deletion masks can produce the same observed string, even when the original input is fixed. Trace lengths are visible, and an undeleted trace would reveal the entire input, but its probability \((1-\delta)^n\) decays exponentially for a fixed nonzero deletion rate. The definition therefore has a finite elementary upper bound while still leaving room for vastly better sample complexity.

Chase proves a worst-case lower bound of \(\Omega(n^{3/2}/\log^7 n)\) for every fixed deletion probability and constant success threshold. The proof exhibits pairs of strings whose trace laws are hard to distinguish. This is an information-theoretic obstruction, not a running-time hypothesis or a limitation of one reconstruction procedure. It rules out near-linear sample complexity, but is consistent with a larger polynomial bound.

Chase’s earlier general upper bound uses \(\exp (\widetilde{O} (n^{1/5}))\) traces. This substantially improved previous subexponential bounds, but left a large gap above the polynomial lower bound. The saved ICALP 2025 source accurately described that frontier at publication; it is no longer the latest general sample upper bound.

Burudgunte, Valiant and Wang’s July 2026 preprint gives a quasipolynomial sample upper bound for every fixed positive retention probability. Its Theorem 43 bounds the number of traces by \(\exp(p^{-7/3}(\log_2 n)^c)\) for an absolute constant \(c\), where \(p=1-\delta\). This considerably narrows the earlier gap, but neither proves polynomial sample complexity nor gives matching lower bounds. In particular, it does not determine the multiplicative-constant growth rate requested here.

The same paper explicitly separates samples from running time. It gives quasipolynomial sample complexity for reconstructing an arbitrary unknown string and quasipolynomial time for distinguishing two supplied candidates. It leaves a quasipolynomial-time general reconstruction algorithm unresolved. Since this card permits unrestricted processing, its upper-bound progress remains relevant even without that further algorithmic guarantee.

A local statistical-query procedure receives approximate expectations of functions inspecting a short consecutive block of trace positions. Chen and coauthors prove strong accuracy requirements for that restricted model, nearly matching the earlier subexponential sample bound. Their theorem does not apply to arbitrary processing of individual traces. The later general upper bound is therefore compatible with the local-query lower bound.

Structural promises can also make the problem easier. Aamand, Liu and Narayanan show that \(O(n \log  n)\) traces suffice, with polynomial processing time, when successive ones are separated by sufficiently many zeros and the deletion probability is a sufficiently small constant. Their definition requires polylogarithmic separation. The theorem cannot be applied to arbitrary dense strings or to every constant deletion probability without additional arguments.

Circular trace reconstruction adds an unknown cyclic shift to each observation and asks for recovery up to rotation. The 2026 circular lower bound of roughly \(n^{5}\) is consequently a theorem for a different observation model. It should not replace the linear-model lower bound in this card. Likewise, deletion-channel coding permits a chosen codebook, while the worst-case reconstruction requirement here must cover every binary string.

A September 2026 preprint studies reconstruction of graph degree sequences from vertex-deleted subgraphs. Its introduction separately cites the quasipolynomial upper bound and polynomial lower bound for binary strings. Its new graph theorems do not supply a matching bound for the linear string observation model of this card.

cards.title: Constant-factor edit-distance approximation in \(O(n\operatorname{polylog} n)\) time
cards.formal:
Do there exist absolute real constants \(C\geq1\), \(K>0\), \(d\geq0\), an integer word-size constant \(B\geq3\), and one uniform classical randomized algorithm \(A\) such that for every integer \(n\geq1\) and all explicitly given \(x,y\in\{0,1,\ldots,n^2+1\}^n\), every execution uses at most
\[Kn\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^d\]
word-RAM instructions and its integer output \(D\) satisfies
\[\Pr\bigl[\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\leq D\leq C\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\bigr]\geq\frac23?\]
The constants and program are chosen once for all input lengths and all pairs. The distance is unit-cost Levenshtein distance; the probability is over the algorithm’s internal randomness on that fixed pair.
cards.definitions:
Write \(\Sigma_n=\{0,1,\ldots,n^2+1\}\). The input is \(n\geq1\) followed by two arrays of \(n\) symbols from \(\Sigma_n\), stored in consecutive memory cells with one symbol per word. Binary strings and strings over any fixed alphabet are included after relabeling. The arrays are explicitly present; there is no compressed representation, access oracle, preprocessed database or promised input distribution.

The distance \(\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\) is the minimum number of single-symbol insertions, deletions and substitutions that transform \(x\) into \(y\). Inserted and substituted symbols belong to \(\Sigma_n\), and intermediate strings may have any finite length. Each operation has cost one; leaving an equal symbol unchanged has cost zero. No transpositions, block moves, variable symbol weights or affine gap penalties are allowed. A substitution costs one, not two. The optimum is an integer between zero and \(n\).

The word length is \(w=B\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits, with one fixed integer \(B\geq3\) for the algorithm. A word represents an unsigned integer from \(0\) to \(2^w-1\); memory addresses are words and all cells outside the given input are initially zero. The machine has a fixed finite instruction sequence and fixed integer constants, independent of \(n,x,y\). The unit-cost instructions are random-access reads or writes of one word, comparisons, conditional branches, bitwise Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient or remainder with a nonzero word divisor. Shifts fill with zeros and discard overflow; a shift amount at least \(w\) gives zero. Address calculations obey the same costs. Larger integers occupy several words and require several charged instructions. No arbitrary-precision arithmetic, advice, oracle or quantum instruction is available.

One fresh independent uniform \(w\)-bit random word costs one instruction; its individual bits are independent fair bits, and different draws are independent. All preprocessing, memory operations, random draws and output writing count toward the bound. The output is an integer in signed binary notation. Only its value is requested, not a sequence of edits. Every execution must terminate within the stated bound, including those that produce an incorrect estimate. An incorrect execution may return an integer outside the interval. The success guarantee is separate for every pair, not an average over an input distribution.

The quantifier order is \(\exists C,K,d,B,A\;\forall n,x,y\), followed by the displayed probability and all-execution time requirements. Neither the approximation factor nor the logarithmic exponent may grow with \(n\). There is no promise that the distance is large or positive. In particular, when \(x=y\), successful output must be zero. There is no additive error. The shorthand \(O(n\operatorname{polylog}n)\) refers exactly to one bound of the displayed form with fixed \(K,d\), not to \(n^{1+\eta}\) for each fixed \(\eta>0\) or to an arbitrary \(n^{1+o(1)}\) overhead.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence of one algorithm and fixed constants meeting both requirements on all input pairs, or of its logical negation. A negative answer must rule out every finite approximation constant, every fixed logarithmic exponent and every permitted randomized algorithm and word-size constant; failure at one chosen factor or for deterministic algorithms alone is insufficient. A conditional lower bound gives only a conditional conclusion unless its hypothesis is also proved. An \(n^{1+\eta}\)-time algorithm for a fixed positive \(\eta\), an approximation factor growing with input length, an additive-error guarantee, an expected-time bound alone, or a theorem only for distant pairs does not settle the question. A large but fixed approximation constant is acceptable. This is an existence question, with no additional numerical approximation tolerance on its answer.
cards.why: This asks whether allowing one universal constant loss of alignment accuracy reduces worst-case sequence comparison to the cost of reading the input, apart from a fixed polylogarithmic overhead. The result would locate a basic computational boundary that remains beyond the known fast constant-factor algorithms. Even a large universal factor would resolve this existence question.

importance.reason: A central remaining precision–runtime boundary for edit distance, distinct from the established n^{1+ε} constant-factor algorithms and from exact-computation hardness.

context_blocks.text: Alignment matters because insertions and deletions shift later positions. For \(x=(01)^r\) and \(y=(10)^r\), with \(r\geq1\), every corresponding position differs, while \(\operatorname{ED}(x,y)=2\). Thus Hamming distance, which counts unequal corresponding positions, is \(2r\) and is not a universal constant-factor estimate for edit distance. The task concerns the optimum over all alignments.

The multiplicative guarantee includes nearby pairs. Equal strings require successful output zero, and distance-one pairs require an estimate at most the same universal constant used at all lengths. An additive error that grows with length cannot be absorbed into that bound. Reading both complete inputs is allowed; this is a total-runtime question rather than a sublinear-query question.

Andoni and Onak’s early theorem already gives a subpolynomial approximation factor in \(n^{1+o(1)}\) time, including for binary strings. Here subpolynomial means bounded by \(n^\eta\) eventually for every fixed \(\eta>0\). Such a bound still permits a factor that grows without bound, and an arbitrary subpolynomial runtime overhead need not be a fixed power of a logarithm. Their result therefore does not supply either fixed quantity required on this card.

Koucký and Saks prove a guarantee \(\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\leq U\leq R(\operatorname{ED}(x,y)+n^{1-\zeta})\) with high probability, for constants \(R,\zeta>0\) depending on a fixed runtime parameter. Their full Theorem 1.1 uses time \(\widetilde O(n^{1+1/T})\), with fixed \(T\geq1\); the tilde hides logarithmic factors. This gives a constant factor on sufficiently distant pairs, but the additive term prevents that conclusion uniformly for all distances.

Andoni and Nosatzki remove the distance restriction: for each fixed \(\eta>0\), their algorithm has time \(O(n^{1+\eta})\) and factor \(f(1/\eta)\). Theorem 1.1 of the full manuscript and its following paragraph specify dependence on the runtime slack, described as doubly exponential. Their journal article was published online on August 17, 2026. The publication does not change the fixed-slack theorem into a fixed-polylogarithmic-overhead theorem.

For every fixed \(\eta>0\), the factor \(n^\eta\) eventually exceeds every fixed power of \(\log n\). Making \(\eta\) depend on \(n\) also changes the theorem’s approximation factor and hidden constants. Thus the existing family does not automatically supply one algorithm with fixed \(C,K,d\). The open question is this remaining simultaneous control of approximation and overhead, rather than the already established existence of a strongly subquadratic constant-factor algorithm.

Mao and Rubinstein’s STOC 2026 theorem gives a different tradeoff: \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximation for each fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), with stated time \(n^2/2^{\log^{\Omega(1)}n}\). It achieves near-exact accuracy, but its stated runtime does not meet this card’s much smaller overhead. Their separate LCS theorem is not substituted for the ordinary edit-distance theorem.

Backurs and Indyk’s conditional exact-computation result relates a fixed exponent saving for edit distance to a fixed exponential saving for CNF satisfiability. It does not rule out the coarse approximation required here. The known fast constant-factor algorithms already show that approximation must be distinguished from exact computation.

TCS-7220 asks for every fixed \((1+\varepsilon)\) accuracy with some positive fixed saving from exponent two, and TCS-7235 asks for the same accuracy in \(n^{1+o(1)}\) time. Neither stated guarantee alone supplies this card’s fixed polylogarithmic overhead. Conversely, one unspecified fixed factor here does not imply arbitrary near-exact accuracy. These user-approved targets remain distinct. Weighted or tree edit distances, codeword promises, quantum algorithms and data structures with separate preprocessing have different models.

cards.context:
Alignment matters because insertions and deletions shift later positions. For \(x=(01)^r\) and \(y=(10)^r\), with \(r\geq1\), every corresponding position differs, while \(\operatorname{ED}(x,y)=2\). Thus Hamming distance, which counts unequal corresponding positions, is \(2r\) and is not a universal constant-factor estimate for edit distance. The task concerns the optimum over all alignments.

The multiplicative guarantee includes nearby pairs. Equal strings require successful output zero, and distance-one pairs require an estimate at most the same universal constant used at all lengths. An additive error that grows with length cannot be absorbed into that bound. Reading both complete inputs is allowed; this is a total-runtime question rather than a sublinear-query question.

Andoni and Onak’s early theorem already gives a subpolynomial approximation factor in \(n^{1+o(1)}\) time, including for binary strings. Here subpolynomial means bounded by \(n^\eta\) eventually for every fixed \(\eta>0\). Such a bound still permits a factor that grows without bound, and an arbitrary subpolynomial runtime overhead need not be a fixed power of a logarithm. Their result therefore does not supply either fixed quantity required on this card.

Koucký and Saks prove a guarantee \(\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\leq U\leq R(\operatorname{ED}(x,y)+n^{1-\zeta})\) with high probability, for constants \(R,\zeta>0\) depending on a fixed runtime parameter. Their full Theorem 1.1 uses time \(\widetilde O(n^{1+1/T})\), with fixed \(T\geq1\); the tilde hides logarithmic factors. This gives a constant factor on sufficiently distant pairs, but the additive term prevents that conclusion uniformly for all distances.

Andoni and Nosatzki remove the distance restriction: for each fixed \(\eta>0\), their algorithm has time \(O(n^{1+\eta})\) and factor \(f(1/\eta)\). Theorem 1.1 of the full manuscript and its following paragraph specify dependence on the runtime slack, described as doubly exponential. Their journal article was published online on August 17, 2026. The publication does not change the fixed-slack theorem into a fixed-polylogarithmic-overhead theorem.

For every fixed \(\eta>0\), the factor \(n^\eta\) eventually exceeds every fixed power of \(\log n\). Making \(\eta\) depend on \(n\) also changes the theorem’s approximation factor and hidden constants. Thus the existing family does not automatically supply one algorithm with fixed \(C,K,d\). The open question is this remaining simultaneous control of approximation and overhead, rather than the already established existence of a strongly subquadratic constant-factor algorithm.

Mao and Rubinstein’s STOC 2026 theorem gives a different tradeoff: \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximation for each fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), with stated time \(n^2/2^{\log^{\Omega(1)}n}\). It achieves near-exact accuracy, but its stated runtime does not meet this card’s much smaller overhead. Their separate LCS theorem is not substituted for the ordinary edit-distance theorem.

Backurs and Indyk’s conditional exact-computation result relates a fixed exponent saving for edit distance to a fixed exponential saving for CNF satisfiability. It does not rule out the coarse approximation required here. The known fast constant-factor algorithms already show that approximation must be distinguished from exact computation.

TCS-7220 asks for every fixed \((1+\varepsilon)\) accuracy with some positive fixed saving from exponent two, and TCS-7235 asks for the same accuracy in \(n^{1+o(1)}\) time. Neither stated guarantee alone supplies this card’s fixed polylogarithmic overhead. Conversely, one unspecified fixed factor here does not imply arbitrary near-exact accuracy. These user-approved targets remain distinct. Weighted or tree edit distances, codeword promises, quantum algorithms and data structures with separate preprocessing have different models.
